EM&A proposes a Phase II project to enhance to Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6 the proof-of-concept runtime assurance (RTA) technology that it created during the Phase I project. The method uses fast, real-time reachability computations to provide dynamic boundaries of operation for the advanced controller and a decision module with stored command sequences and dynamic run-time checks to enable use of unverified controllers. Our Black Box Simplex with Online Reachability (BBSOR) RTA system aims to let the advanced controller act most of the time but applies safety control action when its reachability and safety checks find that the advanced controller would result in unsafe trajectories.   Intelligent, fully autonomous air, ground, surface, underwater, and space vehicles and stationary systems can enable performance, accuracy, repeatability, and safety levels that are either impossible or too costly to accomplish with their manned counterparts. A critical challenge for intelligent autonomy systems such as those based on reinforcement learning (RL) is that they must guarantee their correct performance in all scenarios, but design-time verification for autonomous systems is often intractable. In standard RTA, an advanced, not fully verified controller is designed to operate at most times and a safety controller to replace it when needed to ensure safety.   Our proposed approach enables expansion of the portion of the state space where the advanced, higher performing controller can operate. In Phase I, our team demonstrated our BBSOR RTA method and software on simple problems including aircraft formation flight examples that used RL for the advanced controller and simple models of the aircraft dynamics. Our online reachability features could only handle linear dynamics.   In Phase II, we will adapt our method to black- and gray-box models of system dynamics. We will develop a framework for gray-box aircraft 6-DOF dynamics models. We will populate them based on simulation data and use them for controller training. These models will be of higher dimension than the original nonlinear models but will be equivalent in the system-theoretic sense. We will also explore training controllers using nonlinear simulations directly. The main benefit of linear models is that they are fast and compatible with many system-theoretic and computational tools We will also modify our fast reachability algorithm and efficient safety checking as necessary be compatible with the new models.   To enable software-only and hardware-in-the-loop demonstrations, we will convert our code from MATLAB to software C and C++.  We will integrate it into a modular software architecture. We will then evolve the software functionality. When the software is mature, we will develop an approach for implementing it in embedded hardware. That will culminate in a real-time, hardware-in-the loop demonstration using high-fidelity flight simulation of aircraft flight dynamics.
Physics-Informed, Data-Driven Dynamic Run-Time Assurance using Online Reachability

Autonomous systems and semi-autonomous systems are integral to a number of domains like aerospace, transportation, and robotics. Market pull to deploy new features at an unprecedented time to market scale, requires experimenting with and deploying untrusted and partially tested technologies. However, this is at odds with the need to avoid catastrophic failures especially in safety critical systems. Runtime assurance (RTA) addresses this tension. The  idea is to introduce a  decision module that somehow chooses between a well-tested safety controller (SC) and the experimental untrusted controller (UC), assuring safety of the overall system while also allowing experimentation with the new untrusted technology where and when possible. RTA is seen as a key enabler for autonomy in safety-critical aerospace systems. In Phase I of this project, we introduced a novel formulation of the RTA problem where the goal is to identify a decision logic that guarantees hard safety constraints and at the same time optimizes performance metrics. We should how this problem can be reduced to one where the goal is simply to optimize a single reward (instead of the competing goals of safety and performance) using a technique called reward shaping. Having reduced the RTA problem to a simple optimization problem, a number of off-the-shelf techniques can be brought bear, including approaches like reinforcement learning which can find optimal policies in a model-free manner. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach a number of design problems that arise in the context of defense-relevant aerospace applications, such as, formation flight and wingman aircraft following a leader while assuring safety with respect to ground and air collision requirements. In Phase II of this project, we plan to extend this novel approach to accomplish three main thrusts. (a) Algorithm development of the optimal RTA design with hard constraints that go beyond safety, including liveness and temporal logic constraints, and stochastic and nondeterministic plant models. (b) Development and implementation of RTA systems for multi-agent scenarios including distributed and de-centralized communication and control across heterogeneous teams of agents that is robust to system failures. (c) Evaluation of new algorithms and design strategies via more realistic simulation of fighter-class aircraft models and commercial grade aircraft simulators such as X-Plane.
Scalable Physics-Aware Runtime Assurance for Autonomy

The burgeoning demands in the military sector, encompassing electronic warfare, advanced sensing, and other multifaceted missions, come head-to-head with the inherent restrictions on the size, weight, and power of energy subsystems in autonomous vehicles. These constraints can critically hamper the vehicle's ability to effectively execute its mission. As today’s Unmanned Air Systems (UAS) capabilities are constantly being pushed, the efficiency and management of energy have become paramount. As the solicitation underscores, there is a pressing need to develop, mature, and implement innovative energy-aware autonomous algorithms that can enhance the electrical power and thermal capabilities of UASs across diverse flight phases. Our Energy Saving Collaborative Autonomy for Performance Enhancement (ESCAPE) solution addresses four key technical challenges related this problem byCollaboration across multiple aircrafts using a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) solution;Developing trust of ML/AI technology by human operations through using of Explainable AI and smaller sub-task primitives;Incorporation of weather forecasts for pre-flight planning; andDynamic adaptation to changes in the environment and mission during execution.To address these challenges our solution uses a combination of technologies to provide the Air Force with an energy aware collaborative capability for UASs. To address the collaboration challenge, we are proposing to extend our MARL solution to work for multiple mission primitives. In the area of Explainable AI, we are proposing to use a LLM that is capable of decomposing larger mission tasks into smaller primitives that can be executed via collaboration and coordination algorithms. For the weather challenge, we will extend the first-order models that were demonstrated in Phase I for wind currents and fuel consumption to be more realistic and in line with current state-of-the-art. Finally, to demonstrate the dynamic adaptation we will demonstrate our capability in a software environment where we can inject changes to weather forecasts as well as to inject new mission requirements or changes in the UAS mix. The solution progress will be monitored regularly and every 6 months we will perform a development checkpoint that will objectively measure the technical progress of the research. These checkpoints will provide AFRL with an understanding of the impacts of each of the research areas on the overall system performance during the 24-month development.

Magnetic aerospace particle materials, such as carbonyl iron powders (CIP), are crucial additives in aircraft coatings and composites for enhanced radar absorption. Protective treatments like surface alloying improve the survivability of these particles but increase volume and weight, impacting overall system efficiency. Alloying can add up to 30% more weight. Therefore, developing a lightweight encapsulating coating that offers the same level of environmental protection without alloying could significantly reduce weight. For magnetic radar absorbing material (MagRAM) applications like that of stealth aircraft the reduced weight increases fuel efficiency therefore extending mission readiness.To further weight saving of MagRAM particles GVD has created a chemical vapor deposited barrier coating suitable for protecting complex geometries from environmental degradation. This coating can be directly applied to carbonyl iron powders, which are then used in polymer composites or coatings. Replacing alloy treatments with this encapsulation method may yield weight savings of tens of pounds per airframe and cost savings of near 15%. The GVD coating encapsulates particles in a ~1-micron thick shell that shields them from water, salt fog, acids, and oils. PECVD is a high-throughput, air-free vapor treatment process that deposits high-quality, conformal coatings. In this project, GVD will modify existing barrier coating tools and processes for particle substrates and use the use the two decades of coatings development and commercialization experience to successfully complete the project objectives, then quickly transition to commercial reactor production.

AtomBeam’s software is now in use over Inmarsat satellites with live customer data, reducing runtime data in real time by over 75%. No other software technology can, in real time, significantly reduce the size of the small messages generated by machines, such as tracking and telemetry, in real time.   AtomBeam is highly effective for files as small as five bytes. In contrast, compression typically requires file sizes of at least 1KB to operate even marginally, making it unusable for IoT’s typical 5 - 200B messages. AtomBeam’s 13 issued and three allowed patents testify to the originality of the innovation. AtomBeam uses Machine Learning (ML) to identify data patterns in payloads of a sample dataset. Frequently repeated patterns are associated with much smaller indexes, or Codewords, and both are stored in a Codebook that is replicated on both the source and destination. At runtime, a light, fast executable looks up patterns it finds in live message payloads in real time and encodes the patterns into Codewords, a process that is reversed at the destination to regenerate the original data.  As a bit-level, completely new approach to managing data, Compaction’s ability to greatly reduce small individual datagrams in real time is not the only benefit that Compaction provides. Another unique feature of Compaction is its built-in security. For newly generated data payloads, only Codewords, which are much smaller than the original data, are sent. The original data never leaves the source. Compaction obscures encoded data so strongly that a national effort would be required to compromise a Codebook, despite incurring no added computation or hardware resources. A prototyped version of Compaction that encrypts and Compacts in a single, ultra light step will be released in 2023. AtomBeam’s Compaction software is a unique and innovative system that manages data at the bit level to produce unparalleled, unique advantages that are not available with any other technology. Key benefits include: 4x expansion of effective bandwidth is cost effective, rapidly deployable  Battery life is improved, critical for man-portable terminals, by sending less data Added strong security in the same, light computing step Ultra-flexible: can operate on virtually any device, any protocol, any OS Fast recovery/correction with interrupted comms aids in jamming resistance
Effective Compaction of Satellite Transmission to Maximize Bandwidth and Data Security

These proposed experiments will allow us to validate our wind vector estimates over an entire collection footprint. Our adversaries have evolved beyond conventional ballistic missile systems to developing and deploying advanced systems that travel long ranges at hypersonic velocities with the capability to maneuver to avoid detection from terrestrial-based sensor systems. These advanced threats were developed specifically to counter terrestrial sensors, making birth-to-death tracking extremely difficult due to limitations of available operational locations, creating known coverage gaps. These coverage gaps can be exploited by hypersonic, maneuvering threat targets. The sensor track coverage problem can be addressed with space-based sensors. Given enough space vehicles with tracking sensors, birth-to-death tracking is feasible. Emerging signal chain processing algorithms will support meeting mission and system performance requirements. The algorithms will enable recognizing and discriminating fast moving, maneuverable targets from decoys and clutter in complex scenes that overhead persistent infrared (OPIR) sensors capture from space. ExoAnalytic Solutions will demonstrate low-latency acquisition and tracking of highly maneuverable targets in complex environments.  Our robust modeling and simulation framework, along with algorithms previously developed under HBTSS and other space and missile defense programs, provides the basis for design of an open framework algorithm architecture in which algorithms for target recognition, acquisition, and tracking will be tested. For Phase II, the three technical objectives are to enhance the background scene generation tool developed during Phase I, upgrade the Offset Pole Axis Meridian-Parallel (OPAMP) algorithm for off-nadir pointing in the orbital plane, and enhance the object classification and reachable volume method. The approach during Phase II is to add fidelity and perform verification and validation (V&V) of the methods/algorithms developed during Phase I in order to prepare them for insertion into the tracking layer.

This STRATFI will deliver a network of at least four, fully functional, accredited, connected, secure facilities for the DAF and DIB. This STRATFI will expand on the initial concept of CIaaS by identifying, experimenting with, prototyping, and integrating advanced hardware and software technologies.  It will also expand novel operating processes and methodologies and deepen research into underlying policy and legal issues that hinder scaling or implementation. We will also integrate these technologies to increase speed, reduce costs, and enhance compliance during various phases of the classified-program lifecycle beyond directly accessing physical spaces (Reality Gap 2).  “Nooks Shield” is our company’s technology platform designed to prototype and integrate hardware and software technology solutions addressing Reality Gap 1. This R&D effort involves collaborating with government sponsors and cognizant authorizing officials to prototype, test, evaluate, and validate these technologies in operationally relevant environments, such as CIaaS facilities. “Nooks Speed” comprises a set of software solutions aimed at addressing Reality Gap 2.  This initiative focuses on developing and prototyping software technologies that significantly improve speed throughout the industry classified-program lifecycle, reduce overall costs, and provide greater standardization.

To address the Air Force’s need for a device that can measure the ground-to-air atmospheric transmission path for electromagnetic waves in the wavelength range of 0.2 µm–14 µm, Intellisense Systems, Inc. (Intellisense) proposes to develop a new Atmospheric InfraRed Transmission, Recording, And Collection Equipment (AIR-TRACE) system based on a unique combination of a ground-surface blackbody radiator and a drone-mounted spectrometer. To address the Air Force’s need for a device that can measure the ground-to-air atmospheric transmission path for electromagnetic waves in the wavelength range of 0.2 µm–14 µm, Intellisense Systems, Inc. (Intellisense) proposes to develop a new Atmospheric InfraRed Transmission, Recording, And Collection Equipment (AIR-TRACE) system based on a unique combination of a ground-surface blackbody radiator and a drone-mounted spectrometer. Specifically, the innovation in airborne spectroscopy, coupled with a blackbody source in the wavelength range of 0.2 µm–14 µm, will enable AIR-TRACE to perform direct measurement of the transmission path, which will result in a more accurate representation of complex interactions and phenomena within the atmosphere than current mathematical models can provide. Thus, AIR-TRACE will significantly improve the quality of infrared (IR) signature data. The airborne platform will take measurements at a minimum threshold of 1,000 ft above ground level (AGL) with the goal of extending measurements to an altitude of 10,000 ft AGL or more. The drone will collect/calibrate the atmospheric attenuation data. In Phase I, Intellisense will determine the feasibility of attaching a blackbody or spectrometer to an unmanned aircraft. We will identify types of spectrometers and blackbodies to be used to gather data from multiple miles away, type of aircraft suited to carry the proposed blackbody/spectrometer, how data will be recorded, as well as necessary training, certifications, and Federal Aviation Administration approvals. In Phase II, the questions answered in Phase I will serve as the foundation for the prototype delivered in Phase II. The prototype will be an aircraft capable of flying at least 1,000 ft AGL while carrying either a spectrometer or blackbody. The delivered device will be tested to confirm that the spectrometer is pointed at the blackbody, recording data in the wavelength range of 0.2 µm–14 µm, and that the data can be used to perform an atmospheric correction on IR signature data.

The OCPÆs long-range optical thermal calibration will enable the USAF to perform self-calibration and temperature reading verification remotely at long distances (>1000 yd), which saves labor and time while reducing traffic. The MoBB can connect with distant operators (>1000 yd) on mobile devices and personal computers for remote control and temperature readings with time-stamped data. MoBB is also fully motorized with environmental sensors to detect inclement weather and autonomously protect its blackbody panels without requiring constant supervision, thus reducing operational requirements and maintenance. Combined with a fuel-power electric generator, the MoBB can continuously operate for long periods of time (40 hrs) without the need of external power. As a result, the MoBB system meets USAF requirements for a next-generation field calibration suite for radiometric sensors. In Phase I, Intellisense will demonstrate the feasibility of MoBB technology by mounting large-frame blackbodies to a mobile structure and evaluating the blackbody and mobile platform used in MoBB. In addition to delivering the prototype in Phase II, Intellisense plans to assemble a mobile platform or trailer which will be towed by a government pickup truck and capable of housing the required blackbodies.

US Forces are pivoting to the Pacific in support of Indo Pacific Command (INDOPACOM) operations.  Crews of aircraft and ships will confront the “tyranny of distance and water” while conducting operations in contested sea and air space against near peer adversaries.  These adversaries are expected to jam and/or spoof our GPS systems across vast areas in an effort to deny our forces position, navigation, and timing.  Satellites, aircraft, fishing vessels, and upper stratosphere balloons are all potential sources of widespread GPS jamming outside of immediate combat zones.  This program focuses on rapidly fielding a portable and federated Alternative-Position, Navigation, and Timing (A-PNT) capability that leverages readily available commercial, dual use technology.  Pocket A-PNT integrates a powerful L1/L5 band, multi-constellation Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver with a tactical grade Inertial Navigation System (INS) to provide very accurate inertial navigation when any one of five GNSS constellations is available.  Pocket A-PNT is a very powerful INS navigator during normal operations.  When Global Positioning System (GPS) is denied, the INS is combined with Doppler navigation based on Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite signals of opportunity, to provide an A-PNT navigation solution.  All of this capability is neatly integrated into a small chassis about the size of a typical smart phone.  Aircrew will be able to easily carry Pocket A-PNT in their flight suit or navigation bag.  When needed, Pocket A-PNT can be placed on the forward glare shield with the L-Band antenna rotated up for LEO signal reception.  A-PNT information is streamed to the pilot’s Electronic Flight Bag (EFB) tablet via Wi-Fi and consumed by apps such as Foreflight natively.  No connection or integration to aircraft systems is required.  On vessels, A-PNT data is delivered to marine plotters via the ubiquitous National Maritime Electronics Association (NMEA) serial interface. Use of charting equipment already carried on aircraft and vessels keeps the cost low and reduces program risk. SBIR funds will be concentrated on the A-PNT solution and not on developing standalone mapping and charting equipment. Although the focus of this research is on providing A-PNT in GPS denied regions, the system will also serve as a backup precision navigation source during airborne and shipboard emergencies where battle damage or equipment failure precludes the use of installed systems.

SpaceŚonce a passive and risk-averse environmentŚis rapidly evolving due to new commercial and military interests. Traditionally, satellite operations were slow and manually controlled, but the increasing presence of commercial non-government entities, the establishment of the US Space Force, and growing anti-satellite capabilities signal a shift towards a more dynamic and contested space environment. This transformation underscores the need for autonomous (or semi-autonomous, human-on-the loop) space capabilities for major phases of spacecraft lifetime, launch and early orbit, normal operations, and end of life. The adoption of a system-level, lifecycle autonomous software architecture would represent a significant advancement in spacecraft technology, leading to more adaptable, robust, and efficient space missions. This shift would transform space operations from a static and reactive approach with predetermined responses to proactive, intelligent decision-making. It would consider the entire state and mission objectives of the spacecraft, enabling a new era in dynamic space operations. Verus Research proposes the Adaptive Autonomous Architecture for Dynamic Operations (A3-DynO), a system-level satellite architecture designed to enhance mission efficiency and performance, tailored to automate lifecycle tasking while navigating the challenges of limited resources and dynamic conditions in an open environment. The primary technical characteristics of A3-DynO are modularity, reconfigurability, and adaptability, which are enhanced through predictive analytics, layered defense mechanisms, and adaptive resource management. The end state of A3-DynO is a tailorable hardware/software payload that is installed onto a satellite bus, ranging from 6U to ESPA class, with interfaces to the other submodules on the bus for ingesting data and sending commands, and that autonomously performs mission and day-to-day operations of the satellite in a trusted and secure fashion.Ā

TrustPoint's commercial C-band APNT system is designed to provide fast Time-to-First-Fix, centimeter-level positioning accuracy, improved resistance to jamming through frequency diversity, and robust, encrypted signals with built-in spoofing resistance. The solution is built on a constellation of cost-effective LEO microsatellites, utilizing Commercial Off-the-Shelf (COTS) platforms and launch services, alongside proprietary innovations in navigation signal generation and processing. With minor modifications, TrustPoint's technology can be adapted to meet the DoD's dynamic requirements, delivering enhanced PNT resiliency and operational effectiveness even in GPS-denied environments. The Lightweight Signal (LWS) is a novel solution designed by the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL/RV) to provide a secure PNT service that avoids the complexities of existing military GPS signals, such as M-code. The LWS represents a streamlined approach to military PNT, offering essential security features without the intricate infrastructure and high SWaP-C (Size, Weight, Power, and Cost) demands of traditional systems. This new signal design ensures robust PNT delivery while maintaining operational simplicity, making it an ideal solution for the next generation of military satellite architecture. The LWS has been developed specifically as a low SWaP-C alternative to M-code, targeting users such as dismounted soldiers, unattended sensors, sonobuoys, small UAVs, wearables, and tactical radios/smartphones. Its design prioritizes low power consumption and cost-efficiency, making it suitable for vulnerable and underserved equipment that requires reliable PNT services but cannot support the complexity and power draw of traditional military solutions. Unlike M-code, LWS is not intended to replace existing systems but to complement them by providing a secure, lightweight option for a wide array of tactical and strategic use cases, including the "Military Internet of Things," according to Dr. Joanna Hinks, AFRL/RV. TrustPoint, Inc. proposes modifying its existing C-band software defined radios (SDR) and demonstrating a 1.5U L-band payload capable of transmitting the LWS. TrustPoint’s existing expertise in compact, C-band PNT payloads presents a strong foundation for adapting to L-band requirements, aligning well with SDA’s goals of deploying small, efficient, and cost-effective PNT solutions within its proliferated Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations.

á In the modern age of warfare, airfields have become a linchpin for achieving strategic dominance. The Rapid Airfield Damage Recovery (RADR) Program, as established by the U.S. Air Force, delineates a thorough methodology to restore airfields after an attack. This method leans heavily on manual labor, necessitating a large cohort of specialized personnel and diverse equipment. This human-centered approach requires an extended time frame, a lot of heavy and specialized equipment, and operates on the premise that the airfield won't suffer additional attacks during the restoration phase. Yet, as global combat theaters evolve, such assumptions are increasingly becoming precarious. ááááOur proposed Robotic Swarm Platform for Autonomous Airfield Repair (RoSPAAR) system marries automation, robotics, and AI to redefine the paradigm. Unlike its predecessors, this platform showcases modularity as its defining trait. Instead of an arsenal of specialized vehicles, the system is architected around foundational vehicles that morph as per the task at hand, leveraging a suite of attachments and tool end-effectors for specialization. This lean, adaptable framework drastically cuts down on the logistical challenges, offering a more streamlined and deployable solution, particularly in remote or challenging theaters. Transitioning to a robotic swarm framework surmounts the traditional challenges, promising expedited repair timelines through the parallel execution of tasks, enhanced safety by curtailing on-site human exposure, and elevating the precision and reliability of the repair process. The versatility of this system is further accentuated by the fusion of Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGV) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV). By harnessing the unique strengths of both aerial and ground vehicles, the operational reach of the system is extended and expedited, creating a more expansive operation envelope. This innovative hardware platform is augmented by Greensightĺs modular Task and Motion Planning software. GS-TAMP provides a framework for jointly generating first-order-logic, geometric, and derivative plans for swarms of vehicles to accomplish physical tasks while also accounting for operational constraints such as battery life and heterogeneous vehicle capabilities. Furthermore, GS-TAMP provides the capability for conducting real-time scheduling and command and control of swarms, and has extensive and distributed communication capabilities, making it particularly well-suited for orchestrating a heterogeneous swarm in unstructured environments with interrelated tasks, such as post-attack airfield repair. ááááThe implications of this transformative approach are not restricted to the military domain. The foundational pillars underpinning this system ľ from its modularity to its fusion of aerial and ground capabilities ľ can redefine civilian infrastructure repair dynamics, making inroads into bustling urban landscapes, disaster-affected zones, or far-flung territories.

Lightweight, robust solutions are sought by the Air Force to replace traditional shielding with a new material that can protect and shield essential sensitive avionics, electronic devices, and other infrastructure from electromagnetic interference (“EMI”), electromagnetic pulse (“EMP”) and other electronic warfare attacks, especially when lives or critical missions are on the line. This proposal is in response to Key Area 1: Advanced EMP Shielding & Hardening Technologies. Through our recent experience in the DLA SBIR program and an ongoing Phase II SBIR program with the Navy, AMT has formed a strategic partnership with CONSOL Innovations LLC, the development arm of the largest coal mining company in the United States (CONSOL Energy Inc.), to provide vitreous carbon foam and graphite foam (“CFOAM”) technologies for shielding and hardening around aircraft brakes and carrier jet blast deflectors (JBDs).  This proposal focuses on the application of an open-celled vitreous carbon foam as a structural material. CFOAM® products are fabricated using coal as a precursor and can be produced at a density as low as 0.27 g/cc, or 10% of the density of aluminum. This material has shown remarkable fire and shock resistance, as well as resistance to flammability. Carbon foam also has significant vibration-absorbing capabilities. CFOAM Carbon Foam has some inherent shielding capability, as the material alone is capable of absorbing over 70 dB within a frequency range of 500 - 7,000 MHz. Standard CFOAM has an electrical resistivity of about 0.06 ohm-cm, making it a suitable material for absorbing electromagnetic radiation.  This research and development program will seek to build on these data to build a case for CFOAM utilization as a passive, failsafe, and elegant solution for shielding against EMP and EMI. This effort will enable rapid analysis of carbon foam’s shielding capabilities for different geometries, interface materials, and support structures. Ultimately, the research team expects to refine and elevate the TRL of this concept with high fidelity, providing a sufficient level of confidence that will support the validation and testing of a larger prototype during a Phase II program.

The Air Force is seeking commercial solutions for protecting critical infrastructure and electronic systems from the effects of EMPs. These EMPs could be the result of anything from solar storms to high-altitude nuclear blasts. The Air Force is looking at five hey areas of interest, and Touchstone Research Lab (Touchstone) intends to focus on key area one, Advanced EMP Shielding and Hardening Technologies. Touchstone has performed work on EMP shielding for over two decades. Most recently, the Faraday shielding system has been developed for use as an integrated lightning and thermal protection system for silo-launched interceptors. Faraday is a carbon-based system providing excellent environmental and thermal stability. Its multi-layer approach to shielding allows it to be custom-tailored to a variety of applications, and each layer can be optimized for unique situations. The Faraday layup includes a lighting protection layer (LPS) that is highly conductive in-plane, but not through-plane. This allows the energy from strikes to be spread across the surface, mitigating damage. The anisotropy of the LPS also has the benefit of shielding against electromagnetic pulses and interference. This has been exhibited through HEMP testing per MIL-STD-461G/MIL-STD-464C, which resulted in a -21dB attenuation of the field strength. The bulk of Faraday consists of CFOAM, a coal-based carbon foam, as the Thermal Protection System of the panels. Faraday also has an optional radiation protection layer that can provide shielding against X-rays and Beta rays. Under the Phase I effort, Touchstone intends to modify the Faraday system to meet the shielding standards desired by the Air Force. This will begin with discussions with the Air Force and research to determine the specific shielding requirements sought in the solicitation topic. Once understood, those requirements can be applied to the current Faraday design to alter it for use in this application. The focus will likely be on adjustments or substitutions to the LPS to optimize it for EMP protection over lightning strikes. Depending on Air Force needs, this layer may be isolated for use as a stand-alone EMP shield. Testing will be instrumental in guiding these design adjustments and verifying the resulting panels. Touchstone will also seek to determine how Faraday needs adjusted for installation onto infrastructure. At a minimum, the reporting of this program will be carried out through four main avenues: 1) Kickoff meeting to clarify Air Force expectations and Touchstone’s plan. 2) Midterm report to convey Touchstone’s progress. 3) Summary Meeting toward the end of the program for Touchstone to present its findings. And 4) a program final report. By the end of this Phase I, Touchstone intends to have a thorough understanding of the Air Force’s expectations and requirements, a feasible Faraday design for infrastructure shielding, and a plan for a Phase II program to refine this design for production.

When assembling RSPs, an airman takes a list of required spare parts and develops a loading plan that specifies how many containers are required and how the spare parts should be arranged into the containers. This process is time consuming and error-prone because airmen often partially develop a loading plan, try executing the loading plan, and then must backtrack in the event the plan is unachievable. Virtualitics can quickly configure a constraint-solving model to encode requirements and constraints of RSP load-planning – e.g. by using a highly expressive and flexible logic, Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) – and then utilize a modern, high-performance AI-based constraint solver (e.g. an SMT-solver) to efficiently identify optimized solutions for the RSP load-planning model. Second, Virtualitics will leverage its expertise in developing AI-based optimization models to ensure the prototype can: (i) generate load-plans optimized with respect to multiple quantitative metrics and (ii) incorporate custom heuristics (designed specifically for RSP Optimization use case) that accelerate the AI-based optimization process, thereby decreasing the web-application’s runtime to align with user operational requirements and expectations.

The Department of the Air Force (DAF) urgently requires a modern, efficient, and reliable system to manage last-mile deliveries on the flightline, encompassing the ordering, fulfillment, and tracking of both non-consumables (e.g., equipment, assets, tools) and consumables (e.g., fuel, fleet services). In an era defined by the peer/near-peer power competition, maintaining sortie generation is not just a priority—it’s a mission-critical imperative. DAF logisticians face relentless pressure to meet the demands of Rapid Global Mobility (RGM) while adapting to the increasing complexities of contested logistics environments. RGM is a force multiplier, enabling the projection of combat capabilities worldwide and ensuring that U.S. forces can quickly confront and surpass threats in any future high-stakes conflicts. Additionally, RGM enhances the agility required to execute the Agile Combat Employment strategy, empowering the DAF to rapidly adapt to emerging threats and sustain operational dominance, even with a reduced boots-on-the-ground presence.  At the heart of this effort are the Aerospace Ground Equipment (AGE), Maintenance, and Logistics communities who ensure sortie generation. However, these critical teams continue to rely on decades-old communication systems, using land mobile radios and landlines that are vulnerable to interference from flightline noise, connection issues, and miscommunication errors.  To address these challenges, an AGE Airmen innovator from the 62nd Maintenance Group envisioned a mobile solution similar to the food delivery app DoorDash.  We partnered with him and brought his vision to life with JetDash, a game-changing mobile platform that enables flightline personnel to request support equipment directly from their smartphones. Now accredited and deployed in the DAF Cloud One environment, JetDash replaces outdated communication systems by allowing secure web- or mobile-based AGE orders to be dispatched directly to drivers’ devices for faster, more reliable delivery. Recognized by AFWERX at the Fed SuperNova summit in August 2023 and validated through multiple operational evaluations—including Exercise Mobility Guardian 2024 at Andersen AFB, Guam—JetDash has demonstrated strong demand and offers immediate and tangible benefits to warfighting capabilities by eliminating communication errors, reducing delivery times, and providing real-time situational awareness.  Currently, JetDash supports only non-consumable AGE ordering and delivery, but with the proposed TACFI funding, we aim to:Extend JetDash’s capabilities to include ordering and delivery of consumables (fuel, fleet services) and other critical inventory types.Introduce a Last-Mile Common Operational Picture to provide real-time situational awareness for supervisors and base commanders, enhancing decision-making.Collect Last-Mile Delivery Data to build future Machine Learning use cases that optimize operational efficiency and predict demand patterns.

This proposal addresses the need for advanced, AI-enhanced privacy preservation architecture tailored to protect sensitive data within military family knowledge systems. Military families face distinct, evolving needs across health, social, and logistical domains, requiring robust, privacy-centric data management solutions. Our project aims to develop a secure knowledge base capable of integrating data from the Department of Defense (DoD), Veterans Affairs (VA), and social networks, offering military families support while maintaining the highest data integrity and confidentiality standards.In Phase I, the project will establish a modular reference architecture as a foundational structure for secure data handling and privacy management. This foundation will pave the way for a scalable Phase II prototype, with high potential for dual-use applications across government and commercial sectors. The solution aligns with DoD modernization priorities in Trusted AI, Autonomy, and Integrated Network Systems, setting a new standard for privacy-preserving data solutions in defense and civilian environments.

Dover Microsystems, Inc. (Dover) is working towards a national defense-related mission-need in the area of cybersecurity. Software, despite our best efforts, continues to have errors (aka bugs) that can be exploited by attackers to modify the intended behavior of software-intensive systems. The only two ways to address this problem are to either (1) develop software without exploitable errors, or (2) detect and block attacks when they occur. While preventing errors in the first place is ideal, the history of software has shown that strict processes and extensive testing find many but not all exploitable software flaws. Furthermore, the formal methods to support “correct by construction” (which implies bug-free) are still in their infancy. The five main categories of technology used to detect and block attacks today are: signature-based, anomaly-based, cryptography, compartmentalization, and instrumentation. None of the aforementioned approaches addresses the fundamental problem facing software-intensive systems today: zero-day (not previously encountered) attacks on running systems can redirect execution, modify data, and exfiltrate data. Every system in the Air Force that is currently running software and is connected to a network is at risk of attack. The aforementioned security mechanisms either detect a small subset of possible attacks or merely attempt to limit the scope of damage of a successful attack.  All USAF systems planned or in development can benefit from incorporating CoreGuard as a key element of their security. We believe technology development under the subject SBIR topic will contribute to solving a mission need. The main goals of our project are to demonstrate both the precision and the breadth of customizable, hardware-accelerated security policies using CoreGuard. Specifically, we will focus on defining and then monitoring safety automata for safety-critical, software-intensive systems. The mission impact of this project on the Air Force and the Department of Defense will be to add instruction level, fine-grained, non-subvertible, oversight of an execution processor used by the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center to keep a finite-state machine-based safety critical system from ever entering a dangerous state. This capability addresses a serious and currently unmet gap in the cybersecurity defenses of USAF systems and can save both civilian and warfighter lives by preventing compromise of safety-critical systems.
Dynamic Enforcement of Safety Automata

With the growth of metal additive manufacturing (AM), the technology has reached a readiness level where aerospace suppliers, such as Lockheed, Boeing, General Electric, and Airbus, are investigating AM solutions to solve significant logistic and technical challenges for landing gear parts. It appears feasible in the near future to replace current forging and machining production with metal AM to produce landing gear parts with equal or improved strength, weight, and corrosion resistance. Phase II efforts will focus on the investigation and development of typical landing gear materials including Aluminum-Nickel-Bronze (AlNiBr) and high strength steel (HSS) alloys 300M and 4340. Along with the developmental work on these alloys, investigations into the effectiveness of typical landing gear processing will be completed to ensure AM developed landing gear parts can be sustained effectively. All of this will be targeted to ensure the certification requirements for the materials and parts are met to support implementation and usage when qualified. The major elements of this Phase II effort include high strength AlNiBr development using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), HSS development using LPBF and electron beam additive manufacturing (EBAM), and the evaluation of landing gear processes on AM parts.

Slip Robotics proposes to develop and demonstrate an omni-directionalaircraft mover designed specifically for the F-16 Fighting Falcon. This novel system—built upon the unique capabilities of Slip Robotics’ commercially deployed SlipBot platform—will combine a high-capacity, all-directional robotic base with an integrated aircraft lifting cradle capable of raising and maneuvering an F-16 in tight maintenance environments. The proposed mover will lift the aircraft at designated jack points (with landing gear up or down), securely transferring its full weight to the platform, and then transport it laterally, diagonally, or rotationally with zero-point turning and high precision. This technology directly addresses a critical Air Force need: reducing tow lane requirements by up to 50% and enabling precision placement of aircraft for automated corrosion control, painting, and inspection systems. Traditional tows and tugs lack this lateral mobility and rely heavily on operator skill, increasing the risk of aircraft damage and limiting throughput in constrained depots.Slip Robotics’ SlipBot technology—currently deployed in more than 200 units across the United States—is field-proven in moving up to 12,000-pound loads in industrial environments including dock levelers and uneven floors. This system will be adapted and scaled through reinforced structural design and synchronized jacking mechanisms to support the higher dynamic loads of fighter aircraft (targeting ~20,000 lbs). The integrated software will support semi-autonomous navigation, sensor-based safety systems, and a user interface suitable for depot technicians. The system’s core capabilities in precise all-directional motion, safety compliance, and repeatable positioning will be enhanced with aircraft-specific hardware to ensure no undue stress is placed on the airframe in directions it is not structurally designed for.All R&D will be performed at Slip’s engineering and fabrication facilities in Norcross, Georgia using in-house CNC, electronics, and assembly resources. No foreign nationals will participate. The project team—led by Dennis Siedlak (CTO, formerly Waymo)—includes founders and engineers with backgrounds at GE Aviation, Tesla, The Aerospace Corporation, and Volley Automation, where they previously developed autonomous vehicle movers for parking systems. This Direct-to-Phase-II proposal is supported by strong commercial traction, demonstrated technical feasibility from SlipBot deployments, and internal investment in mobility and autonomy platforms. The proposed system addresses DoD objectives for next-generation sustainment infrastructure and has compelling dual-use applications in commercial MRO (Maintenance, Repair, Overhaul) facilities and industrial logistics.

Aircraft fleets in the U.S. and around the world are aging and require a sound supply of replacement electronics to maintain fleet readiness. Oftentimes OEMs for electronics printed circuit boards (PCBs) no longer exist or have halted production on critical parts. Lack of original designs or technical data packages (TDPs) for these components leads to extensive reverse engineering (RE) efforts in order to reproduce these critical components to meet form, fit, and function requirements and thereby reduce the need for costly re-certification efforts. Current PCB RE methods are destructive, prone to human judgment & error, time-consuming, and require highly skilled & specialized labor. A technology solution that enables PCB RE to be accomplished in a more robust, non-destructive, and automated way could save the Air Force millions of dollars each year. This project is combing non-destructive X-Ray tomographic (XRT) imaging with novel data processing, simulation, and machine learning techniques along with legacy PCB re-engineering software typically used in destructive settings, to solve this crucial problem and yield and a more robust and automated XRT-based PCB re-engineering framework.

This project proposes the adaptation and certification of a mobile safety system for autonomous robotic platforms equipped with articulated arms, operating in dynamic, human-occupied environments. Built on Sensory Robotics’ proven SR-1 technology—currently deployed in industrial settings—the system enables certifiable safety without the need for traditional physical barriers, light curtains, or fixed-zone programming. The objective is to develop a software-controlled safety architecture using 3D time-of-flight (ToF) sensing and real-time spatial awareness to create dynamic protection zones around mobile robotic platforms as they perform tasks such as material handling, inspection, or servicing alongside human personnel. This will enable safe, flexible, and autonomous execution of high-mix, high-risk tasks without the footprint or rigidity of traditional safety infrastructure. Commercially, the system has strong dual-use potential in manufacturing, logistics, and defense applications. By extending SR-1’s core capabilities to mobile platforms, this project advances the Air Force’s strategic objectives around autonomy, human-machine teaming, and agile operational support.

Edge Case Research proposes the development of an Autonomous Confined Space Inspection Platform (ACSIP) to address the U.S. Air Force’s critical need for safe, efficient, and reliable inspection of aircraft fuel tanks and other confined spaces. To support the DoDÆs need to produce synthetic multi-spectral sensor data for the purpose of training low-shot machine learning models, ARiA has successfully demonstrated the feasibility of the Generative Augmentation Process (GAP). A novel, conditionally generative artificial intelligence (AI) method was used to synthesize infrared (IR) from visible data over multiple target classes using measured data coming from multiple satellites with images sampled globally over multiple seasons and at different look angles. By leveraging edge computing and federated learning, this approach allows predictive models to be trained across a network of assets without centralizing sensitive data, preserving both data integrity and security. Organizations within the DOD generate millions of documents (PDFs, PPTX, DOCX, CSV, XLSX, EMAILS) per month that need to be tagged for Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) content. These documents contain sensitive information, so it is crucial to tag these documents with correct CUI categories to prevent highly classified documents from falling into the wrong peopleĺs hands. However, tagging CUI accurately is very difficult, as the CUI labels correspond to over 100 CUI classifications sitting in the CUI Registry, with classes that include PRVCY, HLTH, and LEI. Knowing how to properly tag CUI data requires subject matter expertise, and involves having a strong understanding of the rules designated in the CUI Registry.áTagging documents with the correct CUI label is mission critical, as CUI tags correlate directly to distribution and dissemination of information. If documents are under classified, people with not appropriate privilege levels have access to information that they are not allowed to access, which is a major security risk. If documents are over classified, DOD personnel that should be able to collaborate and work on solving critical national security problems are not able to have access, which causes inefficiencies in productivity, communications, and collaboration.In order to build a robust CUI tagging solution, there are many complex requirements that need to be met. áThe solution needs easy to use, able to be run on privately on premise, provide accurate predictions with probability scores to measure certainty, have the CUI predictions be recomposed into documents across various file formats, incorporate dynamic taxonomies for evolving CUI categories, and enable SME-involved active learning for enhanced model precision. Anote's CUI tagging solution meets these requirements, and has the following components:Anote - An end to end MLOps platform that enables you to obtain the best large language model for tagging CUI. Anote provides an evaluation framework to compare zero shot LLMs like GPT, Claude, Llama3 and Mistral, with fine tuned LLMs that are trained on domain specific training data (via supervised, unsupervised and RLHF fine tuning). Anote provides a data annotation interface to convert raw unstructured data into an LLM ready format, and incorporate subject matter expertise into your training process to improve model accuracies.Private Chatbot - A private, on premise, chat interface where you could upload documents and download the recomposed CUI markings.áUpreach - An email system such that when you would send the email, determines whether uploaded documents and content have specific categories of CUI, and cross-reference the associated privilege level of email recipients to ensure that they are supposed to receive documents.Software Development Kit - An integration layer between Anote's fine tuned LLMs and dissemination systems within the DOD to plug in CUI tagging models into your system.

The Department of Defense (DoD) increasingly relies on artificial intelligence (AI) systems for operational decision making, strategic planning, and mission-critical activities. However, current generative AI models pose a significant risk due to their potential for unreliable outputs, vulnerability to adversarial attacks, and susceptibility to generating misleading or incorrect information. These issues make generative AI unsuitable for deployment in dynamic, high-stakes defense environments without rigorous safety validation. Aptima's PROACTIVE (Proactive Red-teaming and Operational Agent-Centric Trusted Intelligent Vehicles) framework aims to solve these challenges by ensuring that generative AI is trustworthy, resilient, and ready for deployment in mission-critical applications.áPROACTIVE is an integrated AI safety framework that continuously tests and evaluates generative AI models across multiple stages of the AI lifecycle, from initial development to real-time operational use. Our solution includes sophisticated red teaming tools to simulate adversarial scenarios, proactive safety agents to identify and mitigate risks preemptively, and a multimodal safety evaluation approach that leverages lessons from Aptima's award-winning NAUTICAL system. NAUTICAL, originally developed for the Navy, ensures that AI systems remain adaptive and reliable in complex environments, and this expertise has been expanded for broader DoD applications.áPROACTIVE operates at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3, currently focusing on feasibility validation, with plans for further development in Phase II to create an Authority to Operate (ATO)-ready prototype. The frameworkĺs core goal is to bridge the trust gap in generative AI models by making them resilient to adversarial threats, ensuring that they provide accurate and safe outputs that enhance decision making. By addressing both technical vulnerabilities and operational risks, PROACTIVE is uniquely capable of transforming generative AI into a reliable asset for defense applications, supporting the DoDĺs need for safe, effective, and mission-critical technology.á

Problem: In a peer or near-peer conflict, U.S. and Allied forces must achieve seamless spectrum situational awareness and persistent custody of thousands of friendly and adversary objects across the battlespace. Today’s ISR platforms are largely vertically integrated, relying on closed software ecosystems and labor-intensive TCPED (Tasking, Collection, Processing, Exploitation, and Dissemination) workflows. These fragmented architectures limit interoperability, preventing the dynamic, multi-platform collaboration needed to support effective kill-web operations using kinetic and non-kinetic (electromagnetic spectrum) means.To meet this challenge, MapLarge proposes to develop an Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations (EMSO) Data Fabric that integrates, automates, and extends ISR and Space Responsive Tactical (SRT) capabilities across air and space domains. This solution builds on prior USAF and USSF collaborations, and directly addresses the operational need for automated, scalable, and time-dominant ISR capabilities supporting Find, Fix, Track, Target, Engage, and Assess (F2T2EA) of mobile threats.Opportunity: The EMSO Data Fabric will extend the FAST-GAPS SBIR Phase II feasibility engine by enabling collaborative EMS kill-chains supporting both semi-automated rapid reprogramming and fully automated track custody services. This architecture will enable platforms like the RC-135 RIVET JOINT to function as an EMSO “Quarterback,” orchestrating cross-domain operations via machine-to-machine coordination.Key components include:Hybrid Architecture: High-performance, MBSE-driven framework for data orchestration across ISR/SRT systems.Edge Node Services: Cross-platform transport layer for air/space communications planning and relay/backhaul among collaborating assets.Data Catalog Integration: Seamless access to DoD/IC data sources (e.g., UDL, TacSRT, NGA) via standard APIs.EMSO Automation – Rapid Reprogramming: Human-in-the-loop workflows to expedite threat data coordination and countermeasure deployment.EMSO Automation – Kill-Web Custody: Onboard object custody services with trade space visualization to scale custody operations across sensors and mission policies.This effort aligns with DAF S&T Strategy Objective 1, Strategic Need 3: Rapid, Effective Decision-Making, by compressing the OODA loop through automation and machine-assisted ISR orchestration. It supports the DAF Operational Imperative for Moving Target Engagement by enabling composite tracking across distributed air and space platforms. Finally, it delivers the Information Mobility core competency by unifying the space transport layer with airborne ISR edge capabilities—allowing distributed, survivable EMS operations in highly contested environments.

According to Lt. Col. Robert Knapp, Operations Officer at Air Force Education and Training Command (AETC) Detachment 24 (DET 24), in a traditional pilot training environment, students use paper documents or an iPad with their training documents on it. They then transition from that into an extremely expensive traditional simulator where they can execute the full range of flight maneuvers. The problem with those expensive sims is that there are only a handful of them, and they are constrained on the number of times a student can get into them. Air Education and Training Command’s (AETC) Remotely Piloted Aircraft (RPA) Training Next (RTN) program has a national defense-related mission need to improve the rate and quality of pilot and sensor operator certification for the MQ-9 Reaper. RTN is a competency-based concept where RPA students undergo a tailor-made program based on their capabilities and needs rather than an entire class following a rigid construct and transitioning through the entire pipeline together. Every year, the MQ-9 Formal Training Unit (FTU) is expected to produce 650 Basic Combat Elements (BCE) (a crew consisting of a pilot and sensor operator). However, the FTU currently has the capacity to only graduate 550 BCEs due to instructor and simulator availability shortages. Moth+Flame's READY VR Toolkit accelerates Airmen training by augmenting current solutions with autonomous, scalable technology to help increase pilot production, and  has 10 aircraft already contracted for integration onto its platform (Figure 2.3.1.1-1). This means 10 pilot and maintenance communities benefit today from current Air Force investment. By leveraging current AF investment, VR programs get off the ground faster and cheaper than starting from scratch. With tremendous advances in recent years, VR is the perfect solution to augment both basic skills and advanced training and supplement traditional simulators with an integrated, adaptive, immersive, and low-cost solution. Providing data-driven training enhancements to traditional practices, our mission-oriented VR solution brings technology for learning everything from checklist procedures, to formation flying, fighter maneuvers, and multiparticipant tactical scenarios. READY will refine the MQ-9 RTN training and systems roadmap, equipping RTN instructors and students with state-of-the-art VR training that will accelerate the rate of BCE production.
Modular Multi-User VR Remote Training Platform

There is currently a strong need for compact, JP-8 fueled, high power density electrical generation for use in UAV, auxiliary power supplies, and portable power. Precision Combustion, Inc (PCI) is proposing to evaluate the viability of an advanced, high TRL generator with high power density (250-500 W/kg) and high specific power for these applications. The Phase I Objective will be to develop a detailed cycle map (based on testing at PCI) of the generator, confirm gravimetric and volumetric densities, efficiency, robustness, power quality, and identify modifications/updates required to satisfy targeted Air Force requirements. The benefits, shortcomings, and level of effort required to make it MIL-SPEC compliant will be determined. Additionally, component sourcing, manufacturing, pricing, and application-specific technology licensing for USAF applications will be addressed. During Phase II, PCI will modify, demonstrate, and deliver multiple generators, sized to produce target power output ranging from 1-3 kW. Durability, start-up time, emissions, power conditioning, JP-8 suitability, airframe adaptability, BOP requirements, battery hybridization, scalability, and designs with high fuel to electric efficiency will be examined.

On-orbit satellite servicing (OSS) has been receiving increasing interest from government entities. OSS increases the lifetime of satellites in orbit, but currently requires expensive and limited astronaut time. NASA and DARPA/NRL have both proposed upcoming missions to service satellites using re-usable service satellites -- in both low-Earth and geosynchronous orbits. These missions will rely on mixtures of human-in-the-loop and autonomous control to remotely command service satellites with manipulation capabilities. Through previous projects, TRACLabs has contacts at the Air Force Research Laboratory who have begun to investigate OSS tasks using robotic manipulators. Reliable teleoperation of remote robots in manipulation tasks is a challenging open area of robotics research. To address this challenge, TRACLabs has developed CRAFTSMAN, a toolkit for expert and non-expert users to reliably operate robots. CRAFTSMAN has been adopted in various projects by both NASA and private industry customers. In Phase I of this project, we will demonstrate the utility of CRAFTSMAN in a simulated Air Force OSS domain and will identify extensions to the CRAFTSMAN framework needed to address Air Force OSS needs.
Orbital Mechanic: CRAFTSMAN for On-orbit Satellite Servicing

Using simulation, Shield AI can increase the velocity of AI algorithm development. Shield AI’s high-fidelity simulation framework models the real world and simulates sensor data, which enables the accelerated and parallelized training of robotic intelligence, leading to generational capability leaps measured in weeks, not years. RL is an approach to machine learning that defines a reward function and learns a policy that maximizes the reward. The benefit of framing a problem as an RL problem with an appropriate reward function is that the policy can be learned off of many examples rather than by manually tuning the parameters of the policy.  This effort seeks to apply RL to the development of autonomous behaviors for a team of air-launched effects (ALEs) performing the military mission of environment monitoring within our high-fidelity simulation. The capability development process with simulation and RL is extremely fast, which allows for thousands of iteration and makes for a very robust transition to real-world platforms.

Air Force munitions and support equipment transport operations cannot currently function at peak efficiency. The preferred munitions-loading device of Air Force support personnel, the low-profile Manually Operated Lift Truck (MOLT) MHU-194F, is long, heavy, and takes up two entire pallet footprints on its own during storage, resupply, re-arm, or re-launch missions. Branch Technology ("Branch") specializes in construction-grade 3D printing that produces lightweight and exceedingly strong composite parts. Air For personnel from the Air Force Lifecycle Management Center (AFLCMC) Support Equipment and Vehicles (SE-V) Directorate, along with HQ Air Force Material Command (AFMC) and the Air Combat Command (ACC) Agile Battle Lab, have asked Branch to investigate the applicability of its 3D printing technology to create support scaffold structures that can vertically stack multiple MOLTs - each of which weighs in excess of 2000 lbs.  The proposed solution, nicknamed the MOLT Cubby Unit (MCU) will allow Air Force logistics missions to double their capacity for cargo storage, consolidate the overall number of resupply missions required, and facilitate a more agile, lean, and lethal Air Force - while simultaneously expediting the development of future technology through the first DoD productization of Branch's 3D printing capability.  In place of a normal Phase I SBIR award, Branch has already conducted extensive customer discovery, preliminary research, and CAD modeling to verify that the technology could be used to create a prototype. Branch has also already identified and been in recurring contact with the Air Force end-user, customer, and additional committed stakeholders - and has had 4 concept-design review sessions with these units in preparation for this Phase II scope of work. In Phase II, Branch proposes to dive into the details of customer/user product requirements, produce a set of initial prototypes, vet the products for flight-readiness certification with the Air Transportability Testing Agency (ATTLA), and conduct an on-site demo with the end-users and all committed stakeholders - presumably at the Program Office of the AFLCMC's Support Equipment and Vehicles Directorate at Robins AFB. Branch has received assurances that success in Phase II will lead to Phase III transitional purchasing to fill this immediate capability gap for Air Force support equipment personnel.

In order to enable autonomous or resilient satellite constellation operation, immediate decisions and threat mitigation must be executed by satellites in real-time before an enemy is successful in executing their strategies.  Ground operators are generally unable to respond to proximity threats instantly in current architectures.  Applying edge-computing into a satellite enables autonomous rule-sets to be instantly executed in the new contested and congested space environment.   However, without adequate installed hardware, rule-set software has no use. A recent survey of self-driving car applications found that a minimum of 16 TBytes of computational memory is necessary to enable autonomous functions; however, no current small satellite in the US space industrial base approaches that data storage capacity.  The objective of this project is to perform applied development, transitioning a “best-in-class”, already-existing Commercial, Off the Shelf (COTS) NGD Systems ultra-high capacity 8 Terabyte (TB) solid state drive (SSD) – targeted for autonomous driving applications – to SmallSat application.  This COTS SSD will enable in-situ small satellite processing capability with (1) Machine Learning (ML) applications on-orbit, and (2) secure and reliable storage and transmission of data, leading to transformational US Space Force superiority.  Deployment path(s) will be demonstrated through Space and Missile Systems Center, Los Angeles Air Force Base (SMC) supply chains and proposed missions. Satellite autonomy is vital to USSF; the project will develop a full-fledged software stack for in-storage ML processing in support of deploying an autonomous 2U CubeSat to the TRL 3 level for an autonomy demonstration, leading the way for a next-step “trusted autonomy” project.

Our objective in this SBIR proposal is to adapt our advanced infrared imaging technology, called WISP, to accurately screen for fevers to aid in Decision Support to Combat the Virus (Focus Area 1 of the COVID area of interest) and help slow further spread of the “coronavirus disease 2019” (COVID-19).  As a 500-Mpix, high dynamic range, LongWave InfraRed (LWIR) video system, WISP, or a variation on its design, is well-equipped to measure the brightness temperature of objects at a distance with a precision better than 0.1 oC.  When calibrated, the system promises a very wide field-of-view, up to the entire 360o surroundings.  Accurate brightness temperature measurements of everything visible in the surroundings could be made every few seconds. The system could provide unmatched capability to measure skin temperature and detect probable febrile subjects at a long distance and across a large area. The data could in-turn drive automated analysis to gather febrile subject counts in an area.  Note that it is not possible to identify people using WISP LWIR imagery alone.  The currently deployed WISP system does not yet support accurate temperature calibration and is not easily affordable for a broad commercial market.  As part of this SBIR, we propose to immediately build and deploy a mobile testbed to measure face temperature and detect probable fevers using an existing WISP system. In parallel, we will implement a spiral development plan to understand the optimal CONOPS, implement auto-detection algorithms for febrile subjects, and develop a more affordable sensor solution for future production.

Specifically, the Digital University – part of the “Digital Air Force” initiative – requires capabilities that will enable Airmen to train remotely, using industry leading curriculum, to learn skills associated with a new way of fighting wars. The Digital University (Digital U) needs improved data management and integration that can be delivered by emerging technologies and rapidly deployed to Air Force personnel through a scalable architecture. The Air Force must build resiliency by evaluating, training, tracking, and certifying Airmen against AF-vetted cyber and development paths. Additionally, this initiative will enable AF functional leaders to manage manpower/assignments and facilitate Airmen COVID-19 response while geographically separated from their work centers. Airmen need the ability to browse and conduct online training. By integrating various online commercially available learning platforms, Digital U will provide targeted curriculum that meets the needs of the organization.  Harnessing training data and leveraging advanced analytics and AI capabilities, will provide a best-in-class learning management system for the entire Air Force. Additionally, by integrating with approved Manpower Systems with Airmen training and certification information, Digital University will enable functional leaders to manage manpower and assignments. Omni Federal will use our library of reference architectures, tools, processes, code and testbed to build a customized solution for the Digital U platform.  We will use available data to help develop customized recommendations for each Airman that aligns with their personal profile and history.  AI/ML techniques such as natural language processing, clustering and recommendation systems will be used to personalize and optimize the recommendations to align with individual profiles and overall Air Force needs.  We will also integrate with approved Manpower Systems for evaluating, training, tracking, and certifying Airmen against AF-vetted cyber and development paths and will support manpower/assignments and facilitate Airmen COVID-19 response while geographically separated from their work centers. Omni Federal will also evaluate and integrate with commercial online training platforms such as Udemy and Pluralsight using APIs for modular, extensible and light integration.  This will augment Air Force developed training material and provide a broader set of training options and approaches for Airmen.

Vantage proposes a new form of low cost sensory augmented aerial telepresence for the Air Force. This $10K system enables 50 km2 of < 1 cm GSD coverage anywhere in the world in less than 24 hours, controlled by operators from any location and launched by personnel with no prior training.   This will be realized by extending the capabilities of Vesper, Vantage’s Type 1 UAS, to both meet the Air Force ATO security requirements and enable remote operation with multi-user remote viewing. This capability will increase the effectiveness of personnel and reduce the risks, costs, and lost time from travel. Reduced travel risks include reduced potential for exposure and spread of COVID and other future pandemics. Vesper is an NDAA compliant 1.4 lb UAS, developed as part of an effort funded by the U.S. Army’s Short Range Reconaissance Program. The base system costs $6000 with a GCS, charges, transit and travel cases, and a field repair kit. This UAS built on Vantage’s previous commercially available product, Snap.  Combining Vesper with the new remote operation capabilities developed as part of the proposed program can offer secure sensory enhanced remote presence anywhere in the world.  With our proposed network connectivity solution, Vesper could be operated safely over the network, with access to a real time video stream and full control of the aircraft. This gives Air Force personnel a new set of capabilities for telepresence, reducing the health risks, costs, and wasted time of travel. In addition, we are currently engaged with the Air Force to attain ATO certification. We expect some desired modifications to come from this effort including secure boot, encrypted internal communications, and encrypted data storage and propose completing these modifications as part of this effort. This program will consist of an initial benchtop system demonstration, an in person prototype demonstration, and a final Air Force end user test and evaluation. We expect this effort to cost approximately $970K and take 9 months to complete.

Q-Net Security (QNS) will apply its quantum compute-resistant network technology to secure drone communication. This demonstration will be an example of the remarkable strong protection QNS can provide for airborne wide area networks, wide-band air-to-air communications and mobile ad hoc networks. Secure and robust communications in the field is a non-negotiable requirement for mission success. QNS technology works with existing communications infrastructure, strong enough to enable use of public networks, and is currently deployed in commercial settings that use copper and fiber, Wi-Fi, LTE, and satellite links. QNS products are engineered from immutable, purpose-built hardware and do not use any operating systems or other vulnerable software; they are provably-secure and cannot be changed or respond to malware. This drop-in secure network overlay has attributes that are characterized as a distributed firewall together with session-less VPN tunnels that can also be configured to provide fine-grained network micro-segmentation. In addition to ultra-strong encryption, the QNS solution leverages superior packet authentication to ensure that unauthenticated data packets cannot disrupt or pass through a QNS endpoint. These devices deliver remarkably strong security yet are easy to implement, can provide unified endpoint management, and never need to be updated or patched once deployed.

We propose a solution framework to the problem in Space Traffic Management of unpredictable human-machine interactions during Conjunction Assessment (CA) / Collision Avoidance (COLA) situations.  Factors that make COLA involving autonomous space objects (SO’s) more complex include that SO’s may be uncontrolled, non-communicative, self-directing, and/or adversarial.  Versus COLA with a cooperative or uncontrolled SO, the COLA situation is more difficult when responding to a potential collision between a controlled, "friendly" asset and an unknown, potentially autonomous, potentially adversarial spacecraft. We propose a solution framework to the problem in Space Traffic Management of unpredictable human-machine interactions during Conjunction Assessment (CA) / Collision Avoidance (COLA) situations.  Factors that make COLA involving autonomous space objects (SO’s) more complex include that SO’s may be uncontrolled, non-communicative, self-directing, and/or adversarial.  Versus COLA with a cooperative or uncontrolled SO, the COLA situation is more difficult when responding to a potential collision between a controlled, "friendly" asset and an unknown, potentially autonomous, potentially adversarial spacecraft. Our architecture will be designed to accommodate non-cooperative SO’s, whether disabled, non-communicative, self-directed, or adversarial. High-uncertainty scenarios and autonomous systems can be difficult to model sufficiently, and the goal is to guarantee proper, predictable behavior of the onboard autonomy, to ensure that mitigating COLA actions are in fact achievable, and that the avoidance maneuver will occur safely with high confidence. To do this, we propose a generational leap in autonomy based on: 1) collaborative space-ground networked agents, 2) autonomous onboard COLA, 3) Virtual Agent Autonomy to model intents of other intelligent agents via streaming contextual behavior modeling, 4) and next-generation safe autonomy algorithms using Shielded Deep Reinforcement Learning to prevent the autonomous spacecraft from entering into dangerous or impossible-to-recover situations. The combined technologies will be deployed on an integrated ground and flight software system which leverages existing SSA sensing data, SSA systems, and Defense and commercial space mission operations infrastructure. Initial checkouts of the system performed in a live-virtual constructive environment (LVCE), allowing simulation of the autonomy algorithms using operational data ingested in real-time to develop trust in the autonomy.

This folded mirror blank would then be deployed from a small-sat, unfurled, and coated in space with typically a highly reflective gold coating thus enabling IR signal detection. RUBY SKY will be able to provide high intelligence value to the USAF by tracking/tagging cruise missiles (sub/super/hyper-sonic) is possible high-LEO or low-MEO.
