Aerothermal loads interacting with optical sensors include shock waves, causing strong, sharp density gradients, acting as a lens; turbulent boundary layer or wake flow; high-temperature gas and plasma effects due to non-equilibrium air behind shocks, resulting in background radiation, and in turn interacting with the sensor system. Optical window emissions and thermal deformation can also cause additional optical aberrations at the focal plane of the imaging system. In response to those challenges and needs, and within this proposed Phase II effort, CFD Research will leverage past performance and expertise in high-fidelity physics-based and fast-running reduced-order modeling and simulation to continue to build the Hypersonic Aero-optic Analysis and imaging frameWorK (HAAWK). An experimental campaign at CUBRC’s LENS-I and LENS-XX hypersonic facilities will be executed, addressing aero-optical and spectroscopic wake measurements of a generic Common Hypersonic Glide Vehicle (C-HGV) type geometry, providing wavefront information (OPD), and data derived from the point spread function (PSF) including boresight shift, blur and Strehl ratio, etc. as well as spectral emission lines. The experimental data will serve as validation for the in-house developed optical and radiation simulation tools. Reduced-order and surrogate models will be developed, enabling fast execution of the framework. A proof-of-concept demonstration will show HAAWK’s capabilities of rapidly generating databases along hypersonic trajectories, describing the image aberration due to aero-optical and radiative effects. CFD Research uses scene generation to visualize these imaging aberrations. The database information can then be used by third-party sensor manufacturers to develop an on-board compensation algorithm, or, for software- and hardware-in-the-loop (SWIL/HWIL) simulations, supporting ground test validation and verification (V&V) efforts of sensor systems of interest.

Pumping silicon-based cavities to ultra-high vacuum (UHV) pressure levels is challenging using microfabricated pumps. Among the various technologies that achieve UHV at macroscale, ion-sorption pumps are currently the most promising for miniaturization because of the improved surface to volume ratio. Although they reach and maintain 7E-7 Torr, miniature ion-pumps that have been published use permanent magnets to trap electrons into 100’s meter long mean free path to improve the probability of ionizing gas particles at the UHV levels. However, these magnets are cumbersome, bulky and heavy and can also interfere with sensitive circuits and sensors.   This problem is compounded by the lack of absolute pressure sensors that do not require a calibration curve to measure the internal pressure.  Drift due to real or virtual leaks after bonding can only be accurately measured using a cold atom pressure gauge for pressures below 1E-7 Torr.  This proposal will develop a microfabricated ion-sorption ring-Orbitron pump based on previous theoretical work. This device uses a ring-shaped anode to electrostatically trap electrons and increase their mean free path to favor gas ionization without using magnets. The ionized gas particles, including N2 and other noble gas, are then trapped into the getter-coated sidewalls.  This pump will be accompanied by a gas discharge pump that can operate across a broader pressure range. Neither the ring-Orbitron nor the gas-discharge pump require magnets nor moving parts to function; instead, they rely on electrical biasing which can be easily achieved without complex electronics. The proposed device also includes a cold atom cavity to measure pressure in the target UHV range as well as a graphite specimen to avoid loading the pump with Rubidium gas. The proposed device will be fabricated in phase II using silicon microfabrication technology, such that it will be highly compatible with silicon-based cavities.

Operation of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) from large ships represents a disruptive technology for the Navy as it expands UAV capabilities and sortie rates, including swarm launch and recovery. Recently, the Navy has developed new technical paradigms to solve the many challenges associated with UAV operations from ships other than aircraft carriers, including launch and recovery of Group 3 through 5 UAVs subject to strong winds and high sea-states. Large fixed wing UAVs operating from ships offer tremendous potential to the Navy to provide Intelligence/Surveillance/Reconnaissance (ISR), increased lethality, ship self-defense, and ‘loyal wingman’ support for manned aircraft.   Diversified Technologies Inc. (DTI) proposes to develop a launch and recovery system for Group  to Group 5 UAVs. This system consists of a stowable sponson assembly mounted outside the hull of large ships such as ESB-class vessels. The sponsons consists of rigid lattice frames of stowable outriggers bearing support cables that, in turn, support and guide a carriage to launch or recover the UAV with or without landing gear. The sponsons can be folded upward, downward, or forward for storage. The carriage is controlled by a drive cable that connects to motors that both accelerate and decelerate the system. The motors are located below deck and operated by closed-loop controls. The power system supplies or absorbs the required aircraft energy for launch and recovery, respectively. The system is bidirectional and can launch and recover UAVs approaching from either the bow or the stern of the ship. An articulating arm rapidly loads and unloads the UAVs. The DTI launch and recovery system requires minimal modifications to the UAVs. Many system components are available commercially-off-the-shelf reducing costs and easing supply chain worries. The entire system can also be built as a compact and portable ground-based system. Minimal site preparation is needed, all that is needed is a reasonably flat site. The sponson / outriggers would be replaced by a support frame at each end secured on temporary foundations by ground anchors. The machinery would be located on a skid that can either be truck / trailer mounted or ground anchored on a temporary foundation. The cable based system does not need precise alignment of the mechanical components further simplifying the installation. The work plan summary is: Base period is a system design and critical components testing effort; Option 1 is a scaled launcher system fabrication and testing effort; and Option 2 is a scaled recovery system fabrication and testing effort. Near the end of the effort, we anticipate using Group 3 UAVs to validate the system.

To address the Navy’s need for an automated system to assist in the gauge block calibration process, Intellisense Systems, Inc. (Intellisense) proposes to advance in Phase II the development of a new Autonomous Robotic Calibration (ARC) system, which was demonstrated and proven feasible in Phase I research. ARC is based on (a) a novel implementation of a gauge block handling robot, which supports accurate block placement without user intervention, and (b) a novel integration of machine vision algorithms providing increased placement accuracy and automatic identification of the gauge blocks. As a result, the ARC system will provide a compact, cost-efficient robot implementing repeatable and reliable gauge block calibration with no or minimal user supervision. In Phase II, Intellisense will build working prototypes of the ARC system and test and demonstrate its capability to meet all performance requirements. The ARC system will be capable of operating with gauge blocks of different sizes (from <1 in. to 24 in.), placing the blocks with the ideal accuracy of 0.01 in., and operating with the required target size of the measurement device (1.5 in. by 3 in.), and it will not increase the temperature of the room by more than 0.2oF. The Phase II ARC prototype will be demonstrated in laboratory and live environments. The successful Phase II development will lead to transition of ARC for use in Naval calibration facilities as well as other calibration laboratories of the U.S. military and industrial stakeholders.

Navy aircraft use complex cable harnesses to transfer data and provide power to avionics, weapons, sensors, control surfaces, and landing gear. The cable harnesses and the aircraft must be designed so that interference to an electronics unit does not occur. Design approaches must address the cable harness packing, separation, shielding, and layout to avoid crosstalk between conductors within an individual harness and between multiple cable harnesses. In addition to crosstalk, interference can occur due to onboard antennas coupling into cable harnesses (or vice versa), lightning strikes near or directly to the aircraft, electromagnetic pulse (EMP) events, and High Intensity Radiated Fields (HIRF). EMA3D Cable is a mature simulation tool for addressing these types of cable harness problems in a rigorous manner when design details about the cable harnesses and the rest of the aircraft structure and systems are available. EMA3D Cable leverages decades of full-aircraft validation, including a recent validation for NAVAIR on the Triton Platform. However, a solution does not currently exist for the early stages of an aircraft design when such details are not available or for when designers wish to perform a design trade study without performing a rigorous solution for the entire aircraft. A simulation tool is needed that can be used for all stages of an aircraft design while retaining the investment in the model development from previous stages of design. Electro Magnetic Applications, Inc. (EMA) is the world leader for consulting, measurement, and simulation of cable harnesses in aerospace platforms for the past 40+ years. The company expertise includes lightning direct and indirect effects, EMP, HIRF, RFI, and several other technical areas within EM and RF. The EMA3D Cable software tool was developed specifically for modeling complex cable harnesses in aerospace platforms and has been validated many times including several prominent publications with aerospace companies such as Airbus, Bombardier, Embraer, The Boeing Company, and others. Through this effort, EMA will add multi-fidelity cable harness modeling capabilities to the EMA3D Cable product such that analysts can use the same tool from the very early conceptual stages of an aircraft all the way through final testing and certification.

Additive manufacturing (AM) processes such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) have received a great deal of attention due to their unique capability in producing parts with complex geometries. However, a major challenge limiting the application of LPBF today is the high variability in the quality of finished components. To address this challenge, HIDENN-AI, LLC and Northwestern University (NU) propose to establish a simulation-guided machine-learning (ML) based feedback control approach to additive manufacturing of metallic aerospace components based on Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). The project goal is accomplished by building a data-driven machine learning digital twin (ML-DT) framework that integrates real-time experimental data collection/process control with machine-learning-based process modeling and optimization. This integration is critical as it bridges the gap between high-fidelity physics-based models that are known to be computationally expensive and real-time process control and optimization. Seven technical tasks are proposed in this program for the Phase I base and optional period: Task 1: Calibration and validation of an existing physics-based computational model for LPBF process (Phase I Base for HIDENN-AI, LLC) Task 2: Development of machine learning based digital twin for online monitoring and process control (Phase I Base for HIDENN-AI, LLC) Task 3: Integration of feedback control model with the hardware platform of LPBF process (Phase I Base for NU) Task 4: Demonstration of the feasibility of the developed ML-DT for process optimization through LPBF experiment of simple AlSi10Mg Aluminum coupons (Phase I Base for NU) Task 5: Phase II demonstration plan for complex geometry with select materials and Phase II proposal preparation (Phase I Base for HIDENN-AI, LLC and NU) Task 6: Develop a framework of Convolution Hierarchical Deep Neural Network (C-HiDeNN) to significantly enhance the capabilities of the DT and demonstrate the capability for modeling part-scale LPBF process (Phase I option for HIDENN-AI, LLC) Task 7: Extension of ML-DT based control of additive manufacturing process to other process conditions (Phase I option for NU) The key deliverables of the Phase I project will be a software tool and its demonstration for real-time control of the laser power signal to control the Lack of Fusion (LOF) porosity and surface roughness in LPBF processing of AlSi10Mg material system. Future Phase II efforts will be directed towards the extension of the ML-DT based control system to manufacture complex geometry with varied AM materials and improving the predictive capability of the high-fidelity solver using the novel Convolution Hierarchical Deep Neural Network.
Digital Twin-based Machine Control for Laser Powder Bed Fusion of Metallic Aerospace Components

An autonomous domain control system for US Navy surface ships that deconflicts, decomposes, and triages tasks in Hull, Mechanical, & Electrical (HM&E) control systems may reduce operator burden related to the monitoring, operation, troubleshooting, and recovery of HM&E systems.  A domain control system in operation that can automatically adapt to novel environments from actual experience operating in these situations may improve long-term operations and sustainment of Navy surface combatants. However, for domain control systems to autonomously perform well under significant uncertainties in the system and environment for extended periods of time, the system must be able to learn and compensate for both internal and external changes in a trustworthy manner without significant external intervention.  The Artificial Intelligence Based Ship Domain Autonomous Controller effort will address several key challenges necessary to confidently employ artificial intelligence for the operation of several interconnected systems necessary to meet the mission objectives of the ship.  These challenges include but are not limited to the sufficiency of the sensor and signal data available on the ship, the rules of engagement between the human operator and the supervisory control system, and the trustworthiness of the commands and action from the artificial intelligence-based algorithms as they adapt to the changing environment.  Cardinal Engineering and Applied Simulation Technologies will apply proven tools and techniques to solve these challenges and demonstrate the solutions in a proof-of-concept demonstration. The products and processes resulting from the Artificial Intelligence Based Ship Domain Autonomous Controller effort will demonstrate applicability and scalability to a more capable supervisory control system for US Navy ships, as well as for uses in other markets requiring improved safety, security, and operational effectiveness, such as industrial controls systems, self-driving automobiles, robotics, and other such control-intensive fields.

NAVSEA 04, through the National Center for Manufacturing Services (NCMS), has issued a Phase III SBIR contract to Boston Engineering to advance a commercial above water hull vacuum-hold traversing technology (Vacuum Crawler) developed by International Climbing Machines (ICM). Boston Engineering is under contract to redesign a commercial robotic system with components appropriate for defense applications, including addressing ruggedization, design for manufacturing, cybersecurity, and system certification. Boston Engineering previously conceptually designed a means to convert the above water crawler to operate underwater as part of the execution of SBIR N161-044 to develop Maritime Ultraviolet Antifouling (MUVA) capability. Therefore, we have shown how use one system could be designed to operate above and below water with minimum configuration changes. A system is proposed that will have over 50% of its design leverageable for this program (N231-031), including open architecture software, electronics, and user interface. Advances for the proposed underwater variant will include packaging design appropriate for underwater operation, specific navigation capability for boat and ship hulls, and the automation required to deliver the desired cavitation jetting to remove biofouling. An advantage of vacuum- or suction-hold is the ability to operate on non-ferrous surfaces, such as SHT: Anechoic coating. The envisioned robotic delivery technology uses compliant tracks enabling the ability to traverse non-smooth surfaces and most protrusions typical on the hull surface, including slopes (e.g., conformal arrays) and ridges. Fine positioning features of a robotic arm are compared with simpler but equally effective set of controlled, fixed nozzles on the front of the delivery system.

Verification for deep neural networks and learning-enabled autonomous systems is critical for the safe deployment of artificial intelligence in the wild. Although significant efforts have been made in academia and industry with rigorous techniques and tools developed in this area, several grand challenges still need to be addressed for the applicability and usage of state-of-the-art techniques in real-world applications. optoXense is teaming with University of Nebraska - Lincoln to propose solutions for five key challenges in both open-loop and closed-loop verification, including 1) scalability, conservativeness, memory, and timing performance, 2) quantitative real-time verification, 3) intuitive user-friendly interface, and ROS-integrability, 4) handling temporal time-dependent properties, and 5) all-in-one demand. In Phase I, we aim to develop basic front-end and selected back-end features of the proposed tool to demonstrate feasibility. Dr. Tran of UNL has been developing the NNV (Neural Network Verification) framework for Deep Neural Networks and Learning-enabled CPS (Cited in N231-061 topic reference no. 9). The NNV tool is gaining great attention from industry and academia. It has been used for the DARPA Assured Autonomy project and is currently partially supported by Toyota Research and NSF. This proposal aims to improve on NNV by eliminating dependency on proprietary software. We aspire to deliver a tool that could become the dominant platform for neural network verification. This aspiration could be realized by a flexible architecture that could be extended by a community of fellow researchers and developers.

Store certification is an important step to integrate new weapons and aircraft into the Navy and Marine Corps. The store certification process ensures that stores can be safely separated from aircraft in flight and develops a flight envelope of the conditions required for safe separation. Certifying stores requires proper model development and simulation which is then validated through flight testing. Flight testing is the most expensive part of the certification process and is ideally just a validation of simulated store separation events. If the flight test reveals new information or shows that the store is unable to separate safely, the store may need to be redesigned which will add time and expense to the process. Thus an effective software tool that can accurately simulate store separation events is a critical component needed to quickly and affordably certify stores.        We propose the creation of a software system that uses 6DOF equations-of-motion and data from test and simulation events to quickly simulate, visualize, and assess the safety of store trajectories during separation for fixed wing and possibly rotary wing aircraft. Our approach will focus on creating a high performance, user friendly, cross platform solution that will focus on a matrix and quaternion approach that is able to utilize multithreading and GPU acceleration to provide significant speed increases over traditional approaches. Our approach will include relevant interpolation schemes as well which may include Hermite interpolation, cubic splines, or a moving-average method that can adapt between interpolation and regression depending on the form of the weighting function.  We also propose spending significant time defining the requirements of the system and creating a system design with SysML diagrams. This approach will allow for faster development and a system that is modular, well documented, maintainable, and extensible.

Air-launch weapon system store separation dynamics need to be fully characterized to ensure safety and weapon controllability during the separation phase. The current 6-DOF store separation used by the NAVAIRÆs Store Separation Branch is NAVSEP. As a legacy FORTRAN-based tool, NAVSEP lacks commercial-grade software development, documentation, support, and upkeep, nor can it take full advantage of modern computational capabilities or easily integrate into modern workflows. These limitations on have made it difficult for store separation design teams to keep pace with the advancement in complexity of air-launch weapons systems and aircraft platforms. SpaceWorks proposes to develop a new weapons separation toolset using state-of-the-art computer program methods and software utilities as a replacement to NAVSEP. This toolset will be based in a modern programming language and built from the ground up to take advantage of todayÆs multithreaded high performance computing architectures, and to be integrated into modern automation environments for batch execution and MDAO design studies. This new toolset will be a commercial-grade software product with thorough documentation, ongoing maintenance, and technical support. It will be cross-platform compatible with modern versions of Windows, Mac OS, and RedHat Linux, and would include a visualization tool built in Unreal Engine 5. To develop this new toolset, SpaceWorks will leverage its company background and expertise in store separation analysis and commercial software development. From 2019-2020, under the X-60A development program, SpaceWorks performed the store separation assessment required by the Air Force SEEK EAGLE Office for certification of the X-60A rocket vehicle carriage and release from the Gulfstream G-III aircraft, including the development of a custom 6-DOF trajectory toolset capable of modeling X-60AÆs unique flight profile and handling high-fidelity multibody aerodynamics databases. From 2015-2020, SpaceWorks developed QuickShot under SBIR sponsorship into a fully capable 3-DOF trajectory optimization software suite. SpaceWorks now has over 15 active customers of QuickShot across DOD, NASA, aerospace prime contractors, and commercial space/startup sectors. During the Phase I base activity, SpaceWorks proposes to create proof-of-concept software executables for (1) a 6-DOF equation-of-motion solver demonstrating store dynamics propagation; (2) a miss distance calculator demonstrating two-body geometry proximity calculations based on CAD geometry files; and (3) a visualization tool in Unreal Engine 5 demonstrating integration of CAD geometry files, animation of store separation, and user interface capabilities. SpaceWorks will also use these executables to evaluate execution time for complex problems and on high-performance computing architectures. Finally, SpaceWorks will plan a development roadmap for the prototype software package to be developed under the Phase II SBIR effort.

Recent demonstration of hypersonic missiles by American adversaries poses a significant threat to the US. These missiles can evade early warning systems since they cruise at a lower altitude, are highly maneuverable, travel over five times the speed of sound, and have a very low radar cross section. In the past few years there has been increasing interest in developing new EO/IR sensors to detect such missiles.  Due to their high velocity, they develop a hot plasma around them, with the nose cone and leading edges often becoming hotter than 1500C. Such hot surfaces provide a good thermal signature providing opportunity for novel EO/IR sensors to be developed.  Hypersonic missile early detection requires a highly sensitive wide area EO/IR sensor, identification requires a high resolution sensor, and tracking requires very low latency readout. Having all these features in a single imaging sensor is very difficult. For example, a large format 2K x 2K SWIR or MWIR infrared focalplane array imaging at rates required for tracking (20KHz frame rate) would dissipate over 200W of power, while traditional cooling methods can only handle focalplane arrays with at most a few watts of power dissipation. Moreover, such a FPA will produce 80 billion pixel/second data rate that cannot be handled by contemporary processors to detect and track the missile. SAAZ has been developing neuromorphic event-based readout EO/IR sensor technology that alleviates the above issues, offering the following advantages: In pixel detection of temporal contrast to reduce processing load  Asynchronous readout reduces data rate while maintaining very low latency for tracking  Increase probability of detection Reduce false alarm rate Sensor and processor compatibility enhancement Efficient Algorithms Optimized band  Radiation hardened ROIC and electronics suitable for space The ongoing developments offer a good foundation for starting the work on this Navy SBIR. Under this SBIR SAAZ proposes to add the use case to detect and track a hypersonic missile in its glide phase to terminal phase transition, as follows: To study the phenomenology of the glide phase and the terminal phase, especially developing a radiometric model for the transition between these phases  To develop a model that compares the performance by using a single EO/IR band with respect to several bands provide cost-benefit analysis  Conduct preliminary design of an optimal event driven neuromorphic sensor for the intended use case Develop a plan for sensor demonstration (field test) under phase II and develop a productization strategy to transition the technology to a program of record  The proposed multi EO/IR sensor event-based neuromorphic technology with embedded AI algorithms will greatly enhance Navy’s capabilities in protecting platforms against hypersonic missile threats.
SHOT - Sensor for Hypersonic Object Tracking

CrowdAI specializes in AI/ML for automated target recognition (ATR) on full motion video (FMV). With years of DOD past performance in this mission space (DON, JAIC, MAVEN, USAF), CrowdAI will develop an end-to-end computer vision (CV) system for DON aerial platforms. It will ingest and process video, identify targets, and serve video snippets to onboard sensor operators with automated alerts to their multi-function displays. CrowdAI was the first to develop segmentation models on FMV, and today’s advanced ATR models can detect and identify surface contacts in video. Snippets will be compressed automatically, reducing onboard storage and facilitating immediate backhaul via TCDL. The final system will run in the background and support multiple DON missions. CrowdAI intends to work with Pixspan, the unparalleled expert in lossless compression, to develop the full solution. We will design a representative system that includes an ATR model, a snippet export tool, and the functionality to receive, compress, forward media using the fastest possible upload. For fine-tuning, the system will also include a feedback mechanism to augment training data in CrowdAI’s no-code CV software.  We will add demonstrable improvements to real-time CV analysis and the onboard curation, efficient download, and rapid backhaul of high-resolution data. Our software supports intuitive review and retraining of CV at the tactical edge, providing an end-to-end system that not only continuously improves, but is serviceable by DON personnel without any training in data science or AI/ML. Developed from TRL-9 commercial technologies, DON will be able operate this system with its existing workforce without additional personnel. The system will act as a force multiplier, relieving analytic burden on operators to pursue more advanced tasks.   In the face of a constrained compute environment, the project will investigate the feasibility of dynamic reallocation of GPU/CPU resources to prioritize specific processes. That is, ATR for threat detection may require real-time (sub-second) processing, while search and rescue can accept processing every second. The ability to adjust compute allocation will ensure that more creew needs are met. We will interview stakeholders to identify other features beneficial to their missions for development. As experts in our respective fields, we have the technologies and workforce to rapidly develop and implement this solution while exceeding expectations. CrowdAI is actively providing trusted AI/ML for FMV to both the DON and U.S. Air Force. While this mission set and the unique compute environment are novel, both aspects of this project are squarely within our respective areas of expertise.  Lastly, for an interim project to bridge Phase I and Phase 2, CrowdAI suggests the curation of video data from the DON operations platform and to begin labeling data. This process can add significant lead time to a project. Generally, it is low cost, but high impact.

Singularity-Intelligence Amplified, LLC (Singularity-IA) proposes the development of a multi-perspective hierarchical Centralized Fault Monitoring System (CFMS).  We plan to pursue a Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) by dividing the CFMS functionality into three portions: data import, data storage, and visualization.  We plan to develop each of these functions as separate modules, allowing them to plug into other future systems. Crew members have different training and roles to perform on a ship like the Constellation Class Frigate.  Therefore, our approach to visualization recognizes that different roles might require different methods for visualizing the current situation.  We identify these perspectives as: functional, regional, and system-level.  Essentially, this allows crew members to be presented a perspective and receive information structured within the context of their role on the ship. This accelerates their ability to absorb information. Modeling and simulation, using the Modelica modeling language, allows us to leverage our expertise to develop models of the ship and its important systems, subsystems, and components.  We can use these models to seed fault conditions and run simulations to generate data resembling current data acquisition systems that the ship may use.  This allows us to create a significant number of different fault scenarios, of varying levels of complexity, to provide a strong foundation for testing and analysis of our proposed solution. Adding the modeling and simulation capabilities allows us to leverage some of our existing technologies in the Fault Management (FM) space, which provides an interesting path forward.  Instead of just monitoring fault conditions, we can leverage the data acquired by a monitoring system, process it with a virtual cognitive ability using digital twin models, and leverage corrective action abilities to support autonomous real-time active fault management. The phase I project goal is to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and tease out the requirements for future development and implementation of a Centralized Fault Monitoring capability that incorporates advancements in human & machine cognitive interfacing to yield faster and more effective fault management in adverse, multi-failure conditions.

The US Navy requires unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) and combatants which are affordable, reliable, fuel efficient, and proven hull forms. Procuring commercially available hull designs provide a cost effective means of achieve this. However, commercially available platforms are typically not designed for fuel efficient operations over broad operational speed ranges required for military vessels; i.e., lower transit speed, endurance range speed, and higher sustained sprint speed. The speed time profile for a USV will vary highly between peace time and war time operations, making broad range fuel efficiency more critical. Existing passive Hydrodynamic Hull Appendages (HHA) have demonstrated the ability to reduce hull resistance and vertical accelerations, and thereby, improve fuel efficiency and vessel motions. The benefits of passive HHA are optimized for the operating speed of the vessel and not to provide a consistent benefit across a broad range of Froude numbers (0.15 – 0.75). A reliable, wide-range HHA is required to enable commercially available hull designs to provide affordable, reliable, fuel-efficient capability. To achieve this the HHA will have to be actively controlled to optimize efficiency across a large speed range. Development of a reliable, wide-range HHA will better enable a modified Commercial Off the Shelf (COTS) hull-form to meet USV and combatant operational requirements, improving the autonomous systems endurance, persistence, and reliability. The development targets hulls 150’-400’ in length. Innovation is required to develop an advanced HHA that provides fuel savings across a wide range of Froude numbers and provides reliable operation with minimal maintenance. Additionally, the HHA must be readily integrated into an existing hull form, such that it does not require significant modification of existing commercial hull forms. The advanced HHA will target a minimum 5-10% fuel efficiency benefit across a wide operational speed range and shall target a total acquisition and integration cost of less than $750K per unit to provide a Return On Investment (ROI) within 1-2 years. The number of units required is dependent on how broadly the technology can be applied; for planning purposes ~10-20 units would be required over a 10-year period. The advanced HHA’s performance will be assessed against the power delivered ratio for a hull form without an HHA as compared to a hull form with an HHA. The HHA shall be designed for (a) a 25-year service life, (b) fail safe operation, (c) 80% reliability, and (d) preventative maintenance requirements of no more than once per year. A reliability assessment shall be completed to assess the whole system’s reliability, broken down by subsystems and components, to validate improvements relative to current systems.

NAVAIR has created a custom process for managing model-based definition (MBD) parts, linking manufacturing and inspection data to the part model using the Quality Information Framework (QIF) Standard. However, this workflow has three capability gaps that need to be addressed: 1- criticality-based guard banding (CBGB), 2- measurement uncertainty quantification (MUQ) for non-contact articulating arms (NCAA), and 3- optimizing inspection planning to reduce the time and cost of inspecting parts based on their criticality. Global Technology Connection (GTC), in collaboration with the University of Georgia (UGA) and Metrologic Group (MG), is proposing the development of a model-based enterprise workflow (MBEW) that aligns with the QIF MBD. In Phase I, the objective is to address the above mentioned three categories and demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed workflow in a laboratory setting. Furthermore, as part of the Phase I Option, the team will work on the interoperability of the proposed tool chain, alignment with the relevant standards, improvement of the selected ML model in Phase I Base, and integration of the developed software into the MBD tools. In Phase II, the team will improve the new proposed process workflow (MBEW) for the organic industrial base by building upon Phase I solutions. This workflow will integrate with existing manufacturing practices, minimizing deployment challenges. It includes repackaging and deploying the workflow directly on Navy databases. Operations will be integrated into a Digital Enterprise Tool and the workflow will be demonstrated and validated using real Navy data in a prototype manufacturing environment. The team proposes the integration of QIF Model-Based Quality Workflow with the criticality assessment of a product within a MBEW. The innovations of the proposed solution are listed below: Modeling the criticality of a product using FMECA (Failure mode, effects, and criticality analysis) in a unified architecture framework (UAF), and subsequently defining an acceptable level of PoF (probability of failure) for that product Performing an uncertainty-back-propagation from stress level to the geometries and defining a CBGB based on the new acceptable PoF for each measure and Using Bayesian Inference and machine learning (ML) to quantify MU of NCAA Optimizing scanning path and configurations to achieve expected measurement quality considering the feature criticality and measurement uncertainty. Demonstrating feasibility of the proposed solution in a lab environment

Identifying and tracking developing threats across a large and growing set of data sources remains a critical unsolved problem. Currently, multi-modal data (images, video, audio clips, satellite images, etc.) as well as OSINT data (social media platforms like Twitter, Telegram, etc.) must be manually inspected by an analyst to extract relevant metadata, such as ōwhoö, ōwhatö, ōwhereö, ōwhenö, and ōwhyö. Subsequent correlation across multiple modalities, required to identify and track developing threats in operational domains, is also a manual process. Recent advances in computer vision, machine learning (ML), and natural language processing (NLP) technology have resulted in the creation of innovative algorithms capable of assisting an analyst in understanding, cataloging, and characterizing multi-modal content automatically. However, these advances have seen limited application to defense and intelligence problems. Vision Systems Inc. (VSI) with support from STR proposes TALON, an innovative multi-INT analysis framework designed to generate information-rich metadata across multi-INT data streams and use the context provided by this metadata to detect emerging threats. In Phase I, TALON leveraged advances in ML and NLP to discover events from publicly available social media and online sources and produce flexible and semantically rich natural-language descriptions of associated multi-modal data. The proposed SBIR Phase II program will build on Phase I results, enhancing and expanding metadata generation capabilities, analyzing metadata using the latest in state-of-the-art NLP systems such as Large Language Models (LLMs) models, and considering operational data sources of interest to potential stakeholders across the defense and intelligence community. The VSI and STR team is uniquely suited to this project, offering unparalleled expertise in machine learning, natural language processing, and remote sensing; extensive experience in the development of innovative software solutions for challenging defense and intelligence problems; and a thorough understanding of the needs of image analysts across the defense and intelligence community.
TALON: Multi-INT Metadata Extraction for Threat Detection

Textured piezoceramics’ recent expanded commercial availability in wide range of size, quantity, and form factor as well as the successful demonstrations poised to ignite strong further interest in their integration into undersea acoustic systems as to significantly improve operational capabilities.  As is now known, textured ceramic materials have electromechanical properties between those of conventional PZT and relaxor PMN-PT single crystals with large advantages over both.  Textured piezoceramics show ability to increase source level and improve sensitivity; their larger bandwidth relative to PZT for a specific design and form factor opens new design space for acoustic systems as it can enhance both the probability of target detection (i.e., ability to detect quieter enemy submarines), enable longer operational life of power source limited systems (i.e., expendable sensors), and extend target detection ranges in physical volume limited applications by enabling lower frequency transducer designs in a smaller form factor. Because of the combined gains in key metrics, Textured ceramics emerge as an alternative transduction material filling the gap between legacy PZT and Single Crystal. Despite the growing interest and successful demonstrations, there remain key obstacles towards a widescale market acceptance in terms of production capacity, yield, and comparable purchase costs to legacy PZT materials. These limitations represent a critical risk to transition into major high volume Navy applications, specifically in expendable systems where transduction materials are required to be high volume manufacturable without shape and size limitation with high yield and at comparable costs and consistency to PZT equivalents. The identified manufacturing issues are rooted in non-standard textured piezoceramic specific processing steps (i.e., template, slurry, wet forming, and BBO) that are not part of a PZT production causing yield issues. This program will focus on addressing these yield, throughput and cost issues as to enable textured piezoceramic parts approach the baseline cost and availability of standard piezoceramic parts in use by US Navy.

The NAVY seeks an active machine learning database to guide the development of polymer matrix resins and composites that meet metrics for time to ignition, maximum heat release rate, and smoke density from a cone calorimeter. The current fire evaluation and certification of composite materials to be used for naval vessels are heavily reliant on tests such as cone calorimeter and TGA tests. Due to the strong thermo-chemo-mechanical interactions on material fire behavior, there is no reliable physics-driven relation between the chemical structure of a resin / additives and the fire performance of its associated composite materials. The presence of limited test data and the high cost in generation of material test data have prevented the development of a machine learning (ML) model to predict the flammability index parameters of a given resin for use in optimizing the design and selection of a resin to achieve the desired fire requirements. To address these challenges and bridge the existing technology gap, Global Engineering and Materials, Inc. (GEM) and its team members proposed to develop a multiscale machine learning (ML) database and a data-driven platform to predict the flammability index parameters for polymer matrix resins from their chemical structures. In this database framework, physics-based digital twins, data-driven models, and machine learning models are combined to generate a machine learning database that relates the chemical structure to the cone calorimeter data. Actual data from the literature will be augmented with synthetic data generated from a digital twin of a cone calorimeter with input based on the chemical structure and a data-driven model. A machine learning model will then be developed to accelerate the discovery of new polymer systems to more rapidly expand the database and allow for inverse design of polymers based on desired flammability index parameters. In Phase I, the research team will demonstrate the capability of the developed ML database using existing test data, generated synthetic data, and new polymer data to predict fire performance based on chemical structure and inverse design for identifying chemical structure based on desired fire performance.

The military currently employs small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for a range of critical operations. These UAVs play a crucial role in surveillance, reconnaissance, target acquisition, and intelligence gathering. They provide real-time situational awareness, support tactical decision-making, and aid in force protection. However, current limitations of small UAVs include limited flight duration, restricted payload capacity, and dependency on external power sources or frequent battery changes, which can hamper their operational effectiveness. Structural batteries offer a potential solution to these limitations by integrating energy storage functionality directly into the load-bearing structures of UAVs. By reducing weight and increasing energy storage capacity, structural batteries can significantly extend flight times, enhance payload capacity, and improve overall mission capabilities. Ā This proposal aims to address the solicitation for novel multifunctional materials and lightweight structures through the development of a structural battery. Our approach includes three key components: Ā Development of a mechanically strong gel-electrolyte with excellent conductivity. We will focus on creating an electrolyte that provides structural rigidity but also enables efficient ion transport. Ā Utilization of carbon fiber as both the anode material and current collector. By incorporating carbon fiber, we can enhance the structural integrity of the battery while also benefiting from its exceptional electrical properties. Ā Development of a high-capacity LMR-NMC cathode with superior cycling stability. Our focus will be on formulating and optimizing a cathode material that offers increased energy storage capabilities and robust mechanical properties. Ā During Phase I, Lynntech will focus on conducting a proof-of-concept demonstration to validate the feasibility of the proposed concept. This will entail synthesizing the necessary battery materials, performing laboratory bench testing, and utilizing computer modeling analysis. In Phase II, we will refine the concept by fabricating and evaluating prototype parts. These prototypes will undergo rigorous testing in simulated or realistic environments. The weight reduction targets will be identified and addressed to optimize the structural battery design. Additionally, the risks, roadblocks, and challenges associated with full-rate production will be identified and addressed. Ā The proposed structural battery aims to achieve a weight that is comparable to or even smaller than commercially used batteries, all while delivering similar or improved electrochemical performance. Moreover, it will serve as a mechanically robust component integrated within the structure, thereby freeing up valuable space currently occupied by conventional batteries.

Electroplating is a popular method for applying a variety of coatings, including Zn-Ni, to metal substrates. However, these coatings can suffer from hydrogen embrittlement and residual stress, which can negatively impact fatigue strength. To better understand these issues, Technical Data Analysis Inc. (TDA) and the University of Cincinnati have joined forces in an STTR effort to develop a cutting-edge computational framework that uses multi-physics and multi-scale models. By applying these techniques, we can gain insight into the microstructure and properties of the coatings and the mechanisms behind hydrogen embrittlement and residual stress.  During Phase II, TDA will focus its efforts on Developing an electroplating CAE software (EP-Software) to assist in improving the production quality and performance of Zn-Ni electroplated components - The software will help in the specific design and optimization of parts to be plated, anodes, shields (masking), and tank configuration. Investigating mechanisms, modeling, and experimental testing of Zn-Ni electroplating process- Here we focus on two aspects: (a) origins of residual stress from the effects of lattice mismatch and of formation of high-pressure gas, (b) quantifying the residual stress at the interface and through the substrate thickness. Developing concept for digital twin for electroplating process - TDA will conduct initial studies towards the development smart tank and digital twin technology. To create a virtual testbed, we will develop a plan for sensors and other monitoring devices to collect data on various parameters such as temperature, pH level, current density, and plating time. This data can then be fed into a digital twin model which would simulate the electroplating process in real-time. This effort is more towards building a framework and plan for future work and initiatives.  The above efforts lead to the assessment of coating quality for consistency and uniformity, and prediction the impact of defects, residual stress, hydrogen ingress, and the environment on the fatigue strength of high strength steel (HSS) aerospace components. Key investigations of the approach include: 1) the development of an electro-chemo-mechanical electroplating simulation using multi-physics and multi-scale models; 2) the creation of an electroplating CAE tool for Zn-Ni coating; and 3) the performance of critical sets of experiments to validate the electroplating simulation module and identify plating defects' types and causes. The framework will allow engineers to reliably predict electrochemical and mechanical behavior and suggest design parameters to optimize the electroplating process for aerospace components, eliminating the need for multiple experimental trials.
Novel Multiphysics Modeling of Electroplating Process for Metallic Aerospace Components

Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR) personnel must approve operations of aircraft for developmental test, operational test, and fleet service. With respect to handling qualities, piloted vehicle specifications have evolved over decades with significant investments in the development of validated requirements that have been verified and validated through extensive flight test campaigns. For UAS applications, the following issues are a concern to NAVAIR because analogous handling qualities specifications do not exist: over-constraint on the design due to application of manned requirements, existing specifications include considerations for pilots that are no longer in the vehicle, new UAS specific missions are not considered in the piloted specification, and supporting toolsets do not exist to examine the above. To address the needs of the UAS community at NAVAIR and throughout the Department of Defense as outlined above, a team led by Systems Technology, Inc. (STI) has developed the UAS-HQ process that features a draft specification including means of compliance test methods (and a software toolbox that supports the analysis of collected test data against the proposed specification requirements). The process begins with UAS classification. Because of the wide variety of UAS types and vehicle size there cannot be a one-size-fits-all set of requirements. Given an appropriate classification, a mission can be broken down into mission task elements or MTEs. Missions are then broken down into specific task elements that include those elements that will be a part of any mission or are mission specific. These MTEs are used to identify specific criteria that predict handling qualities analytically, test demonstration maneuvers, and the means of compliance that verify handling qualities in flight. Initial work in this area conducted by the STI team as part of a Phase II SBIR conducted for NASA Langley Research Center focused on the small UAS that will operate commercially at altitudes below 400 feet. NAVAIR followed with a Direct to Phase II issued the STI team as a discretionary award to adapt this technology for current and future UAS of interest to the Navy and more generally the Department of Defense. The keys to maturing the specification and the accompanying software tools are data and validated assessment guidance. The proposed project below will therefore mature the UAS-HQ SBIR technology through the verification and validation of the emerging specification using existing data sets from current Navy UAS and the collection of new databases using helicopter in-flight simulators that will serve as UAS surrogates. Additional data will be sought through enhanced partnerships with UAS OEMs through simulation studies or companion flight test activities. Further, the proposed work will introduce necessary scaling techniques and updated guidance on system identification methods for autonomous UAS.

U.S. Navy (USN) Command and Control (C2) systems provide not only situational awareness but increasingly are the source for off-hull targeting data in long-range fires scenarios. As a result, USN C2 software has some unique challenges. First, Navy C2 interacts with safety critical systems. Any mistaken cross-interaction would have deadly consequences including the potential for blue-on-blue fatalities. Second, to support long-range fires in a Distributed Maritime Operations (DMO) environment shipboard C2 systems need to “harvest” and correlate on-board weapons and combat system status information for distribution to the Fleet-Level Maritime Operations Center (MOC). This data must be updated and correlated at a rate adequate to support remote engagement and targeting decisions. Additionally, the increasing use of Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) in C2 systems will require that this data is properly correlated, distributed, and rapidly accessed. IDT’s use of its ATRT suite of technologies will enable rapid assessment of C2 system data inputs, data transmission performance metrics, and metrics needed for kill-chain analytics. This proposal describes a mechanism to address these unique challenges and enable USN C2 to accelerate deployment of capability without sacrificing the rigorous analysis needed for long-range fires.

Currently the Department of the Navy (DON) and broader Department of Defense (DoD) do not have an effective aerial delivery method for small resupply items like food, ammunition, and medical supplies. The Navy relies on large-scale aerial delivery from CH-53E, MV-22B, and MH-60S aircraft. These aircraft require extensive logistical support and coordination, have large radar and audible signatures and are vulnerable to enemy fire putting air crews and supplies at risk. The Navy is seeking novel solutions to refuel, rearm, resupply, repair, and revive distributed naval forces down to the last tactical mile. Distributed forces will lack ground delivery options due to rough terrain and enemy activity. To achieve this end, DON recognizes a Research, Development, Testing, and Evaluation (RDT&E) opportunity with TeamSense AI to provide an autonomous system that can perform diverse aerial expeditionary resupply missions at a cost that is considered attritable in contested environments. Here, TeamSense AI proposes to enhance our modular aerial autonomy system and integrate capabilities on the HoverCrane heavy-lift small unmanned aerial system (sUAS) as a tactical aerial resupply tool for contested logistics operations. During this proposed project, TeamSense will perform the following RDT&E on the HoverCrane platform and demonstrate: Automated onboard drop and landing location selection for ship and shore destinations.Ā Automated mission path planning to reduce probability of interception/detection. Enroute autonomous obstacle detection and avoidance, including confined landing and drop sites. The combination of advanced onboard autonomy and a low cost cargo sUAS delivers the following benefits: Increased Autonomy/Trusted AI: Advanced autonomous aerial cargo shifts responsibility for planning, monitoring, and executing resupply missions from human crew and operators to onboard decision making systems. Appropriate sensors combined with artificial intelligence algorithms can perform tasks such as alternative PNT and identifying drop/landing locations with high reliability, freeing crew for other tasks.Ā Covert Attritable Resupply: Aerial autonomy provides an option to remove manned aviators from hazardous missions in challenging conditions. This inherently reduces risk to aircrew by providing an alternative option for critical resupply in situations where pilot risk assessment is deemed marginal. Small advanced UAS do not require continuous C2 links and are less likely than manned aircraft to be detected or intercepted enroute. Increasing the expected rate of completed resupply tasks.Ā Availability and Response Time: Lower cost, relatively small size and reduced system complexity allows for assets to be positioned at ground locations in close proximity to requested missions. This avoids transit time to and from fixed air bases, lowers inspection/maintenance levels and hastens mission briefings. Significantly reducing time to station and cycle time.

ATA Engineering, Inc. (ATA), in collaboration with the National Institute for Aviation Research, proposes a project to advance VIVA (Volume Image-based Virtualization for Allowables), a software toolkit that provides physics-based prediction of multiscale in-situ effective mechanical properties of as-built laminated composites based on numerical reconstruction of X-ray computed tomography (XCT) data. The toolkit takes a multistage digital twin approach to automated property generation, starting with advanced rule-based and data-driven machine-learning (ML)-based image segmentation techniques to generate multiscale subsurface geometric models from input XCT data. These models include laminate structure features (such as ply waviness, orientation, interfaces, and drops) and critical defects and/or damage (such as ply wrinkles, voids, and resin-rich regions). These features and defects are reflected in multi-fidelity finite element (FE) models created by the software, forming a set of multiscale as-built representative volume element (RVE) models. Virtual characterization of the RVEs produces a coherent relationship between the material scales that is ultimately propagated through the component scale as a set of local mesoscale and global macroscale in-situ, nonlinear, anisotropic effective mechanical properties that are output as user-defined material databases encompassing various hygrothermal conditions enabling informed static/dynamic stress, fatigue, and progressive damage analyses. The proposed effort builds upon the Phase I project, which demonstrated feasibility of the approach and produced a software prototype capable of automating the generation of nonlinear, anisotropic mechanical properties for as-built composite structures, including defect effects. The Phase II project will extend the applicability and robustness of VIVA and assess its modeling and predictive accuracy through a verification and validation (V&V) test program. In particular, algorithms will be extended for fast automated XCT image processing, feature extraction, identification/classification, and uncertainty quantification (UQ) with uncertainty-aware ML techniques, as well as scalable data storage/retrieval/management. A key outcome will be generation of localized FE meshes from XCT scan data, capturing ply orientations and manufacturing defects. The integrated VIVA toolkit will be exercised to predict the in-situ effective mechanical properties for representative thick laminate composite structural components exhibiting defects. Experimental mechanical testing and characterization will be conducted to confirm the accuracy of VIVA predictions through comparison with physical data. Once software development and V&V tasks are completed, VIVA will provide an efficient, scalable, and accurate physics-based simulation capability that will enable more confident and cost-effective decision-making for repair limits and disposition of non-conforming composite components.
VIVA: A Software Toolkit for Automated Multiscale In-Situ Effective Mechanical Property Prediction from Computed Tomography of As-Built Composites

Recent advancements in Machine Learning and Computer Vision (ML/CV) have demonstrated the ability to both enhance existing Naval systems and enable entirely new capabilities that would have been impossible with traditional methods. While this period of rapid advancement is exciting, the opaqueness and brittleness of ML methods, specifically deep-neural networks (DNNs), make it difficult to reconcile with traditional system and software airworthiness verification procedures and has prevented their widespread adoption within the Navy and DoD despite their excellent performance. To expedite adoption and equip our soldiers with the best performing tools available, there is a need to establish methods to guide system developers trained in traditional airworthiness through the process of selecting, implementing, testing, and verifying the performance and safety of ML/CV methods onto existing and emerging platforms. System designers must also be equipped with reliable methods of predicting and mitigating failures of ML methods prior to their deployment and effective real-time checks to monitor component and system level performance while systems are in operation. To address these concerns, La Jolla Logic (LJL) and Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) propose the Soteria Toolbox; a collection of ML capabilities and complementary methods for verifying ML/CV performance and mitigating risks and uncertainties. Team LJL combines LJL’s experience developing a wide range of ML models and user interfaces and their capabilities for developing complex software systems with SNC’s vast expertise in a wide range of safety and mission critical applications. SNC is an industry leader in both landing systems and aerial docking as well as multi-sensor fusion, ISR, and air platform integration. As an example, SNC provided the guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) for the first aerial refueling exercise and, more recently, implemented the GNC for DARPA Gremlins providing aerial recovery of UAS in flight. This effort will combine SNC’s experience with LJL’s expertise in AI/ML to develop a collection of ML/CV models that will enhance the performance of fielded systems with supporting tools to ensure they are operationally safe and adoptable by traditional system developers. As the primary focus of this effort, the operational safety and verification components will focus on methods that both verify the individual ML/CV components and aid in developing system level effects and mitigations. This will leverage both recent advancements in ML verification and traditional statistical and outlier rejection techniques. LJL’s expertise will be leveraged to curate selected models and capabilities to achieve the optimal performance with SNC’s experience developing complex safety critical systems. The team will ensure that the developed Soteria Toolbox and its curated models are accessible to engineers who work on these systems and that the verification and mitigations processes.

Elemental Coatings is developing the next generation of anti-icing and frost protection for applications in aerospace, energy infrastructure, industrial applications, and transportation. Heat exchangers, which are common pieces of equipment in a number of applications, must properly manage frost buildup in order to function correctly. Frost negatively impacts heat exchanger efficiency, and thus reductions in frost can lead to significant efficiency improvements and increased uptime. In aircraft, many of these issues are even more difficult to manage, due to the volumes of air involved, the substantial temperature differentials that exist in flight environments, and high air velocities. As a result, a frost-minimizing coating for this application needs to demonstrate several key properties: (1) ability to limit condensed droplets from freezing in the first place, (2) for those droplets that do freeze, the ability to quickly shed those ice crystals, (3) high thermal conductivity (to preserve heat exchanger efficiency), (4) ability to survive the challenging environmental conditions, (5) ability to evenly and cost-effectively coat complicated geometries.  To date, passive anti-icing and anti-frosting coatings have been researched by a number of academic groups and companies. Elemental Coatings has a strong, multi-year history in developing such coatings, and we believe that we currently have the most proven anti-icing coating in the world. It has already flown on a UAV as part of a NASA mission, and it is currently deployed on operational wind turbines in North America. These coatings are very effective at limiting the total extent of ice buildup, which is of course important, but they are not developed to the point where they eliminate ice and/or frost buildup altogether. Building off Elemental Coatings’ deep expertise around anti-icing coatings, this Phase I effort will explore a novel concept for anti-frosting coatings that entirely or almost entirely prevent frost formation. Specifically, we will create hybrid coatings with glycol-absorbing elements that simultaneously reduce the number of potential nucleation sites for ice crystals, lower the effective freezing temperature of water, allow water to quickly shed the surface (high hydrophobicity), and reduce the strength of ice adhesion to the surface. The base portion of the award will involve a fast-paced examination of multiple candidate formulations, and the option phase will then involve a deeper dive into the chosen approach to characterize all critical properties of the coating and demonstrate its technical viability as an effective anti-frosting coating for aircraft heat exchangers.
Novel Polymeric Coating to Minimize Frost Buildup on Critical Components

Etegent will achieve Navy 3D polarization requirements using polarimetric imagery and existing SfP algorithms. Etegent will address ocean surface-based collection scenarios where targets of interest are non-cooperative. Etegent will focus on SfP for detecting ships a few meters on a side, beyond one km, and at the horizon. Phase I work will demonstrate the ability to estimate target shape from polarimetric imagery using SfP techniques. The system will enable improved DRI of small maritime targets at ranges beyond one kilometer: distinguish non-background objects, separate maritime targets of interest and non-targets, and categorize maritime targets. Improved detection helps answer which objects in the image are manmade such as buoys, floating trash, and maritime vessels and which are natural environment such as sea, sky, and clouds. Improved recognition helps answer which non-background objects are maritime targets of interest, such as boats. Improved identification helps answer which targets of interest are adversarial and which are not threats. The Etegent team will collect data of RC model boats and real boats on lakes. Candidate collection sites are a few hours drive from the laboratory facility amd advantageous for controlling times of day and weather conditions. Lake collections can be conducted from land looking out to sea. Lake collections allow increasing range beyond one kilometer and view targets located at the water-horizon boundary. For example, lake freighters have lengths up to 1000 feet and beams of 100 feet, corresponding to a range of 43.5 km scaled to the nominal target at one kilometer. Lake ferries provide another collection opportunity. The ferries are 90 feet long with beams of 40 feet, and at 3.9 km equivalently scales to a nominal target at one kilometer. The lake ferries and freighters allow Etegent to evaluate SfP performance as a function of air path transmission and Rayleigh scattering and depolarization while maintaining a meaningful number of pixels on target.  The DoLP and Fresnel equations are used to estimate zenith angle. However, zenith ambiguity exists, with a value on each side of the Brewster angle, when using specular reflection relationship. Two polarimetric spectral bands disambiguate the specular zenith ambiguity, relying on radiometrically calibrated and well registered band images. Alternatively for monochromatic cameras, the diffuse relationship can be used, which is monotonic and lacks zenith ambiguity. The refractive index of the reflecting surface must be known to solve for zenith angle. Etegent will use normal reflection measurements and engineering tables to determine refractive index for the articles under test. The azimuth angle is inferred from AoP, however there is azimuthal ambiguity; the number of possible values equals the number of polarization filters used to generate AoP. The Etegent team will use published strategies to determine specular and diffuse contributions and resolve ambiguity.
Single-View Polarimetric Long-Range Maritime Target Shape Recovery

The Navy seeks an ability to sustain superconductor operating temperatures for extended periods in the absence of active cryocooling. The Navy is currently developing small, unmanned, magnetic mine-sweeping vehicles that employ superconducting magnets, and one simple approach to minimize the vehicle size, weight, and power is to employ a solid-state heat absorption system that keeps the superconducting magnet system cold and operating for several hours after it is disconnected from a ship-based cryocooler. Navy ships are also transitioning to superconducting systems for power distribution and degaussing, and cryocoolers maintain the cryogenic temperatures required for superconductor operation. When cryocooler electrical power is lost or interrupted for more than a brief period (such as during power source transfer), these systems begin warming to temperatures at which the superconductors no longer function. When power is restored, the superconducting systems must be re-cooled to restore functionality, resulting in additional time without full power distribution capability. In a prior Phase I SBIR project, Creare showed the feasibility of our solid-state heat-absorbing technology for sustaining superconductor operating temperatures for up to several hours in the absence of active cooling. Our technology is dimensionally stable during thermal cycling and efficient in terms of added size and weight. In this proposed Phase II Base project, Creare will advance the technology designs and performance estimates and then produce and test a sub-scale heat absorption assembly. The test results will confirm the technologyÆs effectiveness and further tune and validate our performance models. In the proposed Phase II Option, Creare will design and produce an operational prototype heat absorption system for the NavyÆs magnetic mine-sweeping application and deliver it to the Navy for testing with a superconducting solenoid system.

For the first time in thirty years, we must contend with a near-peer adversary that is intent on making space a warfighting domain. To meet this challenge, the Navy is developing new beyond line-of-sight (BLOS) communications systems that are far more resilient to adversarial action. To fully realize the potential of these new systems, however, the Navy must also modernize the Automated Digital Network System (ADNS). ADNS manages IP network traffic between Navy afloat units and the shore. Several shortcomings of the Navy’s current approach to Quality of Service (QoS) management in ADNS can be identified. First, a common static policy is applied to all data traffic from each subnet. Second, strong bandwidth guarantees are not provided, only percentages of link rate. Finally, there is a single set of policies applied to every surface ship in the fleet, regardless of its role and regardless of its mission. In this SBIR, Caliola will develop a network orchestration tool that generates dynamic, mission tailored ADNS configurations which ensure traffic priorities are aligned with the Commander’s Intent while respecting BLOS bandwidth allocations. We call our tool AssuredConductor. Prior to a mission, AssuredConductor uses combinatorial optimization and network emulation to plan ADNS configurations. During a mission, reinforcement learning is used to change those configurations in response to an evolving threat environment, an evolving Commander’s Intent, or evolving traffic requirements. In Phase I, we will demonstrate key components of the AssuredConductor architecture. In Phase II, we will develop and demonstrate a Technology Readiness Level 6 prototype of AssuredConductor that builds on the software architecture and human machine interface constructs of WAMPS. WAMPS is the mission planner for the Wideband Anti-jam Modem System (WAMS) that we are building for PMW/A 170.

With advances in applying random finite set theory to tracking, along with increases in computational power, it is now possible to incorporate the multi-target nature of the multi-static air anti-submarine warfare (ASW) sonar tracking problem into the solution as well. Probability Hypothesis Density filtering will be used for track initiation and track maintenance and will jointly estimate target and clutter intensity. Multiple Hypothesis Tracking will be used for track state estimation and association. This approach allows for the use of the strong points of each algorithm to create a tracker which can better achieve performance necessary for the warfighter than either technology alone.

Rotorcraft turboshaft engines within the Navy and DoD fleet are frequently exposed to harsh environments, particularly during takeoff and landing, which contribute to degraded engine health.   Existing modeling approaches of engine health are highly sensitive to the operational conditions on which they are trained while individual models have varying degrees of accuracy for a given set of operating conditions.  To circumvent these shortcomings CFD Research has identified the integrated multimodel scheme proposed here. CFD Research, in collaboration with University of South Carolina, will address each challenge encountered during this effort through the development of Data-Driven Monitoring and Maintenance (D2M2) engine software, with a focus on Navy-relevant engine platforms.  A prototype ensemble of predictive models for remaining useful life will be defined during Phase I by leveraging benchmark datasets of simulated engine health to be generated by the NASA C-MAPSS code. The accuracies and inaccuracies of the individual models will be improved through a graph-based hybrid approach capable of autonomously deciding which models are most trustworthy for a given set of operating conditions. Uncertainty quantification and model justification techniques will also be investigated. Additional health monitoring metrics such as anomaly detection and fault prediction will be explored during the Phase I Option and beyond.  D2M2 capabilities for any Navy provided dataset will also be investigated thereby demonstrating the broad applicability of D2M2. A fully functional prototype of D2M2, including graphical user interface with continuous model refinement through a robust data acquisition and active learning pipeline will be developed by the end of Phase II.

Method Security proposes adapting and extending its commercial product for the purpose of automated attack path enumeration and hardening in the support of Department of the Navy’s (DON) missions. Method Security builds autonomous security robots that can conduct the work of expert security engineers, pen testers, and red teamers 24/7. The outcome is an enumeration of every attack path and automatic hardening within your security stack. All of this happens within your rules of engagement. Method Security deploys on-prem, in the cloud, at the edge, or fully air gapped to protect the most critical environments and mission systems. This proposed Phase 1 Technical Effort involves taking the Method Security product that has already developed, and conceptually adapting and extending it to  DON-specific connectivity-disadvantaged tactical environments, DON-specific data signals, and DON security objectives. Cyber attacks are about to undergo a great acceleration primarily due to advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI). In the same way that AI developer co-pilots have democratized better coding skills to more novice developers, AI will do the same for hackers. Soon thereafter, malware and other cyber weapons will become partially or completely autonomous. This presents a challenge for Defensive Cyber Operations (DCO) in commercial, government, and military environments alike. Traditional security tooling that is often slow, non-interoperable, and requires significant human operator expertise, already can’t keep up with traditional threats, and stands incapable of a more capable adversary. These more capable adversaries will easily throttle between sophisticated attack techniques vs. trivial attack techniques and fast drive by operations vs. low-and-slow operations. DCO has to outmatch this new adversary, and to do that new autonomous defensive cyber solutions are needed that can predict, preempt, and identify threats at machine-speed. In tactical environments, where data may be unique, the bandwidth is Denied, Degraded, Intermittent, or Limited (DDIL), and compute is constrained, even greater challenges are faced for DCO. The luxury of clean environments and abundance of processing resources is thrown out, forcing operations at the tactical edge to be smarter and self-sufficient. Nation State attackers know of this capability gap at the edge, and will seek to exploit these weaknesses until superior DCO capability at the edge is deployed. We propose building a technical conceptual architecture to deploy Method Security’s autonomous defensive cyber product in DON’s tactical environments to enable a multi-stage forensics approach to cyber event analysis and investigation, with the goal of rapidly predicting and preempting threats. This effort would involve a conceptual software architecture to command and control multiple instances of Method Security in edge environments, and multiple scoped security workflows to be automated in a production environment.
Trusted Autonomous Cyber Robots for Multi-Stage Cyber Attack Investigation
