The plasma sheath around hypersonic vehicles prevents radio communication, telemetry, and Global Positioning System (GPS) signal reception and makes it impossible to use electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) imaging sensors for navigation as well. Thus, to address the Navy’s need for a navigation system that can provide precise navigation for the entire flight trajectory of a hypersonic vehicle operating in GPS-degraded/denied environments, Intellisense Systems, Inc., (Intellisense) proposes to develop an innovative, completely autonomous and closed Hypersonic Vehicle Intelligent Alternative Navigation (HYVIAN) system providing drift-free GPS-accu

The plasma sheath around hypersonic vehicles prevents radio communication, telemetry, and Global Positioning System (GPS) signal reception and makes it impossible to use electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) imaging sensors for navigation as well. Thus, to address the Navy’s need for a navigation system that can provide precise navigation for the entire flight trajectory of a hypersonic vehicle operating in GPS-degraded/denied environments, Intellisense Systems, Inc., (Intellisense) proposes to develop an innovative, completely autonomous and closed Hypersonic Vehicle Intelligent Alternative Navigation (HYVIAN) system providing drift-free GPS-accurate (<5 m (<15 ft) of circular error probability) positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) of hypersonic vehicles without GPS at all, along the whole trajectory, including its terminal phase, as specified by the Navy. Specifically, innovations in HYVIAN are based on precise local measurements of gradients of geophysical fields (which penetrate through plasma sheaths, unlike GPS and other radio signals) along the hypersonic vehicle’s trajectory and projection of measurements on precise geophysical field maps using a Bayesian nonlinear filter algorithm. HYVIAN is reinforced by artificial intelligence/machine learning algorithms to significantly increase the accuracy of PNT output. Finally, HYVIAN provides GPS-accurate longitude, latitude, altitude, heading, and precise attitude (roll, pitch, yaw with accuracy ~1 arcmin) of the hypersonic vehicle with a frequency of 1000 Hz, delivering GPS-compatible output signals. The proposed HYVIAN uses commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) sensors only, and satisfies the size, weight, and power constraint because it uses microelectromechanical system sensors and fiber-optic gyros. In Phase I, Intellisense will develop HYVIAN system concept solutions for use in hypersonic vehicles and establish  HYVIAN to meet the Navy’s requirements. We will perform modeling and simulation and preliminary experimental demonstration of a HYVIAN that will meet the required navigation success metrics in the hypersonic vehicle terminal phase. Simulations will be run in three different Navy scenarios to verify the effectiveness of HYVIAN. We will develop an initial prototype design to be implemented in Phase II. All hardware and software requirements will be defined. In Phase II, Intellisense plans to develop a HYVIAN prototype and evaluate, test, and validate the system’s feasibility to meet Navy objectives. The final test and evaluation of HYVIAN will be carried out under relevant operating conditions as close to hypersonic flight conditions as possible.

Triton Systems, Inc. plans to create a secure digital twin-based system for distributed additive manufacturing (AM) to ensure trusted, authenticated, and intellectual property (IP)-protected production of high-quality metallic structural parts.  AM has the potential to demonstrate great utility in both low-rate production as well as in the manufacturing of just-in-time part generation at the point of need. The security of files and transmissions can lead to vulnerabilities in terms of data integrity, cybersecurity, and quality control. All additive manufacturing (AM) methods will require strong cyber-security. Triton aims to expand the securely available AM routes to the Department of the Navy (DoN) while allowing for the fabrication of larger parts through the use of digital twins for in-situ fabrication monitoring. This will be coupled with Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) to enable real-time quality control/assurance of the part build. The digital twin combined with AI/ML will enable comparative analysis of the part design file with the printed file to detect part tampering during a cyber-attack.Triton is collaborating with an esteemed academic partner who is an accomplished researcher in the field of secure cyber-physical additive manufacturing. This partner has made significant contributions through wide-ranging publications in the areas of cyber-attacks, IP protection, and side-channels for additive manufacturing. Additionally, Triton is working with a large corporation to enhance the cybersecurity of their commercial product lifecycle management (PLM) software suite. The goal of this collaboration is to develop a digitally engineered twin and digital thread that meets the stringent demands of the Department of the Navy.

Abstract and Benefits SummaryAbstractThe evolution of radio frequency (RF) systems has been integral to military communications, intelligence, and operations since their inception in the early 20th century. As RF technology has advanced, so has the volume and complexity of the data these systems generate. Modern military operations must contend with voluminous RF data streams, presenting significant challenges in identifying which signals warrant immediate action or storage. This summary explores the historical context of RF use in the military, outlines the current challenges, and presents a proposal for intelligent signal processing to enhance decision-making and operational efficiency.RF technology has been a cornerstone of military communication since World War I, providing crucial links for coordination and intelligence. In World War II, RF systems became more sophisticated, enabling radar and secure communications. The Cold War era saw further advancements with the development of satellite communications and electronic warfare capabilities. Despite these technological leaps, the fundamental problem of managing and interpreting large volumes of RF data has persisted. During a recent military exercise, a task force was overwhelmed by the sheer amount of RF signals intercepted, leading to delays and missed opportunities in critical decision-making.Today’s military RF systems generate data at unprecedented rates due to the proliferation of advanced sensors, communication devices, and electronic warfare systems. This deluge of data presents two primary challenges: Signal Prioritization: Identifying which RF signals are critical and require immediate action versus those that can be deprioritized or ignored.Data Storage: Efficiently storing relevant signals for future analysis without overwhelming storage capabilities.These challenges are exacerbated by limited processing resources and the need for rapid, accurate decision-making in dynamic operational environments.Context Aware Processing Optimization (CAPO) addresses these challenges through an intelligent allocation of processing assets and a decision agent designed to maximize the utility of RF streams. By leveraging advanced algorithms and machine learning, our system can dynamically prioritize and manage RF data, ensuring that the most critical signals are processed and acted upon promptly.Our solution leverages advanced computing, integrated sensing, and trusted AI/ML and autonomy to provide a self-learning, context-aware pre-processing system.  MTRI will leverage their Multi Armed Bandit (MAB) approach to determine the most relevant signals of interest to be tasked on the hardware.  DornerWorks will implement the AI/ML algorithm on the most appropriate hardware based on evaluation to maximize the throughput and speed of the system.
Context Aware Processing Optimization

Barron Associates, Inc. (Barron) proposes to develop and commercialize the Assurance for Uncertain Systems via Robust Estimation (ASSURE) system. The solution focuses on utilizing existing sensors to estimate aircraft states in real time while in-flight, which could lower the number of redundant sensors, lower the likelihood of mission abort, and/or increase pilot situational awareness. By addressing this goal, a system could increase the safety of existing aircraft that have redundancy while also enabling operation of smaller and cost-constrained aircraft that may not possess redundant systems. Such aircraft may not have high-fidelity models typically found in modern commercial aircraft but lower-fidelity approximates with increased uncertainty. ASSURE addresses these situations with a novel estimation scheme based on a generalized polynomial chaos Kalman filter (gPC-KF) that explicitly accounts for uncertainties and noise with arbitrary distributions in nonlinear systems. The gPC-KF utilizes a similar predictor-corrector form found in the Kalman filter but represents the system response using probabilistic machine learning gPC methods. The gPC-KF is not constrained to assumptions of linearity, or weak nonlinearity, and additive Gaussian noise found in the family of Kalman filter estimators. In most realworld systems, these assumptions are violated to a greater or lesser degree, requiring tuning to achieve satisfactory performance which may reduce robustness and filter stability. The gPC approach is not hindered by these assumptions and enables accurate modeling of complex nonlinear, or linear, systems with mixed uncertainty and noise distributions to a defined-level of accuracy. There are numerous applications targeting military and commercial markets, including piloted aircraft, remotely-piloted and UAS aircraft, AAM applications, sUAS used for package delivery, inspection, wildlife monitoring, or counter-UAS. ASSURE is applicable to dynamical systems such as ground and marine vehicles.

Our proposal aims to develop a GigE-Vision-compliant event-based camera (EBC) system that leverages commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components to address the critical need for standardization in capturing and processing dynamic scenes. Event-based cameras operate fundamentally differently from traditional frame-based cameras by detecting changes in the scene asynchronously, closely mimicking biological vision systems such as the human eye. This technology offers significant advantages in terms of high temporal resolution and reduced data redundancy, making it ideal for applications in autonomous vehicles, robotics, surveillance, and defense. Despite these advantages, the lack of standardized interfaces for EBCs has hindered their broader adoption and integration into existing systems. Our proposed solution involves developing both the hardware and software interfaces necessary to ensure compatibility with existing machine vision standards, specifically GigE-Vision and GenICam/GenTL. The project will utilize 10 Gigabit Ethernet (10GigE) technology to facilitate high-speed data transmission and configuration of the EBC. The hardware design will include a small form factor and an intermediary FPGA, similar to the specifications of an AMD Kintex-7, to handle data processing and interface with the 10GigE system. Additionally, the system will feature integrated digital-to-analog converters (DACs) for sensor component biases and an external GPIO interface for synchronization and timing. The software interface will be designed to comply with the Motion Imagery Standards Board (MISB) requirements and ensure low latency operation. Phase I of the project will focus on developing concepts and schematics for the electrical and mechanical components, as well as a block diagram of the software package. Feasibility will be demonstrated through material testing and analytical modeling. Phase II will involve developing and evaluating a prototype to ensure it meets the performance goals and Navy requirements, including cybersecurity and system security planning. The ultimate goal is to transition this technology to practical use in government facilities, with potential applications in manufacturing and other industrial settings within the Department of Defense. By standardizing the interface and utilizing COTS components, this project will unlock the full potential of EBC technology, facilitating its adoption and integration, and ultimately enhancing the capabilities of the warfighter and other defense applications. This effort aligns with the modernization priorities in microelectronics, space technology, and trusted AI and autonomy, and promises to significantly advance the field of machine vision and automated data processing. As part of our commitment to advancing this technology, we will engage with industry stakeholders and end-users throughout the development process to ensure that the final product meets the practical needs and expectations of the market.

Aptima, Inc. and PatchPlus Consulting plan to address the Navy’s problem of defending current and future autonomous aerial systems against counter-counter measures by building a large language model (LLM)-driven development agent named STAR (System for Threat Analysis and Response) that will function to not only generate a taxonomy of the attack surface, but also form a full, future-adapting test suite for AI developers through specialized agents. The Department of Defense (DoD) is accelerating the development of autonomous vehicle sys-tems for complex air combat missions, highlighting the need to identify and mitigate potential vulnerabilities. SSCI proposes the Autonomy Vulnerability Analysis using System Taxonomy (AVAST) framework to address this critical requirement for the Navy. AVAST aims to develop a comprehensive ontology of vulnerabilities within autonomous systems, utilizing Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and expert insights to identify and analyze threats. This frame-work will assess risk levels, pinpoint attack vectors, and create both exploitation and mitigation strategies, providing a combinatorial view of system vulnerabilities that consider the interac-tions and dependencies between different components.In Phase I, AVAST will focus on creating a detailed model of the autonomous system, identify-ing vulnerabilities through Model-Based Vulnerability Analysis (MBVA). This includes em-ploying threat modeling, attack trees, and simulation-based security modeling. The approach will integrate digital twin and digital thread development, ensuring a thorough traceability of vulnerabilities across the system's lifecycle. Combinatorial optimization techniques will be used to discover complex attack sequences, leveraging tools like OptaPlanner to convert MBSE ob-jects into constraint satisfaction problems. The results will be documented and presented in both human-readable and computer-readable formats, facilitating comprehensive stakeholder under-standing and automated cybersecurity analysis.Looking ahead, Phase II will shift to red-team analysis, exploiting the identified vulnerabilities to understand potential attack sequences and their impact. SSCI will integrate MBSE with simu-lation tools to model these sequences accurately, employing a hypergame approach to simulate adaptive tactics and countermeasures. This phase will provide critical insights into the weak-nesses of autonomous systems, enabling the development of robust defensive strategies. The AVAST framework's systematic and innovative approach will enhance the resilience and effec-tiveness of autonomous vehicle systems in complex combat environments, ultimately strength-ening the Navy's operational capabilities.

Weather forecasting is undergoing a paradigm shift, moving from physics-based numerical modeling to data-driven solutions using artificial intelligence. Physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems have been used operationally for decades, providing valuable forecasts across spatial and temporal scales for countless applications. While undeniably useful, the technical capabilities of physics-based NWP systems have plateaued due to a combination of factors, including algorithmic limitations, parameter sensitivity, computational resources, and scientific understanding of complex processes. These technical limitations directly lead to lower-resolution forecasts with less than optimal predictive accuracy. In contrast, recent advances in machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) have highlighted new capabilities for more efficient forecasting systems by emulating physics-based systems. The next step in this transition is replacing the dependence on physics-based data assimilation with observation-to-observation AI forecasting. While the advances in MLWP cannot be ignored, the current generation is dependent on reanalysis and physics-based data assimilation systems. The availability of ERA5 and other reanalysis datasets has enabled the machine learning community to develop powerful forecasting models with novel methodologies. This has created a dependence on analysis data from physics-based data assimilation systems, which contain their own uncertainties and are computationally expensive, causing infrequent update cycles.ÝThis project extends our development of EarthNet to generate medium-range forecasts from a pure AI observation-driven system. EarthNet is a multi-modal foundation model that ingests heterogeneous and sparse Earth data from all types of sensing systems. The model learns through masked modeling, where data is randomly removed with a reconstruction training objective. This approach natively handles sparse and missing data, making masked modeling ideal for gap-filling remote sensing data. We have demonstrated EarthNet's ability to reconstruct atmospheric temperature and humidity from geostationary satellites and low-Earth orbit microwave soundings. Here, we will extend our data pipelines with surface observations, radiosondes, and more satellite data to perform forecasting. Once trained on a larger dataset, EarthNet is capable of performing zero-shot forecasting autoregressively, along with fine-tuning for further performance. We will also experiment with initializing open-source MLWP models. EarthNet also has strong scaling capabilities, which indicate that reconstruction and forecast performance will improve with data, compute, and model size.

The U.S. Navy's plan to expand its surface fleet with Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) will need abilities to function autonomously for extended periods.  Specifically, the heart of the operation, the diesel engine(s), will need special attention for providing maintenance tasks, identifying issues, and even making repairs.  The technology for providing such extended duration operations without humans-in-the-loop requires a fusion of proven reliable hardware and cutting-edge learning and training models for the system ability to autonomously identify, act, and even repair systems on and around the onboard engine. Journey Robotics, in partnership with Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, Blue Water Autonomy, and RPM Industries, presents the Shipboard Technology for Engine Work, Autonomous Repair, and Diagnostics (STEWARD) system. STEWARD is an advanced robotic solution designed to enhance USV operational reliability through predictive maintenance and autonomous repairs. The system integrates machine learning (ML), computer vision, and a digital twin framework to monitor engine performance, detect anomalies, and execute maintenance tasks that are critical for long-duration missions without human presence. A key innovation is STEWARD’s physics-enabled digital twin, which enables real-time monitoring and predictive maintenance. Using reinforcement learning-based manipulation planning, the system autonomously inspects, diagnoses, and resolves engine-related issues. The digital twin also allows for offboard system training, enabling operators to refine ML models remotely for new autonomous repair behaviors.STEWARD features an onboard robotic arm with cameras, torque sensors, and specialized tools for inspections and repairs in confined shipboard environments. The robot operates within a gantry system for precise movement, ensuring accessibility to critical engine components. A robust sensor suite, including thermal and borescope cameras, helps detect leaks, cracks, and wear. The system follows a "Human ON the Loop" approach, where operators validate corrective actions rather than directly controlling robotic movements. If a scenario exceeds the system's capabilities, the operator can guide a solution via the digital twin and train the model using human demonstrations, enhancing adaptability over time. Phase I focuses on refining STEWARD’s design, integrating digital twin technology, and developing an initial proof-of-concept system for a Medium Unmanned Surface Vehicle (MUSV) equipped with a Caterpillar C18 Genset module. Testing in a simulated maritime environment will validate its resilience to shock and vibration. By enabling autonomous engine maintenance, STEWARD enhances the Navy’s ability to sustain long-duration, unmanned operations, ensuring mission success with minimal human intervention. Journey Robotics and its partners are committed to pioneering this transformative technology, shaping the future of autonomous maritime operations.

This compact and highly sensitive oxygen sensor technology will be compatible with operation in fuel tanks and in aircraft environments, directly addressing the Navy requirements. In Phase II, Intellisense will refine the system design based on the Phase I results and build an on-aircraft prototype of this new oxygen sensor, conduct testing in a fuel tank environment, verify the system size, power, and interface requirements, and demonstrate the sensor’s performance in a representative fuel tank. The successful Phase II development will lead to a calibrated and environmentally tested fuel tank oxygen sensor reaching technology readiness level 5 (TRL-5) and leading to a final sensor design that is ready for flight testing in Phase III.

Boundary layer transition (BLT) can be an important aspect of hypersonic vehicle performance as it strongly impacts aerodynamic performance and thermal management considerations. Transition to turbulence significantly increases heating rates and drag forces and limits the effectiveness of hypersonic vehicle performance.The proposed work aims to advance the capabilities required by the DoN for viscous flow analysis of next-generation hypersonic vehicles, with an emphasis on laminar baseflow simulations and boundary layer transition (BLT) which includes accurate heat flux prediction, thermo-chemical non-equilibrium (TCNE) flows, fluid-ablation interactions (FAI), and the handling of complex vehicle geometries. The Whoosh team proposes to advance its hybrid computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver, the CHAMPS+ NBS-Cart solver, which has already been successfully ported to GPU platforms. The use of modern GPU hardware combined with specialized simulation codes can provide an order of magnitude reduction in computational resources required for these computations. The Phase I objectives include the evaluation and development of an optimized implicit solver, further validation of the GPU solver for laminar baseflow simulations on a range of blunt and non-blunt geometries, and the demonstration of transition prediction capabilities. Validation will then continue on various low- and high-temperature ablation problems and the application of these tools to complex test cases such as HIFiRe-5b, HyTRV, the High-Speed Army Reference Vehicle (HARV) and various other flight vehicle geometries. This proposal addresses topic areas 1 (Artificial Intelligence) and 3 (Cybersecurity).Building on SIFT's experience in cyber-aware Large Language Models (LLMs) and automated planning of cyber attack campaigns, we propose to develop Joint AI-Cyber/EMSO Knowledge System (JACKS) to address three key challenges required to achieve the envisioned Human-AI partnered workflows for Offensive Cyber Operations (OCO):Building scalable OCO planning models: Symbolic AI planning has been used in small, academic-scale demonstrations of planning for cyber operations. Scaling that approach up to realistic environments faces a knowledge-acquisition problem: how to create and maintain symbolic models of all the available sensors and their possible values, actions and their preconditions and postconditions, and goals that might be desired. JACKS will use fine-tuned LLMs to automatically translate the knowledge that is already available in CVE reports, threat intelligence feeds, and other data sources into the AI planning models required to automatically plan OCO campaigns. JACKS will use active experimentation to establish confidence that these planning models are accurate.Creating sound and diverse OCO plans: LLMs alone are not capable of reliably planning OCO campaigns. For example, they can hallucinate actions that do not exist, and they can make fundamental errors in logical and causal reasoning. Furthermore, military operations frequently require planning diverse, alternative courses of action to provide commanders with choices and backups. JACKS will use diverse symbolic AI planning methods to reliably create logical, sound plans that meet an operator's needs, incorporating rules of engagement and other constraints.Helping human operators develop OCO campaigns: Cyber plans, especially those built by automation, can be complex and difficult to understand. JACKS will use LLMs to help with this problem as well, providing a Natural Language interface that can accept goals and constraints from the human operator, explain resulting plans, and implement an operator's requests for revisions, all while keeping in mind prior conversations and context.JACKS will help humans plan OCO campaigns, using LLMs for scalable knowledge acquisition and natural language tasking and interaction.

There is a global trend in submarine proliferation. This poses a threat to U.S. maritime strategy and naval operations. To address this Navy need, Intellisense Systems, Inc. (Intellisense) proposes to develop a new low-cost Tier 1 Sonobuoy Launched Aerial Vehicle for Anti-Submarine Warfare (SLAVA) system. This innovative unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) integrates a magnetic anomaly detector (MAD) and an ultralow frequency (ULF) sonobuoy. The UAV is designed to fit within a standard A-size sonobuoy launch container (SLC). After it is launched from the P-8A’s sonobuoy launcher system, the UAV wings are unfolded to produce lift and function as the flight control surfaces. It follows a set of pre-programmed waypoints and flight paths to collect MAD data in the area of uncertainty. The onboard processor processes the data in real-time to identify anomaly components measured by the MAD and with the compensation of data disturbance by the UAV maneuvers. If the analyzed data detects a strong anomaly that indicates a target presence, the UAV will transition to autonomous target tracking to collect additional MAD data for target classification. If the target identification confidence is high, the ULF sonobuoy can be deployed to assist in target tracking. The acoustic data is uploaded to the UAV to be analyzed by the processor. Utilizing a swarm of such UAVs and exchanging data among themselves will enable rapid target cued search, detection, localization, tracking, and classification. In Phase I, Intellisense will design the SLAVA to weigh no more than 39 lb and can be launched from A-size SLC. It will have 9 years shelf life, has standard sonobuoy launch envelope, threshold cruise speed and flight time of 70 kts and 70 min, respectively, and operation altitude of 500 ft to 2000 ft. Its radio range exceeds 20 nm line of sight and has a payload volume of greater than 94.4 in.ł. It can operate in -20°C to 50°C and in light rain with 1 nm visibility. Its flight path can be preprogrammed or chosen autonomously based on the target tracking as cued by the MAD. A new sonobuoy will be designed to have >60 min operating time, >200 ft operating depth, and minimum frequency coverage range of 0.01 Hz to 2.5 kHz. Its radio transceiver range is > 20 nm. SLAVA uses a newly available commercial MAD that has dynamic range of ±100 µT on each axis, no dead zones, and an accuracy of 1 nT over the temperature range of -0°C to 50°C and has in-air noise level of <20 pT/rtHz in 0.01 to 100 Hz with a raw heading error of 1 nT. In Phase II, Intellisense will construct the SLAVA prototype and demonstrate its feasibility in a relevant and operation environment. Ruggedized prototypes will be fabricated for a full-system demonstration of the combined MAD and acoustic capabilities on multiple air-launched prototypes from a surrogate platform to demonstrate they can unfold, transition into stable flight, and communicate in swarm configuration to classify and localize targets.

The US Navy operates in diverse and challenging environments where accurate, high-resolution, timely environmental forecasts are critical for mission success. To support the Navy's ability to anticipate and respond to localized environmental phenomena (e.g., tropical cyclone winds and surge effects, coastal winds, aviation visibility, ocean eddies), there is a pressing need for a capability that can generate skillful, near real-time environmental forecasts with horizontal spatial resolution of less than 1 km and vertical resolution on the order of 10 meters, particularly in the atmospheric boundary layer and upper ocean. However, most current-day Numerical Weather Prediction models are computationally too burdensome to achieve such high resolution in the short processing times that the near real-time paradigm necessitates. Furthermore, there is a scarcity of observational data at these fine scales, complicating model validation and hindering the development of reliable high-resolution forecasting tools.ÝATAC and subcontractor NCAR propose this Phase I SBIR work to address these challenges by leveraging several NCAR-developed and non-NCAR cutting-edge machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) techniques that use downscaling, nesting, and other related methods for generating high-resolution, short-to-medium range MLWP forecasts. These techniques include (1) Enhanced Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network-based downscaling, (2) Diffusion-based downscaling, (3) Analog Ensemble-based downscaling, and (4) National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) Super-Resolution for Renewable Energy Resource Data with Climate Change Impacts (Sup3rCC) model. Moreover, we apply existing high-resolution Large Eddy Simulation sets as training datasets for the MLWP models and leverage ATACís big data processing architectures and deep bench of data scientists/analysts to perform expert comparison of the performance of these models and provide summary of strengths/weaknesses of the methods, their operational viability, and relevant metrics. Our Phase I SBIR work rigorously evaluates the above MLWP downscaling techniques and performs a literature survey of other relevant MLWP techniques, identifying their strengths, weaknesses, and best-use scenarios. This comparative analysis combines quantitative metrics (e.g., standard accuracy metrics, spatial coherence metrics, temporal consistency metrics), model explainability analysis (Explainable AI techniques such as Shapely feature importance), robustness testing (using variety of test datasets covering coastal regions, open-ocean environments, etc.), and computational efficiency metrics. This multi-dimensional comparative analysis enables us to determine the most effective approach for near-real time, high-resolution weather forecasting in landfalling tropical cyclone environments, directly addressing the critical need identified in the SBIR problem statement.

The Navy requires relocatable forecasting tools capable of producing high-resolution environmental intelligence at tactically relevant scales, particularly within the atmospheric boundary layer. Current numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, while valuable at mesoscale resolutions, lack the spatial fidelity and vertical resolution needed for forecasting in complex, coastal, or contested environments where phenomena such as sea breezes, low-level jets, and terrain-induced flows can significantly impact mission operations. This proposal aims to demonstrate the technical feasibility of using generative machine learning (ML) to downscale coarse-resolution NWP forecasts (such as HRRR) into high-resolution fine-scale atmospheric fields at 10-100?m horizontal and approximately 10?m vertical resolution. The solution integrates the open-source Sup3r framework, developed by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), with high-fidelity training data generated from Aeris’ in-house GPU-accelerated large-eddy simulation (LES) model, JOULES. Paired JOULES-HRRR datasets enable supervised training of ML models to recover sub-kilometer structure from operational NWP inputs, grounded in physically realistic simulations. Sup3r supports a modular architecture for generative modeling, enabling flexible integration of diverse ML architectures. During Phase I, we will configure and evaluate several candidate models, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), conditional diffusion models, latent diffusion models (LDMs), and flow-based models. These will be assessed for spatial accuracy, boundary-layer fidelity, uncertainty quantification, and inference performance. Sup3r’s compatibility with PyTorch allows rapid iteration across model types and supports multi-variable outputs such as wind, temperature, and humidity. The Phase I effort includes the creation of a representative JOULES-HRRR training dataset for a Navy-relevant littoral domain, adaptation of Sup3r for this domain, and prototyping of a reduced-scale downscaling pipeline focused on a single architecture. A structured comparative analysis will inform model selection for Phase II. All activities are aligned to a Navy use case involving a carrier strike group operating near an island chain, an environment where small-scale environmental effects directly impact forecasting accuracy and mission planning. By enabling fast, relocatable, high-resolution downscaling from operational forecast inputs, this approach directly addresses the Navy’s need for ML-enabled forecasting under the Machine Learning Weather Prediction (MLWP) initiative and broader METOC modernization priorities.

The U.S. Navy seeks the development of an advanced fretting fatigue life prediction tool to address critical gaps in understanding fretting fatigue mechanisms and to enable the evaluation of novel mitigation strategies for metallic aerospace structural components operating under diverse conditions. The U.S. Navy seeks the development of an advanced fretting fatigue life prediction tool to address critical gaps in understanding fretting fatigue mechanisms and to enable the evaluation of novel mitigation strategies for metallic aerospace structural components operating under diverse conditions. Despite numerous test-based studies and the development of empirical models aimed at improving the durability and performance of metallic components under fretting conditions, no consistent correlation has been established between operational parameters and the associated failure mechanisms or fatigue life variability. The inherently complex nature of fretting fatigue—governed by the coupled effects of fretting wear, multiaxial non-proportional loading with steep stress gradients, contact geometry, slip amplitude, coefficient of friction, and loading frequency—poses significant modeling challenges. As a result, a robust, physics-based life prediction approach capable of accurately capturing fretting fatigue behavior across different materials and loading conditions remains elusive. Compounding this challenge is the high uncertainty associated with current test methods, which limits the utility of experimental data for gaining deeper mechanistic insights. To address these challenges, Global Engineering and Materials, Inc. (GEM), in collaboration with its team member, proposes to develop a comprehensive, physics-informed modeling framework supported by a rigorous verification and validation (V&V) plan. The proposed modeling approach will integrate the following key elements: 1. Advanced interface contact modeling to capture stick, partial slip, and gross slip regimes. 2. Evolution of the contact interface including fretting wear as well as debris accumulation and depletion. 3. Degradation of interface properties and accumulation of plastic deformation under cyclic loading. 4. An enhanced multiaxial stress-driven fatigue damage indicator to account for steep stress gradients for accurate fretting fatigue life prediction. In Phase I, the proposed methodology will be demonstrated using representative case studies from the literature to validate the modeling framework. The validated multiphysics modeling tool will then be used to identify alternative operational regimes aimed at reducing the risk of fretting-induced failure. Additionally, a novel and targeted experimental plan will be developed to generate high-quality, low-uncertainty data that will support model validation and further mechanistic understanding, thereby enhancing model fidelity and practical utility.

This project aims to enhance hardware security through advanced logic obfuscation using threshold-voltage-defined (TVD) logic families. Traditional approaches to chip securityósuch as dummy gates, programmable cells, or logic lockingóare increasingly ineffective against reverse engineering, side-channel analysis, and Boolean satisfiability (SAT) attacks. While techniques like look-up tables and finite-state machines provide better protection, they suffer from significant area, power, and delay overheads and remain vulnerable to advanced imaging and machine learning-based attacks.To overcome these limitations, we propose improvements to E-TVD logic, which encodes logic functions using transistors with identical layouts but different threshold voltages. This technique offers strong resistance to imaging, SAT, and side-channel attacks, while maintaining robustness across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variations. Compared to earlier TVD implementations, E-TVD significantly reduces transistor count and power consumption without compromising security.Building on E-TVD, we will develop two advanced variantsóE-TVD+ and E-TVD++óthat offer greater efficiency and expanded resistance to emerging threats such as laser fault injection and transistor self-heating. E-TVD++ will also support limited post-fabrication reprogramming, enabling each chipís logic functions to be dynamically redefined. This feature further complicates reverse engineering and enhances resilience against both physical and electrical probing.These improvements promise to deliver compact, energy-efficient, and highly secure logic suitable for deployment in sensitive systems and advanced commercial applications.

Wargaming exercises are essential to preparing the U.S. Navy for large-scale combat with a near-peer adversary. However, constructing naval wargames means relying on a human-centric approach to predict potential adversary actions. This runs the risk of introducing to wargames human errors, biases, and omissions, potentially distorting the insights and analysis the Navy seeks to glean from wargaming. Thus, it is desirable to utilize AI-based immersive technology (e.g., augmented, virtual, mixed, and/or extended reality) to construct C5ISR environments for wargames. This in turn calls for leveraging generative AI to create time-varying digital content for use in immersive simulations. The effort we propose would contribute a component to the Virtual Sea Shield (VSS) content generation environment for wargame content.The proposed effort focuses on a specific aspect of VSS: generating static 3D assets that represent objects found in real-world images, using text prompts for controllable generation. This capability is a powerful tool in the context of 4D content generation for the naval domain. For example, using text-conditioning, we could ìupgradeî a 3D model of a scene to 4D by leveraging a text source providing updates on scene changes over time. This would enable seamless integration of text-based ISR reports with imagery to assess and simulate the state of the battlefield. Additionally, using image-conditioning, we could extract photorealistic shapes and textures from open-source imagery intelligence, enabling us to ìremixî scenes by recombining them in fresh orientations, resulting in novel situations that enhance the generality and adaptivity of constructed wargames.Any successful approach to the task of extracting models of domain-relevant objects from open-source imagery must utilize the massive amount of available open-source 2D image data while also leveraging components designed specifically for 3D generation (in particular, it must avoid naÔve use of VLMs to generate meshes). The approach must also simultaneously condition on text and images, whereas prior state-of-the-art approaches have conditioned solely on either text (e.g., MeshDiffusion) or images (e.g., ReconFusion).ÝWe present TICGEN, a novel neural architecture for Text-and-Image-Conditioned content GENeration. Inspired by DreamFusion and ReconFusion, the general structure of the proposed architecture is as follows: given images containing a common object, we first extract the relevant pixels from each image and separate these extracted images into sources and targets. We learn a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) conditioned on the sources which faithfully reproduces the targets. This NeRF is regularized via a Diffusion that has been previously trained on internet-scale data. When provided source images as input, the NeRF can be exported to an explicit representation of the object of interest.

Finite Element Method (FEM) is more integral to the engineering process than ever before, Ýthough it remains rooted in the Engineering Software 1.0 paradigm, where users manually specify each step of the computational workflow. This concept aligns with "Software 1.0," as described by Andrej Karpathy (Tesla, OpenAI), in which software behavior is explicitly programmed by humans. Karpathy's "Software 2.0" envisions a shift where users define the overall desired outcomes, and machine learning (ML) algorithms generate the underlying logic automatically. This transition gives rise to Engineering Software 2.0 (ES2.0), where artificial intelligence (AI) and ML are used to automate learning, calibration, and solution processes into engineering workflows, including FEM, removing user bias and many other errors. This ES2.0 vision as an integration of AI/ML into approaches like FEM is supported by leading voices in industry. Stephen Wolfram (Mathematica) suggests combining AI with computational methods as the best approach to advance science, and researchers at Google DeepMind write that AI will enhance, rather than replace, traditional numerical modeling approaches.ÝWe propose an AI-based toolkit grounded in the ES2.0 paradigm and Convolutional FEM (C-FEM), an AI/ML technology developed under Wing Kam Liu at Northwestern University and at HIDENN-AI, LLC. C-FEM can provide instantaneous physics-based solutions to a dense spatial, parametric, and temporal space with AI/ML through automated and optimized mesh generation from geometric input lists (e.g., CAD) and by assessing accuracy impact and providing error mitigation advice via cutting-edge supervised and unsupervised learning techniques.ÝKey capabilities of the proposed C-FEM framework include: (1) Automated, adaptive CAD-to-mesh generationÝvia HiDeNN-FEM, which enables CAD-aware automatic rh-adaptivity for mitigating discretization and geometrical approximation errors; (2) Linear meshes capable of arbitrary polynomial reproducing order with high smoothness, alleviating element formulation errors; (3) Interpretable, adaptive neural network structure with trainable element-wise hyperparameters such as patch size, polynomial order, and activation functions that are optimized via unsupervised and reinforcement learning to minimize modeling errors; (4) Built-in post-processing accuracy as C-FEMís interpolation framework preserves solution fidelityÝwhen the node-wise FEM solutions are interpolated for post-processing; (5) Multiscale coupling viaÝSelf-consistent Clustering Analysis (SCA) enhancing computational efficiency and reducing material modeling errors; and (6) Scalable hardware-accelerated approach by combining ML/AI hardware and software.ÝThis project aims to advance FEM simulation tools for aerospace structures by transforming FEM modeling into an automated, efficient, and accurate AI-driven analysis framework suitable for forward and inverse problems and optimization tasks.Ý

Contemporary military planning is constrained by the time, labor, and subjectivity required to transform unstructured open-source data into actionable Intelligence Preparation of the Battlespace (IPB) products. Frameworks such as the Marine Corps Planning Process (MCPP) and Joint doctrine depend on timely IPB to inform force disposition, adversary intent, and civil-terrain overlays. Prior automation attempts lack doctrinal fidelity, symbolic reasoning, and calibrated trust modelsŚlimiting their utility for real-world mission planning.Blinkly ODIN introduces an AI-native platform that autonomously extracts, evaluates, and synthesizes heterogeneous open-source inputs into machine-readable, doctrinally aligned IPB artifacts. ODIN integrates three core components: (1) a schema-constrained COA-GPT transformer for generating structured IPB products, (2) a symbolic reasoning engine for adversary COA extraction, and (3) a Bayesian trust model for source-level reliability estimation. The system ingests multi-format OSINTŚincluding HTML, PDF, GeoTIFF, and JSONŚand outputs structured adversary orders of battle, civil overlays, and NetCDF mobility grids. Each artifact is annotated with uncertainty scores and cryptographic provenance for mission transparency and downstream validation.On adversarially perturbed OSINT corpora, ODIN achieves ?90% alignment with SME-generated IPB products, ?5% hallucination drift, and ?0.75 correlation between Bayesian trust scores and human-rated source accuracy. COA-GPT produces outputs for 20-document clusters in under 60 seconds. The symbolic planner constructs multistep adversary narratives with spatial and temporal consistency, while the trust engine filters misinformation with ?88% precision. All outputs are compatible with automated post-hoc auditing and doctrinal red-teaming.Phase I will deliver a validated prototype with containerized ingestion, reasoning, and generation modules, a command-line interface, and modular APIs for integration with C2ISR environments. A reproducibility harness, doctrinal testbed of red-teamed planning scenarios, and evaluation protocol mapped to MCPP and IPB Annex C structure will be included. All components will conform to CUI restrictions and DoDI 3000.09, NIST RMF, and DoD AI Assurance guidelines for trusted autonomy.By uniting transformer-based schema generation, symbolic inference, and probabilistic trust modeling, ODIN establishes a secure, scalable, and mission-aligned foundation for IPB automation from open-source intelligence. It directly supports JADC2, expeditionary planning, and contested-domain intelligence fusion under emerging multi-domain operational requirements.

In this research effort, AMT will investigate a replacement for the braking system located on test sleds at the Supersonic Naval Ordnance Research Track (SNORT) at Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake. The current water braking system is based on last-century technology that is characterized by unnecessary complexity and high cost, especially regarding the labor hours spent on repair, calibration and regular maintenance of the system. Regulatory compliance and safety are ongoing concerns of the current setup. The goal of this research is to design a passive eddy current braking system that accomplishes the same results of the current system and fits in the existing allocated spaces, while offering higher reliability, shorter setup time, lower maintenance and lifecycle costs, and minimal calibration setup. The proposed eddy brake uses a magnetic field to induce current within a conducting secondary. The process is completely passive. There is no water, electricity, fuel or coolant required. The eddy currents are induced because of relative motion between the magnets and the conducting secondary. The design is also inherently self-centering. Technical objectives of this Phase I project include computing the braking force resulting from the induced eddy currents for speeds ranging from 1 – 3,000 ft/s; simulating the kinematics of a braking event on a sample mass from several thousand ft/s down to zero; and verifying compliance of the system design to the provided Navy requirements.
Passive Eddy Current Braking System for SNORT

Parry Labs proposes a non-traditional approach to solve the requirements stated in SBIR N201-012, Multi-Octave, High Power Efficiency Electronically Steerable Array (AESA).  The design will employ a novel and disruptive technique in order to meet bandwidth, efficiency and power over the target frequency range of 2 to 4GHz.  Our solution is to combine several amplifier design techniques, the fundamental being a Load-Modulated Balanced Amplifier, or LMBA.  Compared to traditional Doherty, Out-Phasing, class J, or switched mode PA’s, the LMBA offers unique advantages over bandwidth and efficiency.   It employs a simple and cost-effective architecture using many off-the-shelf components.  Using this approach, Parry Labs will demonstrate through end-to-end simulations greater than 50% efficiency for a 2x2 AESA with 40dBm of output power. A Quantum Cascade Laser's (QCL) core material is a series of nanometer scale layers of conduction band barrier and well materials designed to induce lasing electron energy levels. The key design feature of a QCL is the ability to repeat the laser core superlattice design to cascade electrons through the superlattice repetitions by repeated stimulated emission. Such designs are generally carefully created manually by well trained scientists with a strong intuition for quantum behavior and quantum well simulation programs. A method is proposed to design and evaluate superlattice designs by training a neural network to replicate the intuition of the superlattice designer and the quantitative results of the superlattice simulation. Training such a neural network with thousands of example designs and evaluations will allow the network to produce usable QCL superlattice designs without human assistance.

In response to the Navy’s need for an ultra-lightweight electromagnetic interference/electromagnetic pulse shielding material for protecting sensitive electronics/avionics, Triton Systems proposes to develop a conformable graphene-based nanostructured composite material capable of 70 dB shielding effectiveness across the frequency range from 500 MHz to 100 GHz. The proposed shielding material will have an electrical conductivity of at least 3000S/cm and a weight of 10% that of an equivalent performance aluminum shield. The selected graphene-based nanocomposite fabrication process is readily scalable and suitable for producing large area articles at low manufacturing cost. During Phase I, Triton will design, build and test the nanocomposite shielding material systems to meet the performance requirements stated above. We will develop and optimize nanocomposite shielding materials and fabrication methods using laboratory test samples. Triton will fabricate shielding materials of at least 6” x 6” in size and validate shielding performances across the frequency ranges from 500 MHz to 100 GHz by an independent test laboratory. In Phase I Option, we will further optimize shielding material structures and fabrication procedures, including effective electrical contacts and ground planes.  In Phase II, Triton will demonstrate and validate the shielding performance of a three-dimensional enclosure prototype of dimensions of 12” x 24” x 6”. Reliability testing of the prototype enclosure will be done in accordance with MIL-STD 810 and other required Standards.
Ultra-Lightweight Protection Shielding Material Against Electromagnetic Interference/Electromagnetic Pulse for Avionics

During the successful Phase I program, Systems & Processes Engineering Corporation (SPEC) demonstrated, through modeling, the potential to significantly increase transmission through a hypersonic plasma layer by utilizing a combination of novel approaches.  Current drones use large 24 to 30 inch high gain Ku band antennas, which cannot be used on hypersonic vehicles.  Instead, our proposed baseline antenna design uses a phased array composed of transmit and receive patch elements separated into rows along the outside of the vehicles body.  Plasma electrons are forced into “rivulets” with low electron concentrations along the antenna rows interspersed by rows of high electron/ion concentration.  The DC magnetic field and RF clearing field then form a resonate structure in the plasma, which is maintained along the flow direction length of the antenna. The proposed Phase II technical effort builds upon the comprehensive modeling, analysis and trades studies conducted in Phase I to experimentally demonstrate prototype performance in a high enthalpy hypersonic environment. The Phase II technical objectives are configured to demonstrate, through analysis and prototype fabrication, the S- band ponderomotive electron sweeper, permanent magnet electron stabilizer and phased array satellite communications antenna design. The prototype systems will then be experimentally tested in a relevant Mach 6.6 high-enthalpy environment: single patch first, row second and full phased array third to demonstrate innovative solutions for efficient radio communications with a hypersonic vehicle for both GPS and for a phased array satellite communication antenna array in the 7.25 to 8.4 GHz band. Hypersonic computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of the near-wall boundary layer will be verified over the vehicle surface to support the evaluation of: antenna performance though the plasma layer, transmissivity through the plasma, and S-band Ponderomotive effectiveness in reducing electron density. The prototype antenna design, fabrication, integration, and test will be matured during the proposed Phase II effort. The prototypes will be exhaustively tested in a high enthalpy hypersonic facility wind tunnel at Texas A&M University (TAMU), under the direction of Dr. Tichenor. The Hypervelocity Expansion Tunnel (HXT) housed within the TAMU National Aerothermochemistry and Hypersonics Laboratory (NAL) will produce true Mach 6.6 flight enthalpies, enabling verification of the RF transmissivity through the hypersonic plasma layer. The proposed Phase II Program Plan focuses on the development of the antenna, ponderomotive-based plasma electron sweeper, and rare-earth magnet electron stabilizer assembly. The work plan is a logical, chronological progression, which will result in a verified and demonstrated design and delivery of operational phased array satellite communications system prototypes that can operate through plasma at Mach 6.6.
Radio Communication with Hypersonic Aerial Vehicle

The Dynovas team’s Structural Health Integrated for Enhanced Lightweight Design (SHIELD) rocket motor cases (RMCs) enable lightweighting of composite motor cases, rapid case qualification, and real-time assessment of non-visible damage. The SHIELD rocket motor cases can be >30% lighter weight then metallic cases (driven be case bending stiffness) and with more volume available for propellant than traditional composite cases (driven by higher temperature capable motor case and reduced insulation requirements). The benefits of SHIELD RMCs are realized through the integration of composite hard points (bosses, lugs, rails), hybrid processing with tension optimized filament/tape winding and load path tailoring around embedded hardpoints via tailored fiber placement (TFP), and use of emerging insulations that enable higher temperature processing of higher temperature capable composite materials (>550 °F). The structural build can be completed with existing reinforcing fibers (such as domestically sourced IM7, IM10, or T1100) for which significant material data exists both in CMH-17 and AGATE databases. The reinforcements can be coupled with damage resistant matrices and ply stack-ups to improve the composite cases lifecycle performance (toughened high temperature resins, thermoplastic interleaves, and/or thin ply architectures). The statistical material properties can be correlated to case performance through strain measurement by a network of fiber optic sensors (FOS). The FOS network produces 10,000’s of strain data points for rapid correlation with less test articles. The FOS can be automatically integrated into the wind (reducing cost associated with touch labor) and produce a 3D map of the composite structures’ strain life and identification of non-visible defects (fiber angles, residual strains, pressure cycles, delamination, fiber gaps, etc.) from pre-cure through the entire lifecycle of the motor case.                Dynovas’ SHIELD RMCs replacement of traditional metallic rocket motor cases utilizes a three-fold comprehensive approach: 1) a clear path towards integration as a complete rocket motor assembly; 2) TRL and MRL advancement of the composite case itself with a realized weight and/or performance (e.g., volume of propellant) benefit when considering missile assembly and attachment to aircraft suspension equipment (MIL-STD-8591); and 3) qualification that includes compliance to insensitive munitions requirements (MIL-STD-2105), missile structural integrity (MIL-M-8856B), E3 stability (MIL-STD-464), and risk burn down through empirically driven data. At the completion of Phase I, Dynovas will demonstrate the SHIELD RMCs at TRL 3. In Phase II, the SHIELD RMCs will be demonstrated at TRL 6 via ground based relevant environment testing, including thermal cycling, shock, vibe, and combined load structural testing. Dynovas will also conduct a risk reduction hot fire test.

Archem LLC proposes to develop a high-energy-density synthetic fuel under this SBIR Phase I project, supporting the U.S. Navy’s (USN) mission to enhance cruise missile propulsion efficiency and range. This effort focuses on molecular modeling, computational simulations, small-scale synthesis, and property validation to establish feasibility. The fuel aims to exceed JP-10’s volumetric energy density while maintaining a flash point above 60°C, viscosity below 200cSt at -40°C, and improved thermal stability to reduce coking and enhance combustion efficiency.Phase I will employ an analysis-of-alternatives (AOA) modeling-first strategy, integrating density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to evaluate fuel architectures within the C12-C22 hydrocarbon range. These computational models will guide formulation selection, prioritizing molecular structures that optimize energy density, stability, and compatibility with naval propulsion systems. Machine learning-assisted blend optimization and design of experiments (DoE) will refine candidate formulations before laboratory synthesis.Following computational screening, a 250 mL prototype will be synthesized and characterized using GC-MS, NMR, and FTIR to confirm molecular composition. ASTM-compliant testing will assess heat of combustion, density, viscosity, flash point, and freezing point, ensuring alignment with USN operational criteria. Thermal stability and heat absorption capacity will be evaluated using the Compact Rapid Assessment of Fuel Thermal Integrity (CRAFTI) rig at Johns Hopkins University (JHU) Energetics Research Group (ERG) to assess high-temperature decomposition and coking resistance. Comparative testing against JP-10 will quantify energy output, heat absorption efficiency, and reliability under operational conditions.At the conclusion of Phase I (Base Period, 6 months), Archem will deliver 250 mL of synthesized fuel, computational models, and a feasibility report to the USN’s Technical Point of Contact (TPOC). If successful, the Phase I Option Period (6 additional months) will extend laboratory testing, thermal validation, and cost analysis for scale-up feasibility at production-relevant levels. This structured approach ensures a strong foundation for Phase II development and future transition to operational missile platforms while considering environmental impact and maritime suitability.
HIGH-ENERGY LIGHTWEIGHT INNOVATIVE OPERATIONAL SYNTHETIC-FUEL (HELIOS)

1. Executive SummaryThe U.S. Department of State’s Embassy Algiers is launching a competitive program to catalyze innovation and commerce between the United States and Algeria and advance key U.S. foreign policy priorities. The initiative aims to strengthen commercial ties, expand market access for American companies, and promote American business models and technology, particularly in entrepreneurship and artificial intelligence as well as English language development. Target audiences include Algerian students and young leaders (ages 18-35), entrepreneurs, and mid-career professionals, with a focus on building partnerships between U.S. and Algerian institutions and improving knowledge relevant to U.S. business and technology standards. The Embassy may play an active role in guiding and monitoring the program, while recipients will manage implementation and outreach. Competitive proposals should support a priority program area (see below) and should include a connection with American expert/s, organization/s, institution/s or private sector companies that will promote increased cooperation between the people of the United States and Algeria even after the program has finished. A. ELIGIBILITY1. Eligible ApplicantsThe Public Affairs Section encourages applications from U.S. and Algeria and any othercountry for projects that would have any significant bonds with the priority programsAreas and will be implemented in Algeria.· Registered not-for-profit organizations, including think tanks and civil society/nongovernmental organizations with programming experience. Public and private educational institutions· Individuals: Specialized professional individuals· Public International Organizations and Governmental institutions· Non-profit or governmental educational institutions· Governmental institutions· Social enterprises: public or private.· Museums· Press and media: Including public and private traditional media outlets.· Entities specialized in the project fields.For-profit entities, even those that may fall into the categories listed above, are not eligible to apply for this NOFO. Organizations may sub-contract with other entities, but only one, non-profit, non-governmental entity can be the prime recipient of the award. When sub-contracting with other entities, the responsibilities of each entity must be clearly defined in the proposal. For more information on the difference between sub-contract and sub-recipient, please refer to 2 CFR 200.331. 2. Cost Sharing or MatchingCost sharing or matching is encouraged, but not required for this funding opportunity. 3. Other Eligibility RequirementsAll organizations must have a Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) issued via SAM.gov as well as a valid registration in SAM.gov. Please see Section E.3 for more information. Individuals are not required to have a UEI or be registered in SAM.gov. Optional: Applicants are only allowed to submit one proposal per organization. If more than one proposal is submitted from an organization, all proposals from that institution will be considered ineligible for funding under this funding opportunity.4. This opportunity will not support: · Projects relating to partisan political activity;· Charitable or development activities; including direct social services such as medical, psychological, and/or humanitarian support· Construction projects;· Projects that support specific religious activities;· Fund-raising campaigns;· Lobbying for specific legislation or programs· Scientific research or surveys;· Commercial projects;· Projects intended primarily for the growth or institutional development of the organization; · Projects that duplicate existing projects; or· Illegal activitiesB. PROGRAM DESCRIPTION1. Project Background, Goals, and ObjectivesThe Public Diplomacy Section invites proposals for programs that support one of the following U.S. Embassy priority program areas listed below. Examples of Public Diplomacy Small Grants Program programs include, but are not limited to:· Academic and professional lectures, seminars and speaker programs;· Artistic and cultural workshops, joint performances and exhibitions;· Professional and academic exchanges and programs;Priority Program Areas/Goals: Applicants may submit a proposal to address the program goals below. Proposals should focus on one or more of the priority outcomes, but applicants may also recommend their own objective. Goal 1. Advance Commercial Diplomacy The U.S. Embassy invites proposals that strengthen commercial ties between the United States and Algeria. This is a priority for the U.S. Embassy because it expands market access for American companies, supports workforce development, and fosters a business ecosystem that is conducive to American engagement. Applicants should consider designing programs that promote American business models, create new talent pipelines, stimulate entrepreneurship. and include mechanisms for measuring commercial outcomes.Project Audience(s): All programs should focus on audiences in Algeria. Primary audiences are those who will participate directly in the program, and secondary audiences include those reached indirectly – for example, via social media or traditional media. Specific audiences who are considered a priority for awards funded under this Annual Program Statement include:· Students and young leaders between the ages of 18-35;· Entrepreneurs and small business owners; · Rising and mid-career industry and creative professionals. Priority Outcomes(s): Applicants may focus on one or more of the outcomes listed below. Applicants are encouraged to propose additional objectives and innovative activities that address the priority program areas. Strengthened Partnerships between Algerian and American universities, research institutions, creative hubs, and business incubators. Increased Pipelines for Algerian students and young leaders to work for, engage with, and promote American companies. Improved Ability among target audiences in English language, American business standards, and American approaches to commercialization and entrepreneurship,Increased Adoption of American business models and operational standards within Algeria’s emerging industries, including in Algeria’s sports and entertainment industries. We seek proposals from teams of at least two alumni that meet all program eligibility requirements below.
