To address the ArmyÆs need for a new rugged, lightweight, compact north-finding technology that can provide a precise measurement of heading relative to true north in GPS-denied environments and in the presence of interference such as magnetic fields or overcast skies, Intellisense Systems, Inc. (Intellisense) proposes to develop a novel low-size, -weight, and -power (low-SWaP), completely autonomous, robust, ruggedized, Geographic North Pole Pointer (GNOPP) based on a combination of compact precise MEMS vector magnetometers integrated with supporting MEMS precise tri-axial accelerometers and gyroscope, all of which controlled by a single-board FPGA-based computer with GNOPP magnetometer calibration, extended Kalman filter, and artificial intelligence/machine learning algorithms and software, providing true North pole finding accuracy of ?0.2o, in the presence of hard- and soft-magnetic field sources and various geomagnetic noises. In Phase I, Intellisense will design a proof-of-concept low-SWAP GNOPP system capable of either stand-alone or platform-integrated operation, and compatible with the Army Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA). This design will include GNOPP hardware and software integration and a detailed description of how a user or system integrator would interact with the system. By the end of Phase I, the final deliverables will include a breadboard demonstration of the GNOPP and a concept design presentation featuring anticipated performance, SWaP, and cost estimates for it. In Phase II, Intellisense will develop and demonstrate GNOPP prototypes based on the specifications identified in Phase I and ensure via documented reports that the prototypes and associated software comply with all elements of the Army MOSA standard, such that it can be integrated into existing and future Army systems for demonstration, testing and evaluation, such as the ArmyÆs Weaponized Universal Lightweight Fire Control (WULF) system across a range of training and operational environments. By the conclusion of Phase II, Intellisense expects to demonstrate and deliver two technology readiness level (TRL)-7 GNOPP prototypes that meet the ArmyÆs operational needs, including results of testing the prototypes and a user manual describing how a user can perform a heading measurement in a stand-alone use case. The developed prototype should be able to measure heading relative to True North to within 1 degree (threshold), 0.2 degree (objective).

As systems become more heterogeneous and distributed, determining optimal actions for each “teammate” within the system becomes increasingly complex. A particular difficulty in guiding the actions of these teammates is the fact that they are not guaranteed to follow suggestions provided by a supervisor, especially when those suggestions are inconsistent with the teammate’s tendencies, preferences, or capabilities. We propose the teammate aware autonomy (TAA) system to provide course of action suggestions to each teammate within such a system, where the suggestions (1) are aimed to optimize overall system performance, and (2) are modulated with respect to models of each individual teammate’s tendencies, preferences, and capabilities. The foundational technologies in TAA are a teammate modeling approach to develop models of teammate policies and latent states based on observations, and a multiagent learning algorithm which can optimize multiagent system performance while incorporating these teammate models to ensure suggestions are likely to be understood and accepted by the teammates.
Teammate Aware Autonomy (TAA)

Based on newly developed radar technology, the use of this system will reduce the time required to generate an RF characterization of a target, and reduce the cost as well. The system provides added flexibility in collecting from various geometries and in various backgrounds, especially when compared to airborne systems or fixed measurement sites. The proposed system natively provides capabilities at Ka-band, X-band, L-band, and UHF, and can be expanded in the future to S-band, C-band, Ku-band, and W-band. The Phase I effort consists of a trade study and system design. The details of system mounting, positioning, control, image formation, data acquisition and calibration are all be carefully designed to maximize the utility of the system.

In Phase I, ISI will demonstrate the feasibility of MARSS technology by conducting a trade study resulting in a preliminary design that establishes the baseline target-in-background signature measurement capability. In Phase II, ISI plans to design, develop, and demonstrate a full MARSS prototype system capable of acquiring, calibrating, and processing RCS imagery at desired bands of military type ground systems.

Under EAGLE, SSCI will develop use of electric (E) and magnetic (H) field sensors on autonomous small unmanned air vehicles (SUAVs) to perform tactical intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) of electric power grids. This enables new capabilities to efficiently assess adversarial dependences on power distribution networks, find hidden assets, quickly track down grid faults, and perform surgically targeted grid disruptions. The flow of electric power generates EH fields that can be measured without interrupting the circuit or making physical contact with power lines. With the right set of measurements, power lines can be located, and voltages and currents can be deduced. By putting field sensors on an SUAV and adding autonomy, such measurements can be sampled from the necessary points in 3D space quickly and accurately. By interpreting data during flight, autonomy also guides the vehicle to collect further samples to fill in gaps or optimally extend the exploration frontier, closing the sensing loop. The key enabling technologies for this application are sensor adaptation and calibration for SUAV-mounted use, and autonomy behaviors which turn an EH field sampling tool into a tactically useful asset. In Phase II these are developed, and power grid ISR capabilities will be flight demonstrated.

The Software Implementation from Rigorous Formal Usable Requirements (SIRFUR) project will develop and deploy model-based system engineering (MBSE) tools to provide formal verification evidence that system-level safety and security requirements represented in system models are accurately reflected in the subsystem components and the code that implements them.  SIRFUR will autogenerate embedded C code to align that component interfaces, the application code that implements those interfaces, and the component's run-time environment in a formally verifiable way.  The departure point for SIRFUR combines the error analysis developed on SSCATE Phase II, Kansas State University's Logika Integrated Verification Environment, the AADL representation of run-time semantics for thread dispatch and inter-process communications developed under the DARPA Cyber Assured System Engineering (CASE) project, and code generation technology to add cyber resiliency to software intensive systems by targeting separation kernels prototyped on the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ISOSCELES program and matured on CASE.  SIRFUR will also leverage an existing MBSE process also in use today by the U.S. Army called the Architecture Centric Virtual Integration Process (ACVIP).  The work will be demonstrated in the context of a CubeSat, a non-trivial system with interacting, mixed-criticality subsystems. This will provide a realistic test case that relies on significant software functionality, as well as the correct interaction of a diverse mix of software, hardware, and mechanical subsystems, similar to that required for many DoD systems. SIRFUR will be deployed as part of Adventium's Curated Access to Model-based Engineering Tool (CAMET) Library, an existing collection of model-based systems engineering (MBSE) tools in use today. SIRFUR combines previous work on the SSCATE SBIR with work from several other programs, including CASE. SIRFUR will increase confidence that the implemented code correctly reflects its model-based specification, providing a formal correspondence between the analyses performed on the models and what is deployed in the real system.

ION, a proposed software platform for Influence Operations aNalysis, will help an end user uncover adversary or competitor strategy and improve capability to influence target audiences. It will help USG and commercial end users alike answer: What will an adversary or competitor do next and how can I preempt or counter them? Our proposed human-in-the-loop system for anticipating an adversary or competitor’s behaviors will directly enable a new way of carrying out analysis of entities’ events (actions) and communications in context to (a) identify tactics and appropriate counter-measures, and (b) inform a better understanding of strategy. This type of technology, built on methodologically sound frameworks for analysis and proven techniques from the commercial marketing and advertising world, will also provide improved rigor to the influence space, build on best practices, and create an environment for the development of high-quality standards in the field. The principal strength of our proposed technical approach for ION is the incorporation of multiple proven methods that reduce the burden on the analyst. The unique combination of these methods sets the system apart from other tools. In particular, pre-trained language models are revolutionizing the Natural Language Processing (NLP) landscape. ION will leverage these advancements to reduce the amount of input required from analysts and adapt to new domains. Similarly, the proposed techniques for integrated modeling and forecasting leverage proven time series methods with demonstrated efficacy in a wide range of data regimes. These methodological approaches provide a strong foundation for automating large components of the analytical process used in the case studies below. The novel application of state-of-the-art NLP methods is a core component of our technical solution. Large language models have advanced the state of the art in a wide range of benchmark tasks over recent years. Our approach uses these technologies to build a powerful foundation that is further aided by the incorporation of analyst feedback. The combination of these methods is relatively unexplored, particular in the joint analysis of communications and events; however, a large body of literature indicates they hold tremendous promise. A final unique attribute of our technical approach is the way we treat sequences of communications and events as a combined pool of complex signals to detect and forecast behavior. This allows for the application of a diverse set of computational methods to address the integrated modeling and forecasting challenge. Many of these methods have been proven over decades of research, thus minimizing risk. Other proposed techniques are derived from more recent breakthroughs and hold tremendous promise for a revolutionary advancement in jointly modeling communications and behaviors.
ION: A Software Platform for Influence Operations aNalysis

Our team is developing algorithms and techniques to model the COVID-19 outbreak. Using a hybrid physics-based and machine learning model, we have developed algorithms that utilize mobility data and high-fidelity simulations to model how the pandemic spread has occurred. Our algorithmic framework already demonstrated the ability to accurately backward predict nonstationary data on short timescales (days to weeks) across the country. We are currently improving our predictive algorithms that allow for accurate forward predictions in nonstationary environments without the need for extensive training at the onset of a new event. Our general solution to modeling complex dynamic systems, as applied to the COVID pandemic, is to combine physics-based individual infection simulation data with observational data at the individual and population level, to develop flexible deep learning models with built-in uncertainty quantification mechanisms, to cope with partially observed complex dynamics for accurate near-term prediction. This technique is broadly applicable for predicting behaviors of non-stationary dynamical systems, such as disease or behavior models, without reliance on stationary longitudinal observation data over a time horizon. We will analyze the likely behavioral patterns of interactions among individuals and how it relates to the spread of COVID-19 (and potentially related infectious diseases) during the modeling stage. The project will generate real-time predictions for new cases and hotspots within 7 days for less than 10% prediction error.  In particular, we will establish a connection between the agent-based spatial movement and encounter models with the population level infection dynamics, where the former provides mechanistic foundation to constrain the possible model class and the latter relates directly to the observations on the population level. We use Bayesian inference to learn the model and quantify uncertainty of it. Predictions and credible intervals are formed by forward simulating the learned model. We will deliver visualized results and prognoses of future infection behaviors including number of infected in a region and locations of possible outbreaks.

There is currently an explosion of the adoption of embedded devices (esp. around Internet of Things, IoT). Based on recent incidents related to attacks against industrial sensor and wireless networks, there are concerns about significant risks related to the quality of performance of such devices. Additionally, embedded systems requirements testing is typically currently done at the DevOps stage. However, for purchased third-party COTS devices, the buyer is not part of the DevOps process and is not supported by the testing tool landscape. We propose ōVeriCoRö (Third Party Verification of COTS Compliance with Requirements), a solution for automated analysis of embedded devices with support for Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) operation. The goal of the current system is to achieve outstanding levels of coverage for both device specifications and operator usability, with as much automation as possible. At its heart, our system is driven by a novel Domain Specific Language (DSL) which acts as a bridge between the operator and low-level implementation of instruments performing binary analysis. The analysis results from lifting operations where binaries are made available in formats including Intermediate Representation (IR), Intermediate Language (IL), Assembly (ISA), and high-level programming language (C). In these forms, and relative to platforms including Ghidra and S2E, lifted binary becomes available for analysis in static and dynamic forms. We have previously identified the ability for static analysis to meet code quality, code inclusion, and library import quality standards and specifications. We have previously demonstrated these functions to be fully automated with a binary input and explicit specification of strings, patterns, and dates to include as constraints. As a dedicated cybersecurity company, ObjectSecurity has over 20 yearsÆ experience in evaluating static code representations for security-related specifications and 15 years of experience encoding security policies and specifications in middle and high-level Domain Specific Languages (DSLs). Our proposal is intended to analyze COTS testbed devices covering a variety of industrial use cases as previously carried out for Navy and DoD initiatives. We present novel experimentation, testing, and validation methodologies (including using Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, AI/ML) that will be incorporated for advanced analysis and feedback features to benefit automation and accuracy of fielded systems. Our solution will support a range of operator expertise, from novice to experts, with dedicated DSL IDE support and reporting features including rendering capabilities to concise textual, verbose/auditable textual, and visual/graphical outputs. Additional features are outlined to support functional prototype development and support for APIs, customizable device specifications, independent validations, and future enhancements

full_descriptions: Binary Assurance Through Proofs Of Properties

Kestrel Technology proposes to extend its Axe toolkit to build a lightweight, easy-to-use tool that can prove important safety, security, and correctness properties of software binaries, such as those used in off-the-shelf embedded systems.  This will combine the strengths of several of our existing tools: our Axe Lifter, which can transform x86 binaries into a logical form for further analysis; our Axe Prover, which can prove properties of lifted programs using a variety of proof tactics; our Axe Equivalence Checker, which can compare lifted programs to specifications or to known good programs; and our Formal Unit Tester, which helps users w

Kestrel Technology proposes to extend its Axe toolkit to build a lightweight, easy-to-use tool that can prove important safety, security, and correctness properties of software binaries, such as those used in off-the-shelf embedded systems.  This will combine the strengths of several of our existing tools: our Axe Lifter, which can transform x86 binaries into a logical form for further analysis; our Axe Prover, which can prove properties of lifted programs using a variety of proof tactics; our Axe Equivalence Checker, which can compare lifted programs to specifications or to known good programs; and our Formal Unit Tester, which helps users without formal methods expertise explore bounded program behaviors.  The latter tool currently operates on Java programs but will be retargeted to binaries.  We plan to target x86 but can pivot to a different CPU type if desired. Kestrel's Axe Lifter can explore a program or subroutine using symbolic execution, obtaining a mathematical term that represents its behavior.  Lifting is done using the Axe Rewriter together with a model of the target machine (currently, the Java Virtual Machine or x86 CPU).  The lifted form represents the operation of the program on arbitrary data.  Axe has techniques to avoid path explosion (rejoining the execution after conditional branches) and can lift entire loops into recursive functions. Kestrel's Axe Prover can then be used to prove properties of the lifted program, such as the fact that program operation satisfies given requirements.  A variety of proof tactics are available, including rewriting with our extensive library of proven rules, case splitting, and calling the ACL2 prover or an external SMT solver. Kestrel's Axe Equivalence Checker can prove the equivalence of two lifted programs, or of a program and a specification.  This provides a convenient way to specify correct behavior, and the proof can be highly automatic when the amount of computation is bounded (e.g., when loops can be unrolled). Kestrel's Formal Unit Tester, currently only for Java bytecode programs, provides a convenient way for users without formal methods training to check desired properties of a program.  Unlike traditional unit tests, each of which covers a single input, formal unit tests are small proofs that can cover very large input spaces.  The user writes small test harnesses in a traditional programming language, and the tool attempts to prove that the tests always pass.  Because the tests can take symbolic inputs, each covers many possible computations.  The tool can provide assurance that all behaviors (perhaps within some bound on the input size) satisfy the desired property.  Or it can produce an input that violates the desired property. The novelty of the project will be to combine all these tools, bringing the above capabilities to binaries.  We will also improve the automation, usability, and scalability of the tools and apply them to industrial use cases.

Mobility superiority is a force multiplier, allowing for military assets to respond to changing battlefield conditions quickly and unpredictably. Ground and sea-based platforms designed to transport troops and supplies have been utilized for millennia; however, they are limited by the terrain in which they are deployed. Aerial vehicles overcome these limitations by operating above the obstacles encountered by surface-constrained platforms. Currently, the individual, dismounted warfighter does not have flight capabilities at his/her disposal. Powered paragliders (paramotors) are aerial platforms that can fill this capability gap at the individual-combatant level. Lynntech proposes an advanced powered paraglider called CHARIOT: Connector High-speed Aerial Resupply/Insertion Over-the-horizon Transport to serve as a common, modular platform that can be tailored to meet the needs of the different missions performed by different branches of the DOD.       The paramotor’s lift will be generated by Custer Channel Wings (CCW) mounted to the device’s dual-propellers and an inflatable canopy that can be rapidly deployed from its pack with the application of compressed gas, even in zero-wind scenarios. The novel canopy provides the higher performance associated with semi-rigid wings while still offering the failsafe nature of classic parafoils constructed from traditional fabrics by maintaining its shape in the event of pressure loss during flight. The channel wings provide improved lift at lower speeds, aiding with short takeoff and landing at reduced speed. These features synergize to allow Lynntech’s paramotor platform to launch from the ground, aboard a ship, and from air vehicles. To reduce training time and increase platform effectiveness, Lynntech will incorporate a control system, similar to existing precision airdrop systems, that will simplify operation and provide autopilot functionality, reducing operator fatigue during long-duration flights. Lynntech’s paramotor platform will be readily adapted for unmanned aerial resupply, allowing for large loads of supplies to be delivered directly to soldiers in the field from ships located beyond the horizon.       Phase I feasibility and trade studies will be performed to determine what aspects of CHARIOT should be kept by future iterations of the designs and what aspects should be eliminated:       A propulsion subsystem test stand will be built and tested to determine the feasibility of the Custer Channel Wings and dual-propeller setup.       Analysis will determine the parafoil size and properties for optimum pairing with the CCW. Additionally, mechanisms for parafoil rigidification (e.g. inflatable support sections) will be explored for further parafoil development into Phase II.       A trade study will identify powerplants best suited for different mission durations. In particular, batteries, internal combustion engines, and fuel cells will be investigated.

full_descriptions: Accurate, Cost-Effective Translation System for Low Resource Languages

Barron Associates proposes a Phase I program that will develop the Accurate, Cost-Effective Translation System for Low Resource Languages (ACE-Translation) to address the objectives of SBIR topic A234-021: Machine Translation for Indo-Pacific Low Resource Languages.Ā ĀDuring Phase I, the team will develop methods to automate collection of training data, explore optimal structures for training datasets given constrained resources, implement machine translation systems for representative languages, develop novel quality assurance methods for the translation systems, and quantify performance of the systems using standard benchmarks.Ā The propose

Barron Associates proposes a Phase I program that will develop the Accurate, Cost-Effective Translation System for Low Resource Languages (ACE-Translation) to address the objectives of SBIR topic A234-021: Machine Translation for Indo-Pacific Low Resource Languages.Ā ĀDuring Phase I, the team will develop methods to automate collection of training data, explore optimal structures for training datasets given constrained resources, implement machine translation systems for representative languages, develop novel quality assurance methods for the translation systems, and quantify performance of the systems using standard benchmarks.Ā The proposed approach builds on proven technologies for translation of low-resource languages previously developed by team members, as well as experience with automated data collection and assurance of critical software systems.Ā ĀThe team will build on open-sourced pre-trained models like mBART, DeltaLM, or NLLB, adapting these pre-trained models to new languages.Ā The team will employ hierarchical adapter units, which are injected between the layers of the pre-trained model and can be trained on a new language, domain, or task. There are two advantages in fine-tuning only these adapter components.Ā Since they consist of only a small number of parameters, they can be adequately trained with a small number of training examples. In addition, as the pre-trained model remains invariant, they render catastrophic forgetting a non-issue. The proposed work will improve existing processes for using these adapter units by incorporating additional phylogenetic linguistic information in their organization, leveraging results of prior linguistic studies that provided the needed information in the form of phylogeny trees.Ā The team will develop innovative automated data collection methods to enable low-cost collection of data to support implementation of translation systems for nearly any low-resource language.Ā The proposed work will also include development of strategies for optimally selecting input data for system training, including targeting data to provide enhanced accuracy in domains of interest to the military.Ā Recognizing the dangers of ōhallucinationsö (grossly inaccurate but often articulately phrased outputs) that can be produced by even the best modern language models, ACE-Translation will employ run-time assurance (RTA) to achieve high reliability.Ā Barron will leverage its expertise in RTA methods for safety critical software systems to enable ACE-Translation to detect and automatically remediate degraded performance, falling back when needed to a robust translation mode that prioritizes accuracy over fluency.Ā Phase I research will position the team for subsequent development of operational translation systems for a larger set of languages, integration of these into workflows that support Army missions, and continued enhancement of the quality of the core translation systems.

InferLink, the research firm, has a strong track record of turning SBIR research into commercial technology, having spawned several startups from government-funded tech in recent years. Our team members from ISI have a great deal of published research, as well as commercial and open source products in the areas related to this proposal, including machine translation, multilingualism, and NLP in general.

The Robotic Operating System (ROS) software stack has been a key enabled to robotic platform and application development.Ā This modular componentized architecture has made it possible for a community of developers to leverage innovations from across the industry while decoupling individual nodes from changes in other parts of the system. Unfortunately, security has been a bit of an after thought in this ecosystem, but it is of critical importance.Ā Industrial robots have a long unfortunate history of accidents involving injury or death of the people working alongside them, even with strict safety protocols and guardrails.Ā The potential for a malicious entity to bypass these guardrails is a major cause for concern.Ā Furthermore, even small robots can be dangerous in the right conditions regardless of their size, locomotion, or manipulator capabilities. Since the availability of qualified warfighters is naturally limited by the population which this force is drawn from, robotics provide a way to surpass this limit to match the force potential of adversaries with much larger civilian populations.Ā Realizing this, the Army has created the Robotics Technology Kernel (RTK) as a key enabler for autonomous ground vehicle applications.Ā However, the removal of human personnel with physical access to the vehicle negates the typical security mitigation deployed by the Army: guards with guns, making cybersecurity a fundamental concern in these applications. Many efforts are underway to harden the ROS software stack such as the addition of security extensions to the Data Distribution Service (DDS) middleware, but since a software stack is only as secure as its lowest layer, moving some or all of the ROS software stack to a more security focused operating environment would go a long way to securing these applications.Ā While some commercial RTOS vendors provide ROS compatible software libraries Āthese offerings are costly and vendor specific reducing portability and maintainability, not to mention their sometimes dubious security claims. seL4, on the other hand, has a strong security posture established through the use of formal methods to prove separation of processes and components running on the microkernel.Ā These separation properties also enable seL4 to run isolated virtual machines (VM) which can be leveraged to quickly support legacy applications such as existing ROS/RTK deployments and in turn incrementally harden these systems.Ā This incremental approach will allow the Army to maximize past investments while addressing security concerns and overcoming hurdles with supporting ROS in limited operating environments such as seL4 as they are encountered.
seROS: Securing Robotic Systems with seL4

The Xwing product is a platform-flexible, autonomous flight technology stack that enables aircraft to operate fully unmanned with an optional remote supervisor. XwingÆs technology includes sensor fusion of flight control systems, collision avoidance technologies, machine perception systems, auto braking systems, and other capabilities that jointly support autonomous gate-to-gate flight. To be clear, our product: fully removes the need for a pilot or crew onboard the aircraft,Ā enables the aircraft to operate a programmed flight plan and automatically respond to off-nominal internal or external conditions fully independently from any human input,Ā optionally allows for a remote human supervisor to interact with and re-task the aircraft in-flight, and is intended for DoD UAS groups 4 & 5, or commercial 14 CFR Part 23 or Part 25 aircraft. While existing autopilots are limited to controlling aircraft attitude and throttle, XwingÆs core innovations addĀcollision avoidance technologies that allow for electronic detect and avoid of both ground and air hazards, mission manager software which is the autonomous decision making function that responds to all off-nominal conditions, and a ground control station that allows the supervisor to optionally interact with the aircraft. Key enabling technologies for XwingÆs autonomous system include perception hardware (e.g., LIDAR and Air-To-Air Radar) and machine learning software. A unique and defining feature of XwingÆs approach to autonomy is that the onboard systems are designed to safety fly the mission and off-nominal scenarios completely independently of any human input. Xwing operates a prototypeĀautonomous Cessna Grand Caravan for regular R&D and market research flights. With that aircraft, Xwing has autonomously flown over 200 missions, 350 flight hours, and 450 landings. Xwing also operates 34 conventionally piloted aircraft on nearly 400 flights per week as a cargo-feeder airline and intends to initially deploy certified autonomous aircraft commercially in this network for UPS. With our technical demonstrator,Āthe world's first and only FAA certification project for an uncrewed aircraft, and airline experience, we are confident we are building the right product and are on track to introduce an autonomous commercial service aircraft. Ā Xwing views collaboration with the U.S. Army under this SBIR as an accelerator of our technical development and transition of our technology the defense industry. Xwing sees substantial opportunities for fully uncrewed and autonomous aircraft to fulfill army capability gaps. We propose to use this Phase I SBIR to elicit clear requirements for autonomous flight from Army stakeholders, identify product-fit opportunities for our technology, and demonstrate our technology to Army personnel. Evaluating the adaptation of our commercial prototype system to Army aircraft and use cases is a critical R&D project to allow for future dual use of the technology.

The U.S. Army faces challenges to operational test (OT) as a growing number of increasingly complex systems become integral to Multi-Domain Operations (MDO). Collecting data from systems under test (SUT) in field conditions that are similar to real-world operational environments has been a staple of OT for many years. The Army lacks a means to adequately collect and process this data in an expeditious and meaningful way to feed artificial intelligence (AI) models for system test and test data analysis. Current methods require human-in-the-loop data labeling prior to the data being made available to AI/ML applications. The process is expensive, laborious, potentially inconsistent, and time-consuming. The automated system proposed in this paper offers to expedite this process by reducing the personnel required for labeling data. It also provides the opportunity to label the data in near real-time for immediate use in other systems to achieve additional test objectives, system evaluations, and test data analysis.

The AIExploit platform is a pioneering automated tool designed to enhance the U.S. Army's operational readiness by detecting and preventing unforeseen risks in AI models. This innovation allows the Army to deploy AI in contested environments, empowering personnel to team effectively with AI, thereby gaining a technological edge over adversaries. Our platform introduces a revolutionary capability: on-demand, automated, no-code AI red teaming. This is a significant shift from traditional operational testing, which typically requires the presence of AI/ML developers. Our solution enables real-time vulnerability assessments in the field, providing immediate insights to commanders without developer intervention. This transformative approach enhances the U.S. Army's operational landscape in human-AI teaming, accelerating the closure of the kill chain more efficiently than adversaries. The motivation behind AIExploit stems from the need for operationalizing emerging technologies like AI, ML, and autonomy, which are crucial for the U.S. National Defense Strategy. These technologies offer competitive advantages but also introduce new security risks. Military leadership faces a dilemma: either adopt new technologies with inherent security vulnerabilities or delay their adoption until a full understanding of the risks is achieved, potentially falling behind adversaries. The AIExploit platform addresses this challenge by enabling operators to understand AI's strengths and limitations better, thus making more informed decisions while leveraging AI capabilities. Yrikka's solution builds on the success of its Phase I feasibility study, which resulted in the development of a TRL 4 prototype automated red-teaming tool for context-based AI Risk Management. This tool will enable Army operators and commanders to efficiently identify exploits and vulnerabilities in AI models, crucial for critical decision-making tasks. Our goal in this Phase II project is to evolve the current TRL 4 prototype of AIExploit into a TRL 7 software module. This module will automate the detection of potential exploits in computer vision AI/ML models used by the U.S. Army, supporting modern armament systems and the development of Advanced Fire Control Technology (AFCT).

For modern vehicles governed by electronically-controlled transmissions, real-time predictions of operating characteristics have become an increasingly significant element in ensuring reliable performance. The practice of using the electronic control system for derating engine torque and power output in harsh environmental conditions or when under heavy loads protects the vehicle against potential malfunction and damage. For these systems, a network of sensors is used to continuously monitor various engine health parameters, including temperature, pressure, and load conditions to provide feedback to the electronic control system. Extrapolating this data to develop a comprehensive picture of vehicle health to identify a potentially unsafe operating state can be a complex, uncertain process, especially in cases of rapidly changing or intermittent conditions. For this reason, the Army has identified a critical need for modern data processing and predictive capabilities for combat vehicle powertrains operating in prototypical wartime environments. To address this need, Creare proposes a physics-informed machine learning (ML) approach to modeling and predicting modern combat vehicle powertrain and cooling system performance. Our approach implements physics-based dynamic simulation tools, calibrated by test data, which then serve as the ground truth for training of a deep learning neural network. The overall framework is designed for near?term implementation at the ArmyÆs Yuma Test Center (YTC) to allow more accurate characterization of vehicle performance, in particular for Full Load Cooling (FLC) tests. Electromagnetic (EM) spectrum monitoring and signal source localization play a crucial role in the Army's efforts to maintain situational awareness, secure communication, conduct electronic warfare operations, detect threats, gather intelligence, and efficiently manage the EM spectrum. These capabilities directly contribute to the Army's overall operational effectiveness, safety, and mission success. As the demand for RF spectrum continues to grow and the spectrum becomes increasingly congested, RF spectrum monitoring becomes even more critical and challenging. This is due to the diverse range of signal frequencies, varying signal strengths, and complex environmental conditions found in both DoD and commercial domains. Furthermore, the widespread use of unmanned aerial systems (UAS) in DoD missions and commercial applications presents an opportunity to leverage their autonomous, robust, and versatile capabilities for RF spectrum monitoring and signal source localization. This offers the potential for enhanced efficiency and effectiveness in addressing the challenges posed by the ever-evolving RF landscape. With the rapid advancement of semiconductor integrated circuits (IC) technology, digital electronics, including high-speed ADCs and DSPs, have become increasingly capable of handling signals with a wide frequency range and dynamic range. However, the performance of antennas, which serve as critical interfaces between the free space propagation of EM waves and ICs, remains a challenging limitation. Presently, antenna technologies are constrained by their limited frequency ranges, restricted field of view (FOV), and time-consuming calibration procedures, necessitating the use of multiple antennas to provide satisfactory system performance. This leads to increased system size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C) requirements. Additionally, even the most broadband antenna solutions currently available lack the required accuracy and precision in azimuth and elevation for applications such as direction finding and geo-location. To address this Army needs, Lunewave proposes a Luneburg Lens Enabled Broadband RF Signal Detection, Direction Finding and Geolocation System in a Drone Network (FALCON-LED). This is made possible by a 3D printed Luneburg lens antenna which is renowned for its unique design, offering a range of advantages such as wide bandwidth, simple beam forming, and complete angle coverage.
Luneburg Lens Enabled Broadband RF Signal Detection, Direction Finding and Geolocation System in a Drone Network (FALCON-LED)

Atolla Tech is pioneering an advanced lidar-based Counter-Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) that rapidly identifies unmanned aerial systems (UAS) using their propeller electronic signatures. This process is enhanced by a machine learning (ML) algorithm that performs waveform analysis in both time and frequency domains, necessitating minimal data points for identification. This approach ensures quick processing and high fidelity in target identification, overcoming radar limitations in resolution and cost while surpassing the range and resolution of electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) systems. Unlike traditional mapping lidars that require 3D point clouds and image processing, Atolla's system meets real-time identification demands, functioning effectively day and night with smaller optics. Originally designed for agricultural use in monitoring insect swarms, the SWAP-optimized lidar sensor and ML algorithm are being adapted for defense applications to extend range and improve precision in detecting and identifying small-UAS threats. This innovative method leverages frequency signature mapping to minimize data processing demands.Atolla Tech's system offers several technical objectives and innovative approaches. The Phase I objective is to design and build a field-ready prototype to determine its limitations and optimize it for real-time UAS detection and identification. Key tasks include specifying field prototype requirements, component sourcing, prototype design updates, building and calibrating the lidar sensor, configuring the system for optimal performance, and refining preprocessing algorithms. The goal is to achieve a working prototype that demonstrates the feasibility of using this technology for C-UAS applications. The prototype will address critical military needs by providing a reliable method for rapid UAS identification, enhancing situational awareness, and enabling timely responses to potential threats.This project also includes the development of an identification algorithm for drones, leveraging existing algorithms used for identifying flying insects. Modifications will be made to accommodate hardware changes and new waveform features specific to drones. The algorithm will analyze preprocessed data, extract key features such as propeller and resonant frequencies, and classify different objects (e.g., birds, drones) using ML or rule-based approaches. Experimental trials with various drones will validate system capabilities, ensuring accurate identification and detection range.By integrating these advancements, Atolla Tech's lidar-based C-UAS system will provide a robust solution for real-time UAS detection, classification, and identification, with potential applications in both military and civilian sectors. The project will contribute to the Army's "Defend the Force" C-UAS initiative by enhancing real-time detection, ensuring constant monitoring, and offering a cost-efficient alternative to traditional radar systems.

Commercial AI image analysis and object detection methods are insufficient for the U.S. Army mission, due to a lack of mission-relevant training data. Traditional labeling efforts are costly and time-consuming, and military applications require higher accuracy and robustness than general-purpose models. To address these issues, Boston Fusion Corp (BFC) proposes Sparse-data Perception And Recognition Classifier (SPARC), an automated object detection framework for EO, IR, and/or SAR images. SPARC will reduce the workload on human analysts and provide faster actionable information to decision-makers by providing reliable, accurate and explainable object detection. The system will leverage BFC’s expertise in few-shot machine learning techniques, uncertainty tracking, and AI explainability to support military analyst workflows, and enhance user adoption and trust. SPARC will utilize a multi-algorithm approach with a small-target object detection model in parallel with a large and medium object detection model. Additionally, SPARC will leverage an ensemble of algorithms for feature embedding and clustering to enable refinement of object classification and confidence values. SPARC leverages the Boston Fusion Engine (BFE), an AI-driven, sensor-agnostic fusion framework, developed through multiple DoD projects for rapid testing and training of ML pipelines. Integrating with Project Linchpin, SPARC will meet the Army's need for efficient, accurate, and agile image analysis systems that can operate effectively with limited labeled training data while maintaining the necessary performance metrics for personnel safety and mission success.
SPARC: Sparse-data Perception And Recognition Classifier

Automatic target recognition (ATR) remains a challenge due to the large variety of Army relevant sensors, sensing modalities, imaging conditions, and environments, nuanced differences in military targets, and the wide range of image scales over which a target may be imaged. Labeling vast amounts of training data to cover all of these conditions and targets is not a feasible approach. With Hi-VALUE ATR Kitware and Johns Hopkins University will enable an analyst to efficiently create new object detectors with zero or only a few object exemplars in the Linchpin Unclassified Environment by describing the object types in plain, descriptive text in addition to providing a few visual examples. We use a hybrid architecture, combining state-of-the-art vision language models (VLMs) with classical algorithmic components (e.g. Gaussian mixture models for motion detection, inpainting for synthetic occlusion generation, feature matching and homography estimation for image stabilization). Hi-VALUE ATR’s detectors will create results without lengthy retraining and quickly adapt to new domains (environments, targets, sensors, sensor modalities, weather conditions, etc.) because we build on modern VLMs and state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods. Preliminary results indicate that our approach is highly effective at ATR while requiring only limited training data.

full_descriptions: Object Recognition of Imagery Entities (ORIENT)

Under this Phase II effort, entitled Object Recognition of Imagery ENTities (ORIENT), Language Computer Corporation (LCC) will leverage our 20+ years of experience developing ML technologies for commercial and government interests – in such diverse fields as video- and image-based scene analysis, image categorization and decomposition, generative AI, knowledge engineering, and question answering – to develop an interpretable, fine-grained object detection pipeline capable of quickly distinguishing hundreds of different types of objects from diverse visual data sources without the need for extensive annotated training data or human-in-the-loop

Under this Phase II effort, entitled Object Recognition of Imagery ENTities (ORIENT), Language Computer Corporation (LCC) will leverage our 20+ years of experience developing ML technologies for commercial and government interests – in such diverse fields as video- and image-based scene analysis, image categorization and decomposition, generative AI, knowledge engineering, and question answering – to develop an interpretable, fine-grained object detection pipeline capable of quickly distinguishing hundreds of different types of objects from diverse visual data sources without the need for extensive annotated training data or human-in-the-loop (HITL). To this end, we will expand upon our existing state-of-the-art image processing technologies to leverage latent object knowledge in support of zero-shot (or few-shot) categorization of detected objects with a focus on electro-optical (EO) satellite imagery, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite imagery, and ground-based EO and infrared (IR) imagery. We divide our research into four tasks. Under Task 1, we will develop an ensemble of probabilistic and self-supervised techniques to identify all objects in a scene under the “open world” paradigm. This will allow us to cast a wide net at ingestion time and to leverage existing open-source datasets for coarse-grained object detection. In Task 2, we will employ a suite of large language model (LLM) prompts in a multi-stage dialogue to surface fine-grained knowledge of each of the program object-of-interest (OOI) classes for incorporation into a collection of probabilistic object profiles. In particular, we will focus on identifying which features of those objects are likely to be detectable (within a particular imagery type) – including their parts and any visible attributes of those parts (e.g., color, size, shape, material, markings). The features defined in these object profiles will then be exploited under Task 3 to develop a portfolio of lightweight feature detectors trained indirectly using publicly available images via text-to-patch retrieval in a fine-tuned foundational model embedding space. Task 4 will be focused on the fine-grained classification of all detected objects using Pre-Weighted Neural Feature Trees (P-NFTs) that iteratively test an image for relevant features using the Task 3 feature detectors. These P-NFTs, which combine the expressiveness of deep learning models with the explainability of decision trees, will be trained using synthetic feature data constructed by intelligently sampling feature information from the Task 2 object profiles along with features from all imagery data made available in Project Linchpin. We will focus throughout this project on integration and deployability, making sure that all developed software and models can be easily delivered, installed, configured, tested, and deployed within Project Linchpin’s AI Unclassified Operations Environment, as well as other relevant Army and DoD platforms.

The Phase I research effort demonstrated the feasibility of ACE-Translation (Accurate, Cost-Effective Translation), a system for efficiently deploying high-performance machine translation for low-resource languages.   The Phase I work demonstrated: (1) high-performing neural Machine Translation (MT) systems could be implemented using very small quantities of parallel data, (2) the effectiveness of novel approaches for exploiting grammar information to improve MT system performance in extremely-low-resource settings, and (3) the feasibility of building robust quality assurance systems for MT in low-resource settings.  A quality assurance system was implemented leveraging a Run-Time Assurance (RTA) framework previously developed by the team for safety-critical control systems, and a complete MT system with quality assurance monitoring was implemented and demonstrated for the Ivatan language.  Building on this success, the team proposes a Phase II program to develop and demonstrate a comprehensive set of tools to support efficient deployment of assured MT systems for low-resource languages, including deployment of new systems for languages not previously supported, and performance optimization for specific domains and/or for specific downstream tasks.  The ACE-Translation design emphasizes assurance of the quality and correctness of outputs.  One aspect of enhancing quality is leveraging as much of the available information as possible to produce high quality translations for a language of interest. In high-resource settings, where abundant parallel data exists, it is not as critical to make use of other types of data. In low-resource settings, significant gains can be realized by using additional types of data.   Grammar descriptions exist for approximately 4,300 of the world’s roughly 7,000 languages, making them a rich source of information with good coverage of low-resource languages.  Expanding capabilities for leveraging this data is an important aspect of Phase II. A second key aspect of enhancing quality is innovative use of RTA methods. In ACE-Translation, the RTA system uses three parallel and independent translation branches along with a monitoring and switching system that employs state-of-the-art Quality Estimation methods.  The overall system produces highly fluent translations in most cases, and reverts to a less fluent but hallucination-free mode when needed to virtually eliminate incorrect outputs.  The Phase II effort will include an end-to-end demonstration of the process, resulting in a deployed MT system for a group of related low-resource language.  The complete deployed system will include a general-purpose translation capability for the selected languages as well as one or more variants optimized for specific Army needs, e.g., optimized for a specific domain of interest to the Army, and/or optimized for use in a specific downstream task such as stance detection.

Traditional manufacturing processes for munitions are limited to monolithic materials and simple designs. This limitation is exacerbated given the very hard and strong metals that interest the military. These problems can be solved using new production techniques in additive manufacturing (AM) where multiple powdered materials can be deposited simultaneously using a directed energy deposition (DED) AM platform. The Kraetonics and The University of North Texas (UNT) team will develop a proof-of-concept (POC) software for printing FGMs on a DED AM platform that consist of metals and/or metal alloys. This POC will generate complex toolpaths and output g-code that can change the metal composition on a single layer. The team will demonstrate the control of material mixtures along the generated toolpaths on a DED AM printer and perform materials characterization of that gradient. The proposed software will enable chemical gradients to be constructed in any orientation, X,Y,Z, in the 3D space for new complex device designs. These advanced gradients will enable the manufacturing of complex devices which are unable to be manufactured through traditional processes.

The energetic manufacturing and storage sectors face critical challenges due to outdated equipment and inefficiencies in meeting growing demands. Human dependence in current processes not only constrains productivity but also exposes workers to hazardous environments. With a heavy reliance on humans, the acyclical and fluctuating demand make it hard to scale up and down to meet the changing requirements and episodic wartime needs. Existing collaborative robots, or cobots, fall short of meeting the stringent electrical safety standards imperative for energetic settings as per Article 500 of the National Electric Code (NEC). This approach necessitates a comprehensive evaluation of available cobot systems emphasizing 6-axis arm manipulators and self-driving mobile robots, culminating in the formulation of a certification roadmap through hardware enhancements in conjunction with the selection of a certifying authority. ICON, a pioneer in advanced construction technologies, has developed compact ground robots called Taskbot, which weigh less than 400 pounds. These robots navigate autonomously around freshly 3D-printed concrete structures, assisting in wetting concrete surfaces post-printing and facilitating the efficient transportation of small tools and equipment across construction sites. In the construction realm, the integration of these robots not only brings down additional labor costs but liberates workers to concentrate on supervisory roles over multiple operational 3D printers, enhancing overall productivity. Leveraging its expertise in collaborative robot technologies, ICON proposes the adaptation of its existing platform for hostile explosive environments, christened the "Inertbot." This transformation involves reconfiguring the site support robot and integrating specialized safety features and robust functionalities to meet the rigorous safety standards mandated for explosive settings. The Inertbot aims to revolutionize the operational landscape within energetic environments by ensuring enhanced operational efficiency, heightened safety standards, and optimized productivity through autonomous robotic interventions. ICON comprehensive phase 1 proposes an evaluation of current regulations in comparison with the current Taskbot platform and proposes a modification and testing plan to create a path to develop and certify the Inertbot platform.

From head and weapon mounted systems on the ground to space-based surveillance for ballistic missile defense, infrared (IR) electro-optic (EO) sensors are needed to overmatch emerging threats. A robust and reliable United States based supply chain for IR optic lens materials is essential to produce optics that perform in these critical defense areas. Unfortunately, the IR lens material supply chain is constrained by high-cost refractive index measurement systems and third-party testing.To overcome this issue, ALLVAR is proposing a novel interferometric method for direct refractive index measurement. This novel system and method are projected to reduce refractive index measurement system and testing costs by 75% while providing dual use for determining thermal defocus of refractive optic assemblies. The novel system has already been proven and tested in the visible spectrum.The goal of this project is to demonstrate that interferometry is a fast and economical method for certifying index of refraction in infrared lens materials. To achieve this goal, the index of refraction measurement concept must be matured by applying the proven technology to the infrared wavelengths and operational temperatures of interest. Then the total combined uncertainty of the apparatus and measurement method must be determined to ensure that a lens material’s refractive index can be certified to 0.001. The present study will determine the various uncertainty contributions to the refractive index measurement and use uncertainty calculations and measurements to explore the solution trade space for each subsystem function. A system will be assembled to measure Type A uncertainty at a single wavelength and temperature. The results of this study will pave the way for a full-scale demonstration across relevant wavelengths and temperatures in a Phase II effort. If successful, this novel measurement technique will impact the entire infrared optic supply chain by enabling certification of refractive index lens materials and thermal defocus of lens assemblies. The result will be a more robust and resilient infrared sensor supply chain.
Interferometry for Refractive Index and Thermal Defocus Determination

Eduworks Corporation (Eduworks) proposes to safeguard the Army’s AI data supply chain, both upstream and during model creation and deployment, with an application called Lorica.  Lorica will monitor the datastreams used by Army AI services, during training and at inference, and will observe the output of AI models. It will then alert analysts to suspected data poisoning, data manipulation, and unexpected changes in model behavior that could signal adversary actions and represent potential threats.  Lorica is a DoD-specific application of our innovative AI architecture and technology, called THIA. THIA uses a self-regulating microservice architecture to implement applications that (a) outperform the current state-of-the-art on reasoning and recall; (b) have low computational demands and can therefore run at the edge of a network on field equipment; and (c) can quickly adjust to new situations, automatically or with small amounts of input from subject matter experts. It includes optimized datastream interpreters for multiple types of data, including language, SQL, sensor, and multimedia data, and that can interpret the data in terms of high-level concepts.  Lorica will be an instance of THIA that has been trained to recognize potential manipulation and threats and that has a dashboard through which Army analysts will interact, receive alerts, and train Lorica without requiring prompt engineering or AI expertise. Lorica’s core model will gather input from microservices that look for drift, malicious data, and malicious intent in datastreams used by Army AI models during training and at runtime and that detect unusual behaviors in external models in Army AI systems. The Lorica core model will be a federation of small models, each of which employs a patent-pending technique that allows models to learn from experience without requiring re-training. The micromodels can be customized to different users or use cases without data being added to the context window. As Lorica operates, the data it retrieves from Army systems and the outputs of its internal microservices will be monitored to ensure they are in-domain, sufficient, and accurate in a way that is far more secure and less easy to attack than the guardrails used in large LLMs and in systems that use classical Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). The core model will examine the data received from Army systems to detect and alert potential manipulation or attacks.
Lorica: AI agent microservices for federated data security

Hardy Dynamics, in collaboration with BigBear.ai (Team HD), proposes to integrate ConductorOS (cOS), an AI/ML autonomy orchestration system, into the US Army Project Linchpin ecosystem. cOS is a critical enabler for AI-based systems, orchestrating and deploying data and AI/ML models across diverse environments. It orchestrates third-party AI/ML models and sensors for real-time data fusion and rapid, platform-agnostic deployment. Its open, modular approach allows for the integration of best-of-breed AI models, creating a multi-node system of edge devices that adapt to changing environments, updated models, and DDIL networks. cOS fosters interoperability among industry partners, addresses mission-critical needs, and supports rapid, iterative deployment of trusted AI models across an expanding network of autonomous and semi-autonomous systems.  ConductorOS boasts a TRL7+ maturity level, with successful demonstrations in DoD-sponsored exercises showcasing its AI/ML, data, and sensor orchestration capabilities. By orchestrating unmanned swarms, cOS empowers the Army to achieve more with less, maximizing the benefits of deployed sensors and enhancing human-machine teaming. Its software-based, containerized solution is ready for deployment at the tactical edge, accelerating the Project Linchpin mission and bridging the sensor-to-shooter gap. Centralized AI-enriched information facilitates faster calls for fire and more informed decision-making, ultimately enabling real-time sensor-shooter matching and increased lethality with reduced resource expenditure.

AiRANACULUS, in association with the University of Texas, proposes to develop Synthetic and Network Assisted Digital Twin Platform for Signal Emulation (SYNAPSE), which will meet and exceed the requirements of the “Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) Ready Synthetic Radio Frequency Data” project. Technical Objective for the SYNAPSE Project is to develop improved techniques for generating and labeling synthetic data across different classes of RF signals. This data will be used to train Electronic Support (ES) and Signals Intelligence (SIGINT) models, enhancing the automation of detecting, characterizing, and identifying Signals of Interest (SoI). Through Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), this effort aims to tackle the growing volume and complexity of RF signals that traditional methods cannot fully address. The innovation seeks to lessen operator workload and boost battlespace awareness and decision-making capabilities in both strategic and tactical Army operations.                   The rapid growth in RF signals has created a substantial challenge in maintaining situational awareness of unit and system surroundings.  Traditional methods for identifying SoI linked to potential threats, targets, or even tracking blue force and civilian activities are struggling to keep up. This surge in RF technology has been fueled by the widespread availability and cost-effectiveness of Software-Defined Radios (SDR) and new communication protocols supporting the Internet of Things (IoT) and related networking infrastructure. To manage this expanding signal landscape, automated detection and characterization are essential. AI / ML are central to this automation, along with large volumes of AI-ready data to train and refine the models that will perform these tasks. However, measured data collections are often costly, time-intensive due to the complexities of coordinating in dense battle environments and carry risks due to the number of involved elements. As a result, synthetic data has become a critical component of the Army's data strategy.                   We anticipate the SYNAPSE Digital Twin to be a standalone self-sufficient Dockerized Software Module that can be delivered to the Army for integration with the core components of Project Linchpin. The SYNAPSE Systems Architecture has following core components: 1. Transmit and Interference Waveform Library. We plan to leverage this Module from the IARPA SCISRS Program. 2. Transmit Waveform and Interference Synthesis, 3. Active Learning, 4. Generative AI Module, 5. Nvidia Sionna Emulation Engine, 6. Data Augmentation, 7. Addition of Hardware Artifacts (OTA Component), 8. Synthetic Data Verification and Validation using Performer Algorithms, and 9. Synthetic Data Scoring. In the following sections, we provide detailed description of all these core components of SYNAPSE.
Synthetic and Network Assisted Digital Twin Platform for Signal Emulation (SYNAPSE)

Current generation Cyber Physical Systems (CPS) including aviation systems were not developed with strong computer security requirements. Past cyber threats, Spectre, Meltdown, current cyber threats, and future cyber threats need to be countered. Embedded system designs are typically based on commodity hardware and software optimized exclusively for size, weight, and power – leading to critical cyber vulnerabilities that can have devastating effects on safety and mission effectiveness. This has also led to the unsustainable “Perimeter, Patch, Pray” Information Assurance strategy that is simply impractical for fielded aviation and missile weapons systems. This SBIR proposal focuses on strengthening Army high assurance system such as an Army Aviation or Missile subsystem currently under development or via technology refresh. We propose Modular and Provably Secure high-assurance hardware/software co-design (MPS-HAHSC) based on the open-source RISC-V instruction set architecture and high-assurance (formally proven) kernels such as seL4. We leverage our existing Modular Provably Security (MPS) mathematical reasoning framework (that encompasses both hardware and software layers) and software verification framework to harden the assurance of the formally verified seL4 kernel which by formally verifying seL4 Assembly language code blocks and boot-up firmware functionality that seL4 relies on but is not presently verified. Further, MPS-HAHSC adds support for multi-core execution and DMA capabilities without affecting the existing proofs. Finally, MPS-HAHSC also support executing legacy unverified kernels such as Linux along with the formally verified seL4 kernel all while preserving the formally verified properties of the entire system. MPS-HAHSC thus enables the vision of a Future Vertical Lift (FVL) system architecture that can support robust, mathematically proven end-to-end high-assurance while seamlessly co-existing with unverified components. With the advent of RISC-V this can also be done in a practical and performant manner with all the available tooling to support rich CPS mission applications. Our proposed approach squarely addresses the "Modernization" transformational strategic capabilities of the Army with an emphasis on “Capability Development for Future Vertical Lift and Air and Missile Defense” as identified by the Vision and Strategy for the Army of 2030. MPS-HAHSC provides mathematically backed ironclad cybersecurity properties that, by design, are immune to adversarial impacts and elevates the Army/DoD cybersecurity capabilities to an unprecedented level to protect against great power competitors who are challenging U.S. dominance in all warfighting domains.
Modular and Provably Secure High-Assurance Hardware and Software Co-design (MPS-HAHSC)

The Robotic Operating System (ROS) middleware has been a key enabler of robotic platform and application development. This modular componentized architecture has made it possible for a community of developers to leverage innovations from across the industry while decoupling individual nodes from changes in the rest of the system. Unfortunately, security has been an after thought in this ecosystem, but it is of critical importance. Industrial robots have a long unfortunate history of accidents involving injury or death of the people working alongside them, even with strict safety protocols and guardrails. The potential for a malicious entity to bypass these guardrails is a major cause for concern. Furthermore, even small robots can be dangerous in the right conditions regardless of their size, locomotion, or manipulator capabilities. Since the availability of warfighters is naturally limited by the population this force is drawn from, robotics provide a way to surpass this limit to match the force potential of adversaries with much larger civilian populations. Realizing this, the Army has created the Army Common Robotics Software (ARCS) as a key enabler for autonomous ground vehicle applications. However, the removal of human personnel with physical access to the vehicle negates the typical security mitigation deployed by the Army: guards with guns, making cybersecurity a fundamental concern in these applications. Many efforts are underway to harden the ROS software stack such as security plug-ins to the Data Distribution Service (DDS) middleware, but since software is only as secure as its lowest layer, running this stack on a more security focused operating environment would go a long way to securing these applications. While some commercial RTOS vendors provide ROS compatible software libraries these offerings are costly and vendor specific reducing portability and maintainability, not to mention their sometimes dubious security claims. seL4, on the other hand, has a strong security posture established using formal methods to prove separation of processes and components running on the microkernel. These separation properties also enable seL4 to run isolated virtual machines (VM) which can be leveraged to quickly support legacy applications such as existing ROS/ARCS deployments and in turn incrementally harden these systems. This incremental approach will allow the Army to maximize past investments while addressing security concerns and overcoming hurdles with supporting ROS in limited operating environments such as seL4 as they are encountered. In phase I, DornerWorks showed it was feasible to leverage this approach to run ROS applications supported by native seL4 Micro-ROS threads to increase the resiliency of those applications. The proposed effort continues this work to seamlessly support a greater portion of the ROS/ARCS software stack, provide the necessary security extensions, and transition this work to a physical robotics platform.
seROS: Securing Robotic Systems with seL4

To address the Army’s need to determine the level of risk when a person uses a personal device to access Army resources (i.e., bring your own device (BYOD)) in accordance with zero trust principles, in Phase II Intellisense Systems, Inc. (Intellisense) proposes to advance the development of a new Secure Handling, Inspection, and Evaluation for Device Access (SHIELD) solution which was proven feasible in Phase I. SHIELD is based on a unique combination of the design guidelines set forth in National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800-207, advanced machine learning, and zero trust architecture. Specifically, the innovation in zero trust architecture with supporting machine learning components determines the level of trustworthiness (i.e., level of risk) when a person uses a personal device to access Army resources. In Phase I, Intellisense implemented the SHIELD zero trust software along with Docker containment for secure system access. We built upon this with our graph neural network component to analyze captured packet capture network access files. The SHIELD Phase I prototype was installed on Amazon Web Services (AWS), and we verified BYOD functionality by accessing a Python threat detection service located on AWS from a smartphone over the internet. Based on the solid Phase I results and feasibility demonstration, Intellisense will, in Phase II, complete the construction of a full-scale SHIELD prototype. The Phase II prototype will implement a set of guiding principles for workflow, system design, and operations to improve the security posture of Army resources. A policy engine and policy administrator will combine to form the policy decision point for user access. SHIELD will significantly lessen uncertainties by focusing on authentication, authorization, and restricting implicit trust zones. This will be accomplished without installing software on the personal device. The SHIELD solution will quantify the technical challenges, the risks and how they will be mitigated, and any resultant dependencies. The approach will be designed with a focus on open architecture and industry standards and protocols, which directly addresses the Army’s requirements. At the end of Phase II, a demonstration of SHIELD determining the trustworthiness of a personal device will be performed (specific device information will be provided by the Army after award). The demonstration will include the ability for observers to determine how the level of trustworthiness for a given device was measured (e.g., what specific device factors were used to determine the level of trustworthiness of the device, any configuration data used in the decision, and how that data was mapped to a level of trustworthiness).

The future operational landscape of the U.S. Army is expected to require significantly higher energy and power to support increasingly complex and demanding mission profiles. With advancements in battlefield technology, including unmanned systems, directed energy weapons, and sensor suites, there is a critical need for hybrid electric powertrains capable of providing enhanced mobility, endurance, and survivability across diverse environments. Hybrid electric powertrains are uniquely positioned to meet these needs by enabling new vehicle architectures—both air and ground—that offer increased operational flexibility. These architectures can deliver key tactical advantages such as improved fuel efficiency, extended range, enhanced onboard power generation capacity for advanced electronics and weapon systems, and the ability to reduce acoustic and thermal signatures through silent, all-electric operating modes. However, the development of hybrid electric platforms faces significant challenges in component availability. For both ground and aerial platforms, balancing power density, weight, efficiency, and reliability is essential to meet the Army’s stringent performance requirements. The current state of commercially available components presents a significant gap for vehicle developers. Many of the existing powertrain components on the market are hobby-grade or foreign-manufactured, lacking the necessary durability, power ratings, and quality control required for military applications. This issue is particularly pronounced in the nascent hybrid electric aircraft market, where there is a dearth of U.S.-manufactured components that meet the Army’s needs for mission-critical powertrains with the right mix of power, weight, and efficiency. As a result, developers are often forced to use suboptimal components for early-stage prototyping, with limited options for scaling to robust, domestically-produced systems. This market gap not only hinders the development of prototype systems that could meet the Army's mission needs but also presents a strategic vulnerability, as it relies on foreign supply chains for critical vehicle components. The U.S. Army requires hybrid powertrains that are optimized to meet its mission-specific demands, including higher power-to-weight ratios, extreme environmental durability, and long-term logistical sustainability through domestic supply chains. Addressing these challenges will be critical to achieving the Army's goals for future mobility, lethality, and survivability on the battlefield.The goal of this program is to develop an American-made 30-50 kW class permanent magnet electric motor/generator to enae hybrid electric powertrains used in air and ground vehicles. CRG has assembled a coalition of small businesses capable of providing an end-to-end solution from clean sheet motor/generator design through prototyping, hybrid powertrain system integration, product sales, manufacturing, and sustainment.

Explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) operations face significant challenges in rapidly and accurately identifying a vast array of ordnance types, particularly under conditions where physical damage, environmental degradation, or limited visual access obscure critical identifying features. Current identification methods rely heavily on EOD technicians using static reference materials, such as photographs and line drawings, which are time-consuming and prone to human error. The lack of automated, high-fidelity imaging solutions limits the ability to train artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) models for robust detection and classification of ordnance in complex and uncontrolled environments. Furthermore, existing photogrammetry systems capture only visible light data, making them incompatible with advanced sensors, such as those operating in shortwave infrared (SWIR) or longwave infrared (LWIR) bands, used in modern robotics and autonomous systems. These limitations highlight a critical need for a comprehensive, scalable solution that integrates multispectral imaging and advanced 3D modeling to enhance EOD safety and operational efficiency.To address this challenge, Eoptic proposes the System for Training Recognition and Identification of Known Explosives (STRIKE), a metrology tool used to gather spatial and spectral measurements of real-world ordnance an EOD technician may encounter. STRIKE leverages structured light stereoscopy and radiometric calibration to achieve precise 3D surface mapping with accurate spectral data, enabling simulations under varying conditions based on proven optical metrology and computational imaging techniques. It completes the process in 4-7 minutes, depending on ordnance size and resolution needed. The system integrates spectral data directly into point cloud generation, creating digital twins of ordnance objects with unparalleled spatial and spectral fidelity. This enriched dataset enables the development of robust AI/ML models for ordnance identification, that can then be optimized for use on a variety of platforms, including handheld devices, ground robots, and unmanned aerial systems (UAS). STRIKE also incorporates an automated calibration pipeline and modular design, ensuring adaptability to evolving imaging technologies and operational needs.
STRIKE: System for Training Recognition and Identification of Known Explosives
