Energized Composite Technologies, LLC (EzCT), in collaboration with the University of Central Florida, is developing groundbreaking Energized Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (eCFRP) technology for military applications. This innovation integrates energy storage with structural functionality, offering a transformative solution to the critical energy-weight challenges in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), electric vehicles (EVs), and soldier-portable systems. Unlike conventional batteries that contribute significantly to weight, eCFRP technology leverages the dual-purpose nature of carbon fiber reinforced plastics, creating "weightless batteries" with exceptional mechanical strength and energy density.This Phase II project builds upon proven Phase I successes, including the fabrication of ZnCFRP structural batteries with energy densities exceeding 180 Wh/kg, high cycle stability, and robust tensile strength of 400 MPa. Using innovative electrode and electrolyte designs, scalable manufacturing techniques, and advanced ANSYS modeling, EzCT aims to achieve energy densities of 200 Wh/kg and lifetimes exceeding 4,000 cycles. The project will deliver five 2ft × 2ft eCFRP panels ready for integration into military platforms such as UAV frames, vehicle panels, and wearable technologies.Key outcomes include:A 30-40% reduction in vehicle weight and a 40-50% increase in operational range.Enhanced UAV flight times by up to 50%, improving reconnaissance and mission reliability.Multifunctional applications reducing logistical burdens while enabling stealth operations.With patented technology and strong academic-industry collaboration, EzCT is strategically positioned to advance structural battery systems to Technology Readiness Level 6, ensuring alignment with Army electrification and efficiency goals. This innovation not only optimizes energy solutions for military operations but also extends to aerospace and disaster relief applications, demonstrating broad scalability and impact.
Energized carbon fiber composite batteries as structural panels for electric vehicles

In response to the Army’s solicitation for an emitter system-agnostic solution for threat representative waveform generation and validation, Alphacore and the proposing team propose to develop an ML Based Intelligent Filter with Real Time Calibration of Transmitter (MIR-CAT). In Phase I, a prototype for assessing the efficacy of applying novel artificial intelligence & machine learning (AI/ML) algorithms to enhance the capability of both legacy and state-of-the art low-cost RF emitters will be developed. In Phase II, a carefully selected combination of hardware, including reconfigurable analog front-end (AFE), analog-to-digital converter (ADC) and FPGA, will be built to meet the low cost goal of the program while able to work with carrier frequencies up to K-band (27GHz, or beyond if needed). This proposed work will integrate advanced algorithms in an open software framework capable of real-time adaptation of pre-distortion techniques on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) radio hardware. While there are numerous ML algorithms under investigation for intelligent control of RF transmitter front-ends (RFFE) systems, many of these do not consider the specific low-SWaP-C and real-time needs and capabilities of Army transmitters, nor the harsh radio frequency environments under which they operate. Digital preconditioning is a form of applying adaptive filters and non-linear functions to compensate for the distortions caused by the RFFE, particularly compression artifacts of the up-converter and power amplification stages of the transmitter. These artifacts reduce the quality of the transmitted signal, reducing the communication capacity of data links or degrading the performance of radar systems. While digital pre-conditioning techniques have the theoretical ability to correct for these impairments, in practice calibrating these effects is extremely difficult as the characteristics of the transmit chain vary over time, temperature, frequency band of operation, and output power. As such, applying a real-time feedback mechanism is considered optimal; however with the large number of configurable parameters comes the need for intelligent control of the digital preconditioning stage. Deep-learning models are a tractable solution to this problem as they allow for online learning, removing the reliance on expensive calibration efforts that are susceptible to unforeseen environmental conditions that would otherwise adversely affect the front-end performance.
ML Based Intelligent Filter with Real Time Calibration of Transmitter (MIR-CAT)

Deployed test and evaluation (T&E) threat representative systems currently face substantial challenges in generating high-fidelity, validated threat signals that accurately represent the intended source waveform. Traditionally, T&E environments leverage digital twins or Threat Model and Analysis Program (TMAP) models integrated with low-cost emitters (LCEs) to mimic radio frequency (RF) threat emissions. However, signals emitted from these systems frequently suffer significant distortion caused by intrinsic hardware-induced impairments. These impairments include In-phase and Quadrature (I/Q) imbalance, clock jitter, quantization errors arising from digital-to-analog conversion resolution limitations, nonlinear distortion from power amplifiers (PAs), and local oscillator (LO) leakage and phase noise. Collectively, these factors degrade signal integrity, resulting in system-specific signatures that diverge significantly from the theoretical target waveform. Software-defined radios (SDRs), despite their flexibility, affordability, and broad adoption within electronic warfare and telecommunications domains, intensify these issues due to inherent hardware limitations and artifacts. While SDRs enable rapid configuration changes and dynamic waveform generation via software algorithms, the transmitted signals still undergo multiple transformations across the hardware transmission chain. These transformations inevitably introduce distortions, leading to reduced authenticity and fidelity of the emitted RF signals. To effectively overcome these pervasive challenges, Durandal has developed Digital Cognitive Adaptive Filtering (DCAF), an innovative solution leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms. DCAF operates dynamically and adaptively at the network edge, identifying and learning specific hardware-induced impairments in real-time. Through iterative calibration, DCAF continuously compensates for these signal deviations, significantly enhancing the fidelity and authenticity of threat signals emitted from low-cost, SDR-based systems. Complementing this dynamic filtering capability, Durandal employs inverse SDR twins—highly precise digital models specifically designed to predict and proactively counteract hardware-induced waveform distortions prior to transmission.Durandal maintains technological leadership through rigorous intellectual property protection strategies, combining targeted patent applications, comprehensive trade secret protocols, purposeful software obfuscation, and controlled deployment on secured, proprietary infrastructure. This strategic and multi-layered IP protection approach ensures Durandal retains a competitive advantage, facilitating sustainable commercial success. Durandal’s solutions directly address critical T&E community needs, improving the realism and effectiveness of threat simulations, thus significantly enhancing warfighter preparedness and operational capability.
Dynamic Cognitive Adaptive Filtering: Enhancing Low-Cost RF Emitters with DCAF

The current Mission-Based Cyber Risk Assessments (MBCRAs), such as Weapon System Assurance (WSA), are resource-intensive and limited in scalability. Alternative approaches, including monolithic LLMs or generic AI-driven tools, carry risks such as inefficiency in processing diverse SSE data, over-reliance on computational resources, and lack of adaptability to dynamic mission requirements. This modular approach optimizes processing across multimodal data types, including engineering designs, intelligence reports, and software vulnerability scans, ensuring comprehensive and precise risk assessments. The solution is engineered to comply with Department of Defense Responsible AI principles, emphasizing transparency, auditability, and scalability for military environments.The Phase I effort focuses on designing and validating this innovative architecture, with tasks including dataset curation, modular LLM design, prototype selection, and feasibility demonstration. Expected outcomes include a transformative LLM framework that integrates seamlessly into Army SSE operations, mitigating the risks of alternative approaches and significantly enhancing cybersecurity efficiency and efficacy across the Army and beyond.

full_descriptions: Computational Game Theory AI for Army Tactical COA Generation Scenarios

Computational game theory is the only sound way of planning against an intelligent adversary: it is the only approach that can properly handle imperfect information (partial observability) and the associated opportunities to deceive and be deceived, as well as a nonstationary intelligent adversary that selects its strategy based on what strategy we select for ourselves.Strategy Robot (SR) has developed the only game-theoretic COA Generation and Execution System (CGES). Computational game theory is the only sound way of planning against an intelligent adversary: it is the only approach that can properly handle imperfect information (partial observability) and the associated opportunities to deceive and be deceived, as well as a nonstationary intelligent adversary that selects its strategy based on what strategy we select for ourselves.Strategy Robot (SR) has developed the only game-theoretic COA Generation and Execution System (CGES). It computes COAs for Blue and Red simultaneously, taking into account that Blue’s optimal COA depends on Red’s COA and that Red’s optimal COA depends on Blue’s COA. So, unlike simulation, single-sided optimization, and single-sided reinforcement learning, it does not need to assume that the user has correctly guessed the adversary's COA (but it can further capitalize on aspects of it being known).Our computational game theory AI has already generated superhuman COAs for armored combat, beyond-visual-range air combat, and no-limit Texas hold’em poker. In this SBIR project we propose to apply it to the Army's desired tactical COA generation scenarios.  The approach in CGES is based on game-theoretically constructing COAs from COA pieces (COAPs). This enables the planning abstraction to be raised so strong COAs can be generated with a reasonable amount of computation.  In Phase I, we will 1) study to understand the relevant Army scenarios and data sources, 2) identify any necessary generalizations to CGES to address them, 3) design a development strategy for those generalizations, 4) conduct a feasibility study, and 5) develop and demonstrate a proof of concept for CoA recommendation. The work will be conducted in Pittsburgh.

Valor leverages rich metadata (e.g., time, geolocation, sensor configuration) to filter and fine-slice model performance, informing model comparisons and uncovering potential model vulnerabilities before our adversaries find them. The Phase II SBIR confidently builds upon these already scalable capabilities, mitigating development and deployment risks.  Striveworks will optimize Valor for speed during evaluation of various AI/MLmodels (CV, LLMs/RAG) and integrate it with our Chariot MLOps platform to improve usability and enhance model selection and monitoring. Integrations with Chariot include: no-code UI support for object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and classification T&E workflows; live dashboards for model comparisons to make model evaluation more approachable to non-technical stakeholders; and remediation pipelines that use automated T&E to detect model failure, trigger retraining pipelines, and redeploy the updated model.  Striveworks will advance Valor integrations, including dataset/model holdings and complementary tooling (e.g., adversarial robustness techniques, drift detection, and DevSecOps pipelines). As a result, Valor will serve as a seamless component in an end-to-end AI/ML stack designed to enhance model development and greatly improve post-production maintenance, including remediation, for both defense and commercial operations at scale.

Phase III consists of third party and field testing and commercialization.

Charles River, with its extensive DoD R&D experience, including AI/ML pipelines in particular, is uniquely positioned to address this critical challenge. We will deliver a practical, fully functional prototype, supported by a comprehensive technology transition and commercialization plan for both DoD and commercial applications.

Modern tactical environments and enterprise settings alike face the critical challenge of integrating data from heterogeneous legacy systems and modern platforms. In the Department of Defense (DoD) context—exemplified by an Army battlefield scenario—commanders must quickly synthesize information from legacy ground sensor networks alongside modern unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems to achieve unified situational awareness. These disparate systems expose data via various APIs, data models, and messaging formats, often accompanied by incomplete or unstructured documentation. Our proposed approach, Conflux, leverages a multi-agent framework to address these integration challenges. In this context, an agent is a software entity powered by advanced large language models (LLMs) that can autonomously reason, generate code, and interact with data. Agents operate by “tool running”—that is, they invoke and execute external programs or code (for example, in Python or another suitable programming language) to perform tasks such as API calls or data transformation. This language-agnostic “tool running” capability allows the agents to flexibly adapt to different execution environments as needed. The multi-agent framework comprises three specialized roles:Integrator Agent: This agent orchestrates the overall integration process by leveraging chain-of-thought reasoning. It uses a tool-running capability (e.g., a Python execution environment) to dynamically generate and execute code that performs API calls and data transformation routines. For clarity, “tool running” refers to the agent’s ability to call and run code procedures, which may be implemented in Python or another language, to carry out specific tasks in real time.Specialist Agent: This agent ingests API documentation—whether in the form of formal OpenAPI specifications or raw, scraped documents—to extract and understand the key endpoints, data models, and mapping rules required for integration. The Specialist Agent translates these insights into actionable instructions that the Integrator Agent can use.Librarian Agent: This agent curates successful integration and transformation examples by deduplicating entries and maintaining a repository of validated “recipes” that can be reused in future integration tasks. This repository aids in ensuring consistency and reliability as the system learns from each interaction.This dynamic, ad hoc approach avoids rigid data standardization by enabling the agents to normalize and transform data on a case?by?case basis. Although comprehensive security measures and human-in-the-loop monitoring will be further developed in later phases, Phase I will also investigate the feasibility of implementing secure, segregated mechanisms for handling sensitive credentials (e.g., API keys) without exposing them directly to the agents.

Data interoperability is a critical challenge for the military as the battlespace evolves into an increasingly complex network of disparate software tools, communication protocols, and bespoke application interfaces. While Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) and implementations such as REST and GraphQL have provided a level of standardization, they remain inherently brittle. Current systems are tightly coupled to the specific APIs they are designed for, meaning any change to the underlying API can break dependent applications. Service Oriented Architectures (SOA) frameworks exhibit issues such as changes in the API definition, third-party service dependency changes, poor error handling, data inconsistencies, authentication issues, and data model mismatches which lead to service disruptions, increased maintenance costs, scalability challenges, and security vulnerabilities. Given that mission requirements demand continuous software evolution, this fragile relationship between applications presents a primary mode of failure for data interoperability.The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) capabilities indicates a promising area of research to overcome these rigid API interface coupling and workflow limitations. Current LLMs excel in open-ended conversation (e.g. chatbots), but without specific instructions fall short in performing sequence of operations to mimic sequential workflows. In contrast, human “agents” typically decompose workflows into API interfaces, as well as the series of actions and programming code to invoke these interfaces, to achieve the desired result. These API workflows are often custom-defined and prone to changes, and human “agents” can adapt to these changes by proactively monitoring API documentation or, more typically, reacting to these changes after a dependent software system function breaks.This presents an opportunity to research API Flow, a universal API (uAPI) Workflow Orchestration concept to alleviate this strong coupling by leveraging recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Agent frameworks. LLMs have proven extremely useful in translation, reasoning, and structured document generation, making them ideal candidates for acting as natural language proxy agents between disparate systems. Instead of direct integration with a rigid API, applications would interact with an LLM-based uAPI endpoint, which dynamically transforms queries into the required format for the target system. This effectively abstracts downstream applications from any specific API implementation, enabling interoperability even as software evolves. This concept is directly applicable to the Army SBIR program’s Army Tech Marketplace (ATM) software and provides a viable alternative to manual data source ingestion pipeline maintenance in order to achieve Innovation Economy business intelligence.

A key technical challenge in deploying autonomous robotic platforms for bridging operations is ensuring robust perception, navigation, and coordination in dynamic and uncertain riverine environments. These platforms must operate effectively in the presence of environmental disturbances such as strong water currents, floating debris, occluded visibility due to sediment-laden water, and unpredictable surface conditions. Unlike structured terrestrial environments, riverine domains introduce significant sensing challenges, where GPS signals may be degraded or denied, sensor data can be affected by water reflections, and communications between multiple unmanned platforms must remain resilient despite interference from natural and man-made sources. Traditional approaches to robotic navigation and perception often rely on GPS-based localization, vision-based scene understanding, and high-precision LIDAR. However, in riverine environments, these solutions become unreliable due to factors such as GPS signal attenuation near cliffs or under foliage, water spray obscuring cameras, and sensor degradation caused by reflections and surface turbulence. Moreover, coordinating multiple autonomous bridging platforms requires advanced situational awareness and real-time decision-making, as conventional collision avoidance algorithms struggle with the fluid dynamics and shifting positions of floating objects. To address this critical need, we propose to develop the Robotic Autonomous Platform Sensors for Intelligent Distributed Bridging Operations (RAPIDS) technology.
RAPIDS: Robotic Autonomous Platform Sensors for Intelligent Distributed Bridging Operations

We propose the development and integration of a hybrid power system for an uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) that is designed for aerial resupply, cargo delivery, loitering munitions delivery, and communications relay missions. The proposed hybrid power system (the “Pelican HPS”) will significantly reduce the acquisition/operating cost, risk to life, and fuel consumption in the performance of such missions and extend the range/endurance of a similarly-sized battery-powered UAV by ten times. An example of a current resupply aircraft is the UH-60 Black Hawk, which costs $6M, has a payload capacity of 2,600 pounds and carries up to 360 gallons of fuel. The Black Hawk is oftentimes used to carry small, inexpensive cargo such as ammunition boxes and food. This presents a mismatch between the cost, payload capacity, and fuel consumption of the aircraft with respect to the cost and weight of its cargo. This mismatch wastes fuel and unnecessarily puts personnel and equipment at risk. The Pelican HPS is based on a proven, heavy-fuel-based internal combustion engine (ICE) used in maritime VTOL UAVs. The HPS produces 16.5 kilowatts (kW) of power, sized for a multirotor/multicopter UAS to carry 100 lb. of payload for one hour/30 miles, or 50 lb. for 3 hours/90 miles. The proposed payload capacity is sufficient for a large swath of missions, such as delivering light machine guns, multiple cans of 5.56 NATO, medical supplies, or water/food to the frontline. For these missions, by using the proposed HPS, the amount of fuel consumed would be reduced from 100 gallons to 3 gallons, and the value of the equipment at risk would be reduced from $6M (the cost of a Black Hawk) to sub-$200k (the cost of a UAV). The proposed work includes integration and test flying of the HPS with an existing heavy-lift UAV produced and funded by Skyfront. The integration validates performance and forces resolution of any potential difficulties in commercializing the Pelican HPS system, such as concerns pertaining to vibrations, aerodynamics, and thermal dissipation. The proposal stands in contrast to simply building a standalone hybrid power system that has been merely bench tested and not actually flown. The integration will serve as a reference for further commercial work and integration onto other, larger UAVs, whose future applications include troop transport and medical evacuation.The proposed Pelican HPS is a scaled up version of Skyfront’s commercially available and proven HPS that is used by the Skyfront Perimeter 8 multirotor, which holds the world record for multirotor flight time and range at 13 hours / 205 miles. The Skyfront team has over 10 years of experience designing and commercializing hybrid power sources. The company has generated over $27.5M in revenue over the last four years selling hybrid-electric technologies to both commercial and military customers all over the world.

Existing C-UAS architectures primarily rely on radar and electro-optical (EO) sensors that are constrained by line-of-sight, generate high power signatures, and are vulnerable to jamming and spoofing. These systems typically require human-in-the-loop operation, increasing cognitive load and delaying response times—especially against swarming or autonomous threats. Near-peer adversaries, including China and Russia, are fielding sUAS equipped with advanced autonomy and sensor fusion, widening the gap between current Army capabilities and emerging operational risks. A scalable, passive, and automated detection layer is urgently needed to protect maneuver forces and critical nodes without compromising mobility or survivability. LAPIS (Low-Altitude Passive Integrated Sensors) directly addresses this capability gap by providing a lightweight, low-size, weight, and power (SWaP), passive sensing system designed for real-time detection, classification, and geolocation of low-altitude threats traveling at variable velocities. LAPIS enables early warning and automated alerting within seconds of threat detection, and can support integration directly with Tactical Assault Kit (TAK) and Army C2 networks (NGC2, FAAD C2, Maven, and Lattice) to streamline operator response.  LAPIS leverages Picogrid’s modular architecture to integrate Guardian RF’s passive RF sensors and Hoverfly’s Spectre tethered UAS (teUAS) into a unified, low-altitude threat detection system optimized for Army use. Guardian RF provides software-defined, passive RF detection and classification capabilities, while Hoverfly’s Spectre platform offers persistent aerial elevation of sensors. Picogrid’s Legion API fuses these inputs—along with EO/IR and acoustic data—into a common threat picture and delivers automated alerts to Army C2 environments. Aligned with the Army’s Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) and designed to support the Army Long Range Persistent Surveillance Program, LAPIS offers a high-impact, low-risk path to expanding the Army’s counter-sUAS capabilities. It reduces the sensor-to-decision latency, minimizes cognitive load on operators, and is purpose-built for mobile operations across multi-domain battlespaces.  Picogrid’s Legion software has been validated in 80+ fielded deployments, with proven ability to integrate and automate workflows for a wide range of sensors. Guardian RF’s detection technology has been used in live operations across U.S. and partner missions, while Hoverfly’s teUAS is widely fielded across the DoD. LAPIS builds on these mature components to deliver a scalable, rapidly deployable capability purpose-built for the Army’s C-UAS mission needs.
Low-Altitude Passive Integrated Sensors (LAPIS)

Occam Vision Group’s Autonomous Optical Sensor (AOS) system is a self-contained, distributed camera network designed to autonomously capture ultra-high-speed missile events in harsh, infrastructure-limited environments. Developed during Phase I, AOS consists of 10 lightweight Pods, each integrating 8 synchronized, high-frame-rate cameras capable of up to 32,000 FPS per Pod and a synthetic system-wide rate of 320,000 FPS. Each Pod includes onboard compute, solid-state storage, wireless communications, and a solar-capable power system, making the platform fully self-contained and deployable in austere field environments.AOS addresses key limitations of current range instrumentation, which relies on manually aligned, fixed-angle cameras tethered to centralized trailers. These legacy systems require significant setup time and fail to adapt when test articles deviate from their nominal flight path. In contrast, AOS leverages reinforcement learning (RL) to autonomously steer camera orientation and dynamically adjust region-of-interest (ROI) selection during flight. This enables real-time adaptation to non-nominal trajectories, tumbling behavior, and unpredictable impact locations—ensuring that critical test data is captured even under off-nominal conditions.Phase I established technical feasibility through a combined hardware/software development effort. Results included a ruggedized Pod with pan-tilt control, onboard AI processing, and real-time synchronization using sub-25 ns clock alignment across multiple cameras and Pods. Calibration, timing, and tracking functions were demonstrated in simulation and lab test environments, using data generated by the Trajectory Analysis and Optimization System (TAOS) from Sandia National Laboratories. These tools enabled scalable training and evaluation of AI models across a wide range of flight scenarios, and support for complex cases such as multi-stage events or intercepts was investigated for future integration.Phase II will complete system integration, validate the platform in live test events at White Sands Missile Range (WSMR) and Yuma Proving Ground (YPG), and deliver a complete 10-Pod system to the Government by Month 18. The final product will include hardware, software, deployment tooling, and documentation suitable for transition to Phase III procurement or follow-on Commercial Solutions Opening (CSO) contracts.Beyond Army test ranges, AOS is also being commercialized as a passive, infrastructure-light airspace awareness system for counter-UAS and drone detection at commercial airports. The first early-adopter deployment is planned for summer 2025, with follow-on beta installations under discussion with five U.S. airports through early 2026.

A Celestial Compass provides rapid and accurate non-magnetic azimuth information for precision handheld targeting systems used by Forward Observers. Typically, solar compasses utilize a multi-element telecentric fisheye lens. To meet the azimuth accuracy requirements, individual lens elements must meet and maintain centricity, spacing and tilt specifications and provide micrometer-level line-of-sight (LOS) stability during environmental cycling over its lifetime. The high stability telecentric fisheye lens is large, heavy, and complex. It is the single most expensive component in a solar compass. Metalens technology provides a basis for development of miniaturized imaging systems containing fewer elements with increased stability. JHU/APL recently developed a metalens structure with most of the functionality of a telecentric fisheye lens. A metalens will greatly simplify solar compass design, while still performing as well or better than traditional telecentric fisheye lenses because all the tolerances between multiple individual lens elements have been eliminated. With the use of a metalens, size, weight and cost of the solar compass will be reduced. It is expected that at realistic military production volumes, unit price of metalenses will be in the range of a few hundred dollars.Proposed program will develop and demonstrate the 1st metalens-based solar compass for Far Target Location  (FTL) systems. Under this program the following results will be obtained. A solar compass using a metalens will be designed, fabricated, calibrated and field tested. The field-of-view (FOV) of the metalens will be increased to cover an entire hemisphere. Time to celestial navigation solution will be reduced by a factor of 3x using FPGA processing. Availability of accurate celestial solutions during daytime will be increased because the metalens solar compass can provide accurate azimuth readings for solar elevations up to 80°. The metalens solar compass design will provide a “drop in place” replacement for solar compasses in Army Joint Effect Targeting System (JETS) units comprising traditional telecentric fisheye lenses. Using proprietary technologies developed at Trex, the metalens solar compass prototypes  developed under this program will meet all required mil-spec temperature and shock & vibration requirements. This will accelerate transition of metalens solar compass technology to Army Programs-of-Record. Trex’s team possesses more than two decades of experience in celestial navigation technology. This will mitigate technical risk.
Metalens Solar Compass (MLSC)

This initiative addresses the logistical challenges faced by the Army in multi-domain operations, particularly in contested environments, where autonomous logistics solutions are vital for sustained resupply. This provides full autonomy from takeoff to landing, including in-flight retasking and handling mission contingencies. RUCK is an affordable alternative to only procuring new optionally piloted aircraft like the UH-60M. The immediate goal is an autonomous UH-60 capable of operating in contested logistics environments, enhancing operational readiness, reducing personnel risks, and enabling resupply missions during future conflicts. Since we use the Army’s Modular Open System Approach, the same technology can be applied to other logistics aircraft like the Lakota and the Chinook with minor modifications. The proposal first substantiates the technical merit and feasibility of RUCK, drawing on Near Earth's past successes with various cargo aircraft. It then outlines the technical approach, objectives, tasks, risk mitigation strategies, and deliverables. The transition and commercialization sections highlight how the team intends to extend RUCK’s applications to civilian helicopters and the emerging Advanced Air Mobility sector. Near Earth Autonomy’s expertise in autonomy comes from its experience with numerous DoD projects, including ONR’s Autonomous Aerial Cargo/Utility System, NAVAIR’s Autonomous K-MAX, and the Army’s heavy vertical takeoff and landing (HVTOL) system. Past achievements include integrating autonomy with the Kaman KARGO UAV, demonstrating successful autonomous logistics missions. RUCK builds on these accomplishments by extending autonomous capabilities to helicopters, significantly broadening their operational role in military and commercial settings. This initiative is strengthened by a partnership with industry leader Honeywell that will support certification and commercialization of the technology with a wide range of aircraft. This synergistic partnership combines each organization’s strengths to deliver a robust and scalable solution, accelerating the deployment of autonomous logistics systems for the Army and expanding their potential for broader applications in both defense and commercial markets.

As robotics technology continues to mature, the Army's operational needs demand more than just simple automation. There is a growing need for flexible manufacturing systems that can enhance operational capabilities, particularly in dynamic mechanical and electrical repair facilities. Traditional systems fall short in providing the necessary versatility, which is critical to maintaining military readiness and supporting the Army's modernization priorities such as Human-Machine Interfaces and Trusted AI and Autonomy. The problem described can be summarized as the need for custom collaborative robots (cobots) for tasks that require precision and flexibility, such as wiring in electronic assemblies or positioning components in tight spaces. Research might include developing advanced sensory and vision systems to enable cobots to work more intuitively with human operators and easily be reconfigured by operators to perform a variety of tasks in LEAD repair facilities. These needs may change over time, but developing new solutions for each one should not require hiring a systems integrator to do a full system design, development, and re-training.  PickNik Robotics (PickNik), a world leader in solving unstructured robotics challenges like the problems described above, proposes to develop, implement, and deploy a cobot system with advanced motion planning using our commercial MoveIt Pro software platform and extensive in-house robotics experience.  During Phase I, PickNik Robotics will conduct a comprehensive feasibility study to validate the technical and operational potential of our proposed cobot system. We will develop supporting features for MoveIt Pro that will enable the software to be used in multiple applications such as component placement, wiring assemblies, spraying, or blasting. PickNik will develop a digital twin of the system in a physics-based simulated environment to aid in development and validation. We will investigate and implement perception-based 3D scanning and develop features that use 3D path planning techniques to create collision-aware trajectory plans.  We will assemble a representative small-scale hardware platform from existing COTS components, ensuring that the solution is aligned with the Army's modernization priorities and is capable of supporting mixed-model production in dynamic repair facilities. By leveraging our MoveIt Pro software and extensive experience in robotic systems, we will ensure that our solution integrates seamlessly with existing Army infrastructure while offering enhanced capabilities for future needs. This proposal directly addresses the Army's solicitation requirements by focusing on developing cobots that can be quickly reconfigured to perform various tasks within repair facilities.

LOGIA, the Local Guide for Intelligent Assistance, is designed to allow the DoD to locally deploy foundational machine learning models. The system is designed from the ground-up with the Authority to Operate (ATO) process in mind.áOur Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) divides the problems into three layers: the interface layer, the foundational layer, and the data layer. The interface layer allows users to authenticate and interact with the system. This layer routes voice or text requests to the appropriate machine learning model but also contains guardrails both for ethical concerns as well as defending against things like prompt injection attacks. The foundational layer contains open-source foundational models such as Large Language Models (LLMs), some of which have been fine-tuned for specific tasks using RAFT (Retrieval Augmented Fine Tuning). This separate layer allows for rapid adding or updating of existing models as the technology landscape continuously evolves. The data layer ensures that the foundational models only have access to the same data the user has access to when answering queries, avoiding the problem of aggregating data and raising the classification level. With this architecture, LOGIA enables rapid adoption of foundational models in the DoD and helps scale proven Al-enabled solutions for enterprise and joint use cases.á

full_descriptions: Real-time Generative Video Restoration at the Tactical Edge

Real-time access to clear video intelligence is critical for military operations, yet bandwidth constraints and network limitations often result in degraded video quality when tactical decisions are most urgent. This Phase I effort proposes a novel generative video restoration system that learns from the actual scene being transmitted to reconstruct authentic detail in degraded video regions - a fundamental departure from traditional AI enhancement approaches that hallucinate details based on generic training data. Real-time access to clear video intelligence is critical for military operations, yet bandwidth constraints and network limitations often result in degraded video quality when tactical decisions are most urgent. This Phase I effort proposes a novel generative video restoration system that learns from the actual scene being transmitted to reconstruct authentic detail in degraded video regions - a fundamental departure from traditional AI enhancement approaches that hallucinate details based on generic training data. The proposed system builds upon the proven Generative Video Codec (GVC) technology, which achieves structural similarity (SSIM) scores above 0.875 in critical regions during normal operation - the threshold at which operators can clearly distinguish mission-critical features. When bandwidth constraints force video quality below this threshold, the generative restoration system activates, leveraging multiple quality levels naturally present within the GVC stream to train scene-specific restoration models directly at the tactical edge. Research objectives focus on achieving real-time generative restoration on standard laptop hardware without cloud dependencies. Key investigation areas include optimizing the training process for real-time operation, ensuring authentic detail reconstruction without hallucination, and validating performance across various operational scenarios. The Phase I effort will analyze product-market fit within CDAO mission sets, particularly for applications requiring immediate access to high-quality video intelligence for critical decision-making. Success in Phase I would establish the foundation for Phase II prototype development of an edge-based video restoration system that maintains both operational security and independence from cloud infrastructure. This capability stands to transform access to video intelligence in contested environments, enabling confident decisions based on clear video when and where operators need it most.

People have always been America’s greatest strength. Today, the Army faces a war for technical talent. To build a vital long-term advantage, we must fill our most consequential ranks. Starting with commissioned officers, we must identify technology leaders who can maximize the effectiveness and deployment of emerging technologies -- by acting as the linchpin between the operational and technical community. Namely, Emerging Technology Leaders (ETLs). At a conference in 2019 by the Association for the United States Army (AUSA), Gen. McConville, the Chief of Staff, told the audience how critical skills are currently hidden in the Army’s personnel system. He found out that during the Afghanistan surge, he had a supply sergeant who ran an engineering design firm -- who as it turns out, designed all the forward operating bases in Afghanistan. And a major who worked for the Texas Highway Department, who helped the troop surge build highways. Yet none of this vital information was visible in the existing personnel system. The Chief had to manually ask people to fill in an Excel spreadsheet to discover their vital skills. This highlights the importance and great potential of the modernization of ETL talent management -- in particular, making ETLs visible. And with a modern data science approach, we can go beyond Excel spreadsheets and incorporate not just hard skills, but also critical human factors.The first step: identify ETL talent by mapping hard and soft skills with the right behavior attributes. At Voltera, our management is composed of serial technology entrepreneurs who have mastered this art in a systematized fashion -- for example, our CEO is an Army-connected disabled veteran who has led the commercialization of multiple emerging technologies. We will apply modern data science techniques such as k-means clustering -- which our Principal Investigator used successfully at Qualcomm to classify 15,000 hardware engineers and subsequently optimize their engineering workforce, including at multi-million dollar projects -- to identify ETLs from input data. To capture the skills needed for the progression to become an ETL, we will describe the clustering models that could be used to segment the augmented input data to show and/or infer the hard skills, soft skills and behavior attributes for ETL identification. We will also consider supervised learning models such as logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, decision tree-based classifiers or neural network classifiers. Our data partner Emsi is the world leader in labor market data and analysis tools and holds the country’s preeminent databank of resumes, job postings, skills classifications and natural language processing (NPL) resume parsing tools. It provides us the ideal warehouse of data to train the envisioned software and revolutionize ETL talent management in the Army.

Product development (PD) remains an uncertain process, especially for highly engineered and complex DoD programs. Historically, PD systems relied on a process that quickly zeroed-in on a single promising “point-solution” concept and most of the effort went into realizing that solution. This is the predominant approach to PD around the globe and is the case with the DoD 5000 acquisition process as well as the recent DoDI 5000.02 Adaptive Acquisition Framework. In recent years, there is growing recognition that point-solution design (PSD) approach limits PD program management and development resilience with respect to changes in requirements and to uncertainties in the availability and maturation of subsystem/component alternatives during system development and integration. Therefore, an effective “set-based design” (SBD) approach is necessary for best addressing program resiliency and trading risks and uncertainties with cost efficiency and program success. While SBD approaches have been entertained in practice, the studies are mostly qualitative in nature. There exist no effective, scalable, and commercial SBD decision support platforms to guide the program management (PM) and development process with multi-stage and multi-criteria considerations, the development of which is the core focus of this Phase II proposal. This proposal seeks to develop an innovative and comprehensive multi-stage SBD tool platform for program management and development to support DoD’s acquisition processes. The resulting Resilient Program Management & Development (RPMD) Tool can fundamentally transform the highly complex and sophisticated DoD acquisition programs to promote on-time and on-budget development of product systems while accounting for the entire product life-cycle. RPMD tool innovatively integrates the state-of-the-art of sequential decision making under uncertainty, as Markov Decision Processes (MDP), with combinatorial trade space exploration and optimization (TSE&O) based on set-based design approaches. To cope with computational complexity in handling large-scale real-world DoD programs, the RPMD tool implements the intelligent and scalable MDP solution algorithms developed in Phase I. The developed novel solution set-based TSE&O algorithms employ state-of-the art multi-criteria optimization algorithms to guarantee optimality of SBD solutions. For highly complex programs, the tool platform also employs meta-heuristic optimization algorithms for scalability. By integrating variable fidelity physics- and simulation-based analysis with efficient SBD driven TSE&O and sequential decision optimization, proposed tool platform increases PM/PD resiliency and confidence. Additional functionality includes extensive and practical sensitivity analysis module, real-time PM/PD program and technical risk-management decision support capability, visualization and characterizations of program and technical decisions in design criteria space and in terms of system designs.

Access to assured Position, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) data is critical to maintaining overmatch on the battlefield. The Department of Defense is heavily dependent on the Global Positioning System (GPS) to provide PNT data to warfighters. With the increasing prevalence of navigation and electronic warfare tactics, this dependence on GPS has created an attractive target. The relatively weak signal power received by GPS devices makes them vulnerable to jamming attacks, which can significantly reduce the availability of position, navigation, and timing (PNT) and jeopardize mission success. Navigation systems for both mounted and dismounted platforms that can operate in a GPS challenged or denied environment are currently a topic of significant research. There are a wide range of dismounted solider PNT solutions, but most rely on dead reckoning techniques, based on sensors such as IMU, camera, magnetometers, GPS, and pedometers, that require accurate knowledge of their starting point for good performance. In a GPS denied environment, initialization (through proper calibration and alignment) of the PNT system is critical. Many vehicle systems utilize high sensitivity GPS receivers, specialized antennas such as CRPAs, or high-grade IMUs to provide a robust PNT solution in challenging environments. However, due to size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C) constraints, these options are not available for the dismounted soldier. In this effort, Integrated Solutions for Systems, Inc. (IS4S) and teammate Auburn University (AU) will develop a PNT initialization system for dismounted soldiers that leverages high quality mounted PNT systems to help calibrate and initialize the dismount soldier's lower-cost navigation system. A system of systems approach will be used to allow collaboration and data sharing between mounted and dismounted navigation systems.
Mounted/Dismounted PNT System Initialization and Collaboration

To address the ArmyÆs need to determine the level of risk when a person uses a personal device to access Army resources (i.e., bring your own device (BYOD)) in accordance with zero trust principles, Intellisense Systems, Inc. (Intellisense) proposes to develop a new Secure Handling, Inspection, and Evaluation for Device Access (SHIELD) solution based on a unique combination of the design guidelines set forth in National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800-207 and advanced machine learning. Specifically, the innovation in zero trust architecture with supporting machine learning components will determine the level of trustworthiness (i.e., level of risk) when a person uses a personal device to access Army resources. SHIELD will accomplish this by implementing a set of guiding principles for workflow, system design, and operations to improve the security posture of Army resources. A policy engine and policy administrator will combine to form the policy decision point for user access. SHIELD will significantly lessen uncertainties by focusing on authentication, authorization, and restricting implicit trust zones. This will be accomplished without installing software on the personal device. The SHIELD solution will quantify the technical challenges, the risks and how they will be mitigated, and any resultant dependencies. The approach will be designed with a focus on open architecture and industry standards and protocols, which directly addresses the ArmyÆs requirements. In Phase I, Intellisense will determine the feasibility of SHIELD and describe in detail the approach to be used for determining its trustworthiness. Also in Phase I, Intellisense will describe the technical challenges, the risks and how they will be mitigated, and any dependencies that are required for the solution to work. In Phase II, Intellisense plans to develop the solution outlined in Phase I. A demonstration of SHIELD determining the trustworthiness of a personal device will be performed (specific device information will be provided by the Army after award). The demonstration will include the ability for observers to determine how the level of trustworthiness for a given device was measured (e.g., what specific device factors were used to determine the level of trustworthiness of the device, any configuration data used in the decision, and how that data was mapped to a level of trustworthiness).

When upgrading or redesigning a complex system, it is crucial to understand the ripple effect of design changes on the system's resulting costs, especially costs related to re-certification. System-level requirements cut across multiple design domains, including size, weight, and power budgets; bandwidth and processor utilization; timing constraints; safety requirements; and security controls.  Small, local changes to a subsystem or component can have broad impacts on system requirements.  The Tooling to Understand Ripple Effect Costs (TUREC) project will make Adventium's existing Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) tools change-aware, implementing a change impact cost estimation from each tool's point-of-view. The change impact cost measurements are then rolled up into Adventium's Trade Space Explorer that enumerates and visualizes for the developer at the system level the impact their changes have on overall costs. The developer defines how change impact is weighted within the individual analysis tools using a customizable Change Impact Function (CIF). The CIF provides the developer a means to drive their system designs to a solution that encompasses the full impact of their system changes, including changes that may propagate through the system.  Phase I established feasibility by adapting an existing tool to be change-aware and demonstrating it in the context of an Army-relevant, comprehensive system model to provide a realistic test scenario. By the conclusion of Phase II, TUREC's change impact capabilities will be integrated into multiple analysis tools  deployed on Adventium's CAMET Library  and supporting AADL and SysML modeling languages. In addition, CAMET sponsors will also have access to the steps and technology needed to convert third-party tools to be change-aware. TUREC will help system developers identify and measure the impact of their proposed design changes on the eventual certification costs. The significance is that weapon system capability will be enhanced by lowering risks to schedule and budget.

Current generation Cyber Physical Systems (CPS) including aviation systems were not developed with strong computer security requirements. Past cyber threats, Spectre, Meltdown, current cyber threats, and future cyber threats need to be countered. Embedded system designs are typically based on commodity hardware and software optimized exclusively for size, weight, and power – leading to critical cyber vulnerabilities that can have devastating effects on safety and mission effectiveness. This has also led to the unsustainable “Perimeter, Patch, Pray” Information Assurance strategy that is simply impractical for fielded aviation and missile weapons systems.   This Phase I SBIR proposal focuses on strengthening Army high assurance system such as an Army Aviation or Missile subsystem currently under development or via technology refresh. We propose Modular and Provably Secure high-assurance hardware/software co-design (MPS-HAHSC) based on the open-source RISC-V instruction set architecture and high-assurance (formally proven) kernels such as seL4. We leverage our existing Modular Provably Security (MPS) mathematical reasoning framework (that encompasses both hardware and software layers) and software verification framework to harden the assurance of the formally verified seL4 kernel which by formally verifying seL4 Assembly language code blocks and boot-up firmware functionality that seL4 relies on but is not presently verified. Further, MPS-HAHSC adds support for multi-core execution and DMA capabilities without affecting the existing proofs. Finally, MPS-HAHSC also support executing legacy unverified kernels such as Linux along with the formally verified seL4 kernel all while preserving the formally verified properties of the entire system. MPS-HAHSC thus enables the vision of a Future Vertical Lift (FVL) system architecture that can support robust, mathematically proven end-to-end high-assurance while seamlessly co-existing with unverified components. With the advent of RISC-V this can also be done in a practical and performant manner with all the available tooling to support rich CPS mission applications. Our proposed approach squarely addresses the "Modernization" transformational strategic capabilities of the Army with an emphasis on “Capability Development for Future Vertical Lift and Air and Missile Defense” as identified by the Vision and Strategy for the Army of 2030. MPS-HAHSC provides mathematically backed ironclad cybersecurity properties that, by design, are immune to adversarial impacts and elevates the Army/DoD cybersecurity capabilities to an unprecedented level to protect against great power competitors who are challenging U.S. dominance in all warfighting domains.
Modular and Provably Secure High-Assurance Hardware and Software Co-design (MPS-HAHSC)

The following objectives are required for this CESU-funded project, which is to understand agricultural processes, inland rivers/reservoirs water quality, weather impacts, and energy-water nexus of the Central US. Year one (1) will establish the initial structure of the project and includes tasks that support the following objectives. If funded, year two (2) and year (3) would continue to expand major elements of the project and build a diverse portfolio of collaborative EWN projects and engagements. Objective 1: Establish Collaborative EWN R&D Enterprise for understanding inland systems in the Central US. This objective prioritizes and subsequently builds a suite of diverse, collaborate R&D projects that expands current research efforts within EWN portfolio. Specifically, these projects will offer insight with respect to: (1) EWN opportunities in the Great Plains Region; (2) EWN opportunities in the agricultural sector; (3) EWN solutions to address hydrologic challenges in inland rivers and reservoirs; (4) assessing the role and impact of weather extremes and global climate change on EWN projects; (5) assessing the direct or indirect water quality benefits of EWN projects; and (6) assessing EWN opportunities in the energy-water nexus. The breadth of projects is strengthened by the caliber of multi-disciplinary researchers that integrate capabilities, resources and expertise to target very deliberative endpoints that advance EWN research. During the first year, it is anticipated that researchers associated with USACE and the selected team will initiate 3-5 R&D EWN projects, which ultimately lead to expanded technology transfer opportunities. Objective 2: Identify and Pursue EWN Field-Demonstration Projects. Demonstrations are applied research projects critical to the overall success of an EWN solution. As such, this objective seeks to establish field-demonstration projects that integrate research projects with a diverse number of collaborators, in addition to the core participants (i.e., members of the successful team and USACE’s EWN researchers). Demonstration projects could include, for example, an EWN pilot demonstration project to address hydrologic challenges in inland rivers and reservoirs. Selection and/or prioritization of demonstration projects would be determined based on a system-level opportunity assessment and/or restrictions as well as other considerations specific to environmental conditions; collaboration with partners; suitability for monitoring and modeling; access to informative data (existing and acquired); public interest; input of collaborative funding, etc. It is expected that 2 to 3 field demonstration projects will be identified and actively pursued in the first year. Objective 3: Launch and Operate EWN Communication Platform for Enhanced Public Communication. A successful communication platform will result in the timely delivery of informational products and/or engagements across the EWN network. This objective seeks to optimize and integrate the collaborators’ proven methods of delivering products and/or successful engagements that advance EWN strategic outcomes for the public benefit. Example products include, but are not limited to: workshops, symposia, news articles, videos, documentaries, graphics, reporting of case studies, technical notes, journal articles, etc. The selected team will work with EWN leadership and researchers to prepare most (if not all) of the referenced products. During the first year, it is expected that a minimum of 2 workshops/symposia, 1 video, 2 or 3 tech notes and 2 journal articles will be produced through a highly successful collaboration. The products derived from this collaboration are expected to generate EWN educational and public outreach opportunities. A successful application would likely include a team of investigators with knowledge in a broad array of disciplines including, but not limited to agricultural science and engineering, biogeochemistry, stream and wetland restoration, numerical modeling, water quality monitoring, ecosystem restoration, and hydrodynamics and sediment transport modeling. Additionally, experience should include, but not be limited to the following: Engineering With Nature®; development, design, and implementation of nature-based strategies in inland settings; ecological monitoring and modeling of restoration projects; incorporating human-use benefits into infrastructure projects; beneficial use of dredged sediment; quantifying benefits derived from restoration projects; and modeling of riverine and reservoir systems.

The government seeks research and technical support for watershed management modeling and analyses for water quantity and quality, impacts to aquatic species, and effects of extreme rainfall events to take place at the Fort Leonard Wood, MO area. Details of primary tasks are as follows: Task 1: Watershed modeling SWAT+ modeling will be completed for the Big Piney River (a HUC 12 watershed) and Roubidoux Creek (part of the Upper Gasconade HUC 12 watershed). The area around FLW is a karst landscape. Models will be calibrated using USGS stream gages and TSS sampling data supplied by FLW and ERDC-CERL. Task 1 consists of 2 (two) subtasks. a) Model(s) will incorporate existing climate and watershed/management conditions, b) model(s) will incorporate the recommended areal coverage of BMP types and management practices into the SWAT+ models to estimate change to water quality and discharge under existing climate conditions, Note: ERDC-CERL will assist with creating recommended BMPs and management practices. Task 2: Assess model output and determine management prioritization Interpretation and evaluation of model results to prioritize watersheds to target with proposed BMPs and management. Analyses will include statistical methods to justify periodization. The cost of BMP implementation and ongoing operations and management cost and the potential water quality and quantity impacts will also be included. Standard maintenance plans for all recommended BMPs will be required. Task 3: Develop a Watershed Management Plan Develop a Watershed Management Plan with recommended preliminary designs and locations for future development of LID features and BMPs to protect imperiled aquatic species, reduce infrastructure maintenance costs, and support current and future land usages. The final Watershed Management Plan will be included in the FLW Integrated Natural Resources Management Plan (INRMP) and used by land management groups on FLW including the Directorate of Public Works (DPW), Training, Mobilization & Security (DPTMS), and Integrated Training Area Management (ITAM) as well as the adjacent Mark Twain State Forest.

The Therapeutic Idea Award is designed to promote new ideas aimed at drug or treatment discovery that are still in the early stages of development. Projects that focus primarily on investigating the pathophysiology of ALS are not within the scope of this Funding Opportunity. Development and/or modification of preclinical model systems or the application of high- throughput screens to define or assess lead compounds for ALS treatment are of interest. Development of methods to adequately measure target binding and proximal downstream effects (target engagement) and the potential for undesirable activities at related but unintended targets (selectivity) are also encouraged. While the inclusion of preliminary data is not prohibited, the strength of the application should not rely on preliminary data, but on the innovative approach. All proposed research projects should include a well-formulated, testable hypothesis based on strong scientific rationale that holds translational potential to improve ALS treatment and/or advance a novel treatment modality. Innovation and impact are important aspects of the Therapeutic Idea Award. Research deemed innovative may introduce a new paradigm, challenge current paradigms, introduce novel concepts or technologies, or exhibit other uniquely creative qualities that may lead to potential therapeutics for ALS. Impact may be near-term or long-term, but must be significant and move beyond an incremental advancement. Identification of treatment approaches using biological correlates of disease activity and progression in pre-existing, de-identified human specimens from well-characterized, adequately controlled, and sufficiently powered patient cohorts is encouraged. Examples of acceptable cohorts for study include controlled clinical trials, observational studies, and registries (e.g., Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC] National ALS Registry and/or Biorepository; (https://www.cdc.gov/als/Default.html). Active duty military and/or Veteran patient populations or resources should be considered. All specimens must exist at the time of application submission; collection of new specimens will not be supported. The Therapeutic Idea Award encourages applications that include meaningful and productive collaborations between investigators. As appropriate, applicants are encouraged to collaborate with established ALS researchers. Applicants seeking support for the development of products beyond drug or treatment discovery should consider the FY19 ALSRP Therapeutic Development Award (Funding Opportunity Number: W81XWH-19-ALSRP-TDA), which supports advanced preclinical development activities (https://cdmrp.army.mil/funding/alsrp). The anticipated direct costs budgeted for the entire period of performance for an FY19 ALSRP Therapeutic Idea Award will not exceed $500,000. Refer to Section II.D.5, Funding Restrictions, for detailed funding information.

In the near future, the Warfighter may face prolonged isolation and sustained denial of support on the battlefield, and may have no access to medical support. To become more resilient to these challenges, the Warfighter will need additional, innovative support to provide Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC). Intelligent decision-support software, teleoperated trauma care systems, and fully autonomous trauma care robotics are intriguing solutions. In addition to intelligently diagnosing multiple injuries, performing patient monitoring, and producing prioritized TCCC treatment plans, solutions must assist Warfighters without specific medical training so they can perform interventions. To meet this goal, the solution must interface with telemedical assistance and provide direction to robotic platforms, all within a modular, unified architecture. To address these challenges, we propose to design and evaluate the Autonomous Ruggedized Combat Casualty Care – Intervention (ARC3-I), a modular, intelligent framework for autonomous combat casualty care. ARC3-I combines behavior modeling based on trauma treatment algorithms and procedures with a human-in-the-loop, human-machine interface and robotic adapter, to provide autonomous medical knowledge of interventions that can be performed by either Warfighters without specific medical training or robotic platforms.

Malaria infection and transmission is a continual threat to military and civilian communities across the world, but there are very low compliance rates with current preventative treatments due to gastrointestinal effects of anti-malarial medications, forgetfulness, and a low perception of risk. In order to address the need for a long-acting malaria treatment that bypasses the issue of compliance, Luna will develop the Malaria SHIELD™ (Sustained-release Hydrogel Injection with Encapsulated Layer-by-layer Drug) delivery system in the proposed program. The hydrogel-nanoparticle formulation, delivered via subcutaneous injection, will be designed to controllably degrade and release drug-loaded nanoparticles into surrounding tissue. In addition to being compatible with multiple therapeutic agents, the formulation will require no removal surgery. In Phase I, Luna will demonstrate the feasibility of this delivery system using in vitro models, and in Phase II will demonstrate the functionality of the system in in vivo malaria models.

The KCRP Academy of Kidney Cancer Investigators Award mechanisms, which are being offered for the first time in FY19, support a unique, interactive virtual academy providing intensive mentoring, national networking, collaborations, and a peer group for junior faculty emerging as potential leaders of kidney cancer investigation. The overarching goal of the Academy of Kidney Cancer Investigators (AKCI) is to develop successful, highly productive kidney cancer researchers in a collaborative research and career development environment. The AKCI will be a virtual career development and research training platform that will consist of Early-Career Investigator (ECI)/Designated Mentor pairs from different institutions, and an Academy Dean. The KCRP AKCIECIA is not a traditional career development award; the ECI is expected to participate in monthly webinars and annual workshops and to communicate and collaborate with other members of the Academy (other ECIs, Mentors, Dean) as well as with the advocacy community. The Academy Dean will serve as a resource for the ECIs and Mentors, assessing the progress of the ECIs, and facilitating communication and collaboration among all of the ECIs and Mentors, as well as with national research and advocacy communities. In addition to fostering ECI scientific development, the Academy, through its leadership by the Academy Dean, will provide for professional and leadership development of the ECIs to include skills and competencies needed to fund and manage a productive laboratory or research team. A separate funding opportunity (W81XWH-19-KCRP-AKCIDA) will solicit applications for the Academy Dean. This FY19 Program Announcement is soliciting ECIs and Designated Mentors to join the inaugural class for the Academy. This award mechanism enables the ECI (the investigator named as the Principal Investigator [PI] on the application) to pursue a kidney cancer project that may be basic, translational, and/or clinical research. The Designated Mentor is not required to be at the same institution as the ECI. The KCRP encourages applications from ECIs whose ability to commit to conducting kidney cancer research is limited by minimal resources or a lack of resources, such as a qualified Designated Mentor at his/her institution, access to kidney cancer research tools, opportunities for establishing collaborations, or other obstacles, which should be identified in the application. Preliminary data to support the feasibility of the research applications and approaches are required; however, these data do not necessarily need to be derived from the kidney cancer research field. The ECI must be in the early-career stage. This award provides the ECI with funding, networking, and collaborative opportunities, and research experience necessary to develop and sustain a successful, independent career at the forefront of kidney cancer research. This award also provides support and protected time for the ECI for 4 years of intensive research under the guidance of a Designated Mentor experienced in kidney cancer research. Although the AKCI will serve as a conduit to share knowledge and research experience among all Academy members, the ECI and Designated Mentor will be responsible for developing the ECI’s career development plans and for designing and executing the proposed research. The ECI must clearly articulate his/her commitment to a career as a kidney cancer researcher and to participating in and contributing to the growth of the AKCI. The Designated Mentor must have a strong record of mentoring and training early-career investigators. With the goal to expand and enrich mentorship capacity within the Academy, a Designated Mentor must agree to also serve as a Secondary Mentor to another ECI in the Academy. The Designated Mentor will be limited to one Primary (applicant ECI-Mentor pair) and one Secondary mentorship. The Dean of the Academy cannot be listed as a Designated Mentor. The ECI and Designated Mentor are required to attend a biennial multi-day DoD KCRP AKCI Workshop and, in alternate years, a 1-day DoD KCRP AKCI Workshop. The proposed research must be relevant to active duty Service members, Veterans, military beneficiaries, and/or the general public. The anticipated direct costs budgeted for the entire period of performance for an FY19 KCRP AKCIECIA will not exceed $725,000. Refer to Section II.D.5, Funding Restrictions, for detailed funding information. The CDMRP expects to allot approximately $4.64M to fund approximately four Academy of Kidney Cancer Investigators – Early-Career Investigator Award applications. Funding of applications received is contingent upon the availability of Federal funds for this program as well as the number of applications received, the quality and merit of the applications as evaluated by scientific and programmatic review, and the requirements of the Government. Funds to be obligated on any award resulting from this funding opportunity will be available for use for a limited time period based on the fiscal year of the funds. It is anticipated that awards made from this FY19 funding opportunity will be funded with FY19 funds, which will expire for use on September 30, 2025. Awards will be made no later than September 30, 2020. For additional information refer to Section II.F.1, Federal Award Notices. The types of awards made under the Program Announcement will be assistance agreements (grants or cooperative agreements). The level of involvement on the part of the Department of Defense (DoD) during project performance is the key factor in determining whether to award a grant or cooperative agreement. An assistance agreement (grant or cooperative agreement) is appropriate when the Federal Government transfers a “thing of value” to a “state, local government,” or “other recipient” to carry out a public purpose of support or stimulation authorized by a law of the United States, instead of acquiring property or service for the direct benefit and use of the U.S. Government. An assistance agreement can take the form of a grant or cooperative agreement. If “no substantial involvement” on the part of the funding agency is anticipated, a grant award will be made (31 USC 6304). Conversely, if substantial involvement on the part of the funding agency is anticipated, a cooperative agreement will be made (31 USC 6305) and the award will identify the specific substantial involvement. Substantial involvement may include collaboration, participation, or intervention in the research to be performed under the award. The award type, along with the start date, will be determined during the negotiation process. Research Involving Human Anatomical Substances, Human Subjects, or Human Cadavers: All DoD-funded research involving new and ongoing research with human anatomical substances, human subjects, or human cadavers must be reviewed and approved by the U.S. Army Medical Research and Materiel Command (USAMRMC) Office of Research Protections (ORP), Human Research Protection Office (HRPO), prior to research implementation. This administrative review requirement is in addition to the local Institutional Review Board (IRB) or Ethics Committee (EC) review. Local IRB/EC approval at the time of submission is not required. The HRPO is mandated to comply with specific laws and requirements governing all research involving human anatomical substances, human subjects, or human cadavers that is supported by the DoD. These laws and requirements will necessitate information in addition to that supplied to the IRB/EC. Allow a minimum of 2 to 3 months for HRPO regulatory review and approval processes. Additional time for regulatory reviews may be needed for clinical studies taking place in international settings. When possible, protocols should be written for research with human subjects and/or human anatomical substances that are specific to the DoD-supported effort outlined in the submitted application as a stand-alone study. Submission to HRPO of protocols involving more than the scope of work in the DoD-funded award will require HRPO review of the entire protocol (DoD and non-DoD funded). DoD human subjects protection requirements may be applied to non-DoD funded work and necessitate extensive revisions to the protocol. Applications that involve recruitment of human subjects must indicate the quarterly enrollment targets across all sites in Attachment 5: Statement of Work (SOW). Successful applicants will work with USAMRAA to establish milestones for human subjects recruitment. Continued support for the project will be based upon satisfactory progress in meeting the established milestones. Refer to the General Application Instructions, Appendix 1, and the Human Subject Resource Document available on the electronic Biomedical Research Application Portal (eBRAP) “Funding Opportunities & Forms” web page (https://ebrap.org/eBRAP/public/Program.htm) for additional information. A Congressionally mandated Metastatic Cancer Task Force was formed with the purpose of identifying ways to help accelerate clinical and translational research aimed at extending the lives of advanced state and recurrent patients. As a member of the Metastatic Cancer Task Force, CDMRP encourages applicants to review the recommendations (https://health.mil/Reference-Center/Congressional-Testimonies/2018/05/03/Metastatic-Cancer- Research) and submit research ideas to address these recommendations provided they are within the limitations of this funding opportunity and fit within the FY19 KCRP priorities. Clinical trials are not allowed. Research Involving Animals: All DoD-funded research involving new and ongoing research with animals must be reviewed and approved by the USAMRMC ORP Animal Care and Use Review Office (ACURO), in addition to the local Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of record.
